It's incredibly unforgiving game but an extremely rewarding one once you get the hang of it.
I play Battlefield mostly and bought this game on whim. I found myself playing it for nearly two days straight.
At its best is multiplayer trench warfare, one of the game's only current two gamemodes.
Each game contains a maximum of 32 players, which consist of four squads of four on each side.
Each side is either the axis or central powers and the allies. Each squad can be a particular regiment or company from the perspective side. For example, you can be french sappers, or british fusiliers or canadian royal infantry. You get to choose which faction you're squad will be. Each faction has it's own unique weapons and uniforms. And each squad has fixed slots with a unique role for each  - (leuitenant, rifleman, sniper, grenadier....etc) so, you can't have a squad of all snipers for example.
The game is broken down in a serie of stages where one side has a certain amount of time to take the enemies trench before the enemy can counter attack and take your trench. Once you succesfully take a trench then you have to hold it during the enemies counter attack. If you survive that then the next part of the map opens up for you to attack. Each time you take and hold a trench you get 1 point.
It's that simple. It's brutal. It's a hell a lot of fun.

It's not often you find an interactive experience with such real human emotion, but that's what Gone Home is -- something that feels real.  A found object mystery game, it unfolds as you explore the environment of an empty mansion inherited from an uncle.  The story is told through the artifacts and music of the protagonist's family that come together like pieces of a puzzle revealing an image of joy, heartache, tension, and ultimately the emotional struggles for identity and place of all of the members.
Although possible to stumble upon just the right pieces necessary to progress in the game, the wealth of information concealed in nooks and crannies gives a fascinating timeline explaining why you are the only person left and some deeper, darker mysteries that, while tangential, are still rewarding in that they provide echoes of an unspoken past as well.
The game can be completed in under 3 hours and the gameplay is composed solely of picking up and examining objects, rotating them, and occasionally putting tapes in tape players, so fair warning if you value time per dollar.  Still, I feel like this is a game that everyone should play at least once to see what this medium can do with storytelling that no other medium can in its own special way.

It's hard to argue with any of the negative comments regarding this game. Yes, it isn't a traditional game per se (at least as we know them now). There are no enemies (other than boredom for the ADD set), a single setting and quest; it's all story, little action, and it's pretty short.
So why do I recommend it?
Because it tells a beautiful story to which many of us who grew up in the 90s can relate, and it does so remarkably well. Aided by a nicely rendered, moody and atmospheric setting, and incredible attention to detail, GONE HOME tells the tale of a woman who comes home to find her family gone and is thus tasked to explore every room in the house for clues as to their whereabouts. A simple enough setup that triggers a superbly written story of teenage angst, alienation, and love. And essentially that's what GONE HOME is: a love story, so inevitably the hormonal COD-crowd will hate it, and that's fine, despite the fact that a game like this--one I suspect, and hope we'll see more of in the future--should appeal to everyone. The women in the game--two of whom form the core of the story--are for a nice change not represented as damsels in distress (stressed, yes; helpless, no) waiting to be saved by some unkillable action hero. They're human and strong, and you'd have to be an absolute coldfish not to find yourself drawn into their story, something made all that much easier by the exceptional voice talents employed to convey it.
Call it a game, call it a story, call it one or the other. What can't be denied is the value of the experience, and GONE HOME certainly proved a worthwhile one for me. Highly recommended.

Well, trench warfare is not fun. It looks nice, but gameplay is very basic - run out of trench, get shot by a sniper or a machinegun. Pretty realistic, but very boring. Even if you eat dirt most of the time you still get sniped as soon as you show a tiniest bit of your body. You occasionally get some kills, especially if you play as a sniper. Which is very satisfactory as per any hardcore game.
The game is badly optimized. Stutters. Animations feel clumsy. Your soldier responds sluggishly. Maybe it's realism again - it's hard to get up fast when you have to carry all the typical soldier's stuff. But again - not fun.
It also features a squad system which basically makes the game not very good for solo play. You have to level up your squad with your friends, and if you don't have them you'll probably wander in different people's squads without many unlocks.
There isn't a lot of guns in the game. Probably realistic, since there wasn't much variation in WW1, I guess.
Maps are nice, though they look pretty much the same. It's no man's land after all.
The trench warfare system is a variant of control points play. One team defends a point and the other team tries to capture it. Maps are huge, but you have to stay in the designated portion of the map. Wandering off the borders will get you killed in a few seconds for desertion. This is rather annoying, since you can't infiltrate the other team in any way. Even connected portions of the trenches are sometimes unaccessable to you. Sections of the map shift towards a team that lost a control point, the battle goes on different, albeit same looking, parts of the maps.
Gases are a nice idea, but gimmicky.
Sound design I didn't like. Guns felt a little like BB guns.
Music is cool. Though it mostly plays in the main menu.

I have generally been a fan of non-game interactive stories such as Dear Esther, but Gone Home just doesn't do it for me. I think there is too much of a disconnect between the "gameplay" and the story. The interactive portion is akin to a horror adventure game (Amnesia comes to mind). You are coming home after being out of the country for some time. Upon arrival, you find that nobody is home and the house has a slight eeriness to it. Lights flicker, there's rain and thunder, you are all alone... It's a perfect setup for a creepy adventure. But this is highly contrasted by the story. The story is provided as pieces of a journal that you discover as you walk around and explore the empty house. Without giving too many spoilers, the story is about a teenage romance. Right from this moment, you can probably see my confusion with the non-game: Horror-like environment and gameplay, romance story. It just doesn't fit together. In fact, I would go as far to say that Gone Home doesn't quite know what it wants to be. With that being said, I wouldn't exactly shun Gone Home completely. I think it might be worth picking up if you happen to stumble upon it during a sale, but I don't think it's worth the $20 it's asking for. There are much better non-game interactive stories to experience: The Stanley Parable and Dear Esther are just a couple that come to mind.

I absolutely loved this game. However, rather than jump straight in with a subjective review, I'll try and give an overview of the game. Okay, so this is what you actually do in the game:
You arrive home from hoilday and wander around your seemingly deserted house, with creepy sounds and lighting effects in full flow. As you explore, you learn about the lives of your sister (through voiceovers discover after interaction with objects), your parents and even your grandfather. This information is all discerned by examining objects. There is no fast paced action, no need to run down a corridor, no sliding or jumping - just interacting with objects, in your own time.
As others have remarked, it technically is possible to complete the game in under a minute, but that's not the point (in the same way any speed run isn't the point). This isn't really a "game", at least not in the traditional sense. It's an emotional adventure, designed to show you an insight into this family. In other words, don't start playing the game and examining every crack in the wall and every spot on the ceiling. Imagine you were in this situation yourself. What would you do? Where would you go first? What would you logically check?
Basically, if you're happy to be taken on a touching story, where your understanding of the story depends on how deeply you immerse yourself, but where your interaction with the world is minimal (i.e. you can't change anything that's happened, only learn about it), then this is the game for you. If you want something fast paced, with more action and strong gameplay, it's probably better to skip it.
Finally, from a price point of view, it's up to you how much you want to spend. As a fairly experienced gamer I got around three hours worth of gameplay from it initially (and much, much more after deeper exploration to tie up "loose" ends (which is obviously not compulsory)). I'm happy paying the asking price to an Indie developer starting off, but if you want to pay less, wait for one of Steam's awesome sales to come around and you can pick this up for peanuts.
Now that that overview is out of the way, I can hopefully be a little more subjective! From my point of view, as a fairly emotional 26 year old male who enjoys thought provoking media, I found this to be one of the most moving, haunting and beautiful gaming experiences of my life. I've never found myself caring about characters in this way in a video game before. I was genuinely touched and found myself wondering about the characters involved for days after completing the game. Certainly it joins a very select list of games that I'll always remember when and where I first played them.
I also need to give credit to Sarah Robertson, the voice actor behind Sam (the sister in the story). Her work really helped immerse me into the storyline.
So from me, I couldn't recommend this game any higher. A pure 10/10 emotional rollercoaster that really did leave me shaking. I'm hugely thankful I got the chance to play and if you're in any way "on the fence" about the game, I'd thoroughly recommend taking a chance and hopefully you'll be left as moved as I was.

WW1 has been crying out for some good fps attention (indeed, it is remarkable that more have not hit the market given the ongoing centenary of the conflict) and Verdun is a more than worthy WW1 entrant to the growing "FPS with brains" genre. If you've played the Red Orchestra series (if not, why not?) you'll be right at home with the moving fronts style game mechanics and this approach works particularly well in a WW1 trench warfare setting.
In particular the attack and counter attack phases are well implemented and fit nice with the subject matter and there are many really nice touches such as the meaningful implementation of gas attacks that all serve to add value and longevity.
In short this is a quality FPS  in the Red Orchestra style mould where you can see the devs passion for the history of the conflict really shining through. The devs appear to be in this for the long haul with a defined road map of further good things coming and the game as it stands is an absolute steal for the price.
Thoroughly recommended by me, go get it. Look forward to seeing you in the Trenches!

WW1 has been crying out for some good fps attention (indeed, it is remarkable that more have not hit the market given the ongoing centenary of the conflict) and Verdun is a more than worthy WW1 entrant to the growing "FPS with brains" genre. If you've played the Red Orchestra series (if not, why not?) you'll be right at home with the moving fronts style game mechanics and this approach works particularly well in a WW1 trench warfare setting.
In particular the attack and counter attack phases are well implemented and fit nice with the subject matter and there are many really nice touches such as the meaningful implementation of gas attacks that all serve to add value and longevity.
In short this is a quality FPS  in the Red Orchestra style mould where you can see the devs passion for the history of the conflict really shining through. The devs appear to be in this for the long haul with a defined road map of further good things coming and the game as it stands is an absolute steal for the price.
Thoroughly recommended by me, go get it. Look forward to seeing you in the Trenches!

Without a doubt the best FPS I have played in a long, long time. Verdun is an extremely addictive, yet insanely hard shooter, which you love and hate at the same time - it is a very abusive relationship.
Forcing you to play as a team, Verdun blows other shooters away in the 'teamwork' department, which Battlefield loves to promote in our faces the entire time. If you don't work as a foursome in your individual squads you will die. Again. And again. And again. And again. And again. And again. This is because you die in a single shot. This is why Verdun is much better than recent shooters: realism. Although no game will ever make you feel like you're truely in a war, Verdun goes for realism and nails it with a nailer. Weapons are fantastic, maps are challenging, and the combat is addictive, as each side attempets to attack and defend their line of trenches.
Progression is simple yet awarding, higher rank players aren't ridculously over powered compared to new ones, and that sweet taste of winning a round of an FPS never tasted so good. In short: Verdun shows how triple A games how to do an FPS right: an original idea, dedication, and NO bloody micro-transactions or pay-to-win tactics. I take my hat off to these developers.
NB: I'm still afraid to stand up straight in real life.

A masterclass in game design, Gone Home is one of the most important narrative based games of this generation. Its design allows it to seamlessly weave together narrative with exploration, making every interaction you have with your environment relevant to the story you are trying to uncover. By stripping away all of the distractions of a first person game (action, shooting, interaction with other characters) all you are left with are the details. These minute details that used to be supplemental to a game's plot (like audio diaries in Bioshock, or books in Skyrim) are now essential to progress through the story. Every detail of the eerie, vacant house gives more and more insight into the reason why it's so quiet there. If you have any interest in narrative driven games, I highly recommend you pick this up. Top that off with top notch writing and voice acting, and it's well worth your time and money.

With the sheer amount of indie games on Steam it requires significant momentum for one of them to stand out and grab the attention of the media. Released in August by developer The Fullbright Company, Gone Home was able to do just that.
It tells the story of a daughter returning home from Europe to find her family home empty. Only by reading notes around the house is she able to determine where everyone is. In turn these notes trigger audio samples that deliver the primary narrative from the perspective of her sister. Unfortunately to obtain these samples there is no need for exploring, there are no puzzles, there are no choices, no critical thinking is required – the entire time you simply move from point A to point B and listen to the dialogue. Certainly at the start of the game you have the whole house to explore, but once you start finding relevant clues they lead you directly to your next point of interest. As a result I find it difficult to even call the overall experience a ‘game’. Rather an interactive short story.
Which makes we wonder how Valve even had the audacity to price this game at $19.99. That isn’t to say that value should directly relate to experience, but there must be some substance and the substance here just isn’t enough. I feel that pricing it under $5 would not only justify the experience, it would also encourage a much wider audience to enjoy the piece.
The highlight of the game is the story telling – a stale cliché in the world of video games. All too often we’re spun the same, tired tales that start to leave you unreceptive. With Gone Home however we are presented with a refreshing narrative, rich with realism. Enhanced by some excellent voice acting it makes for a captivating experience. Aside from the main story arc, certain notes around the house will give you an insight inside other family members, but they leave more questions than answers.
Mechanically I also felt that the game was awkward, and graphically it looked dated. However if you focus on the positives in Gone Home, you can really see that The Fullbright Company had some great ideas. If they could transfer this approach to an actual game with substance, then I’m confident that it would have some real potential.

I followed this game through most of its development over the last year.  I was originally drawn to it for the subject matter, and despite its, at times, quirky aspects, such as somewhat crude character models and cartoonish animations, I found myself sticking with it.  The gameplay always drew me back, and I found myself devoting more and more of my limited gaming time to this intriguing game.
Slowly, over more than a hundred builds(!), the developers changed one thing, then another and another, in a steady march to completion.  It hasn't always been a straight line to the finish - sometimes two steps forward, one step back - but these guys perservered, and succeeded, in ways both surprising and impressive.
What started out as a clever, quaint little Indie game, fun in its own right, has blossomed into something much different.  The talented minds behind this effort could have stopped trying to improve things long ago, and still have it be considered a success.  Instead, through relentless hard work and obvious devotion, they have produced what, to me, is the best looking, most immersive, fun (and intense)  multiplayer FPS I've ever had the pleasure to play.  From the choice of a graphics engine to attention to gameplay elements, they've managed to do what virtually everybody said couldn't be done - create a compelling FPS based on the First World War.  Graphically, this is hands down the most gorgeous game I've ever played, of any genre.  Fantastic artwork, gentlemen!  You've put the big-budget boys to shame!
There may still be some elements that are less than perfect, but it has been a real pleasure to follow the development of the game through beta to release, and I suspect that development will continue.  If you like multiplayer FPS games, you owe it to yourself to try this absolutely stunning effort.  I highly recommend it (as if that was in doubt)!
Thanks to the devs for bringing this game to life.  Thank you, thank you.  I only wish I had the time and the stamina to play it more!

Gone Home is a down-to-earth realistic atmosphere game.  The narrative unfolds in a non-linear fashion as you choose which areas and items around the house to explore.  The more you explore the house the more you feel like you are right there in the shoes of Katie Greenbriar.  This game is basically about discovering the characters and their stories through their belongings.  The 90s Pacific Northwest setting is pulled off brilliantly and really completes the experience.  There is some mystery here, but this is not really a mystery game.  There are a couple of puzzles, but this is not really a puzzle game.  It is basically realistic fiction, but in a game format.  Get it.

I think I'm biased because I was a teenager in the late '80s and so the time period hits me just right, and I have a younger sister like the protagonist of this game... but don't let that scare you off if you don't quite fit those categories.  You might just like this anyway.  This is an 'interactive fiction' exploration game where you play a young adult woman who returns on a red eye flight from some months abroad in Europe, to find no one home waiting for you.  You explore the house and find journal entries (including voiced 'tape' diary entries from your sister), notes, and other things that help you figure out what's been going on in your absence.  Along the way, you unravel what happened to leave the house empty the day of your return, learn a lot about your family, and maybe learn about some other mysterious things and people as well.  I cried my eyes out at the ending; the storytelling was that spot-on.
After I finished the game, the developers released a "director's commentary track" that runs over parts of the game after you've completed it, and I may have to go back and discover more.

Gone Home is an explorational short story. The story is good, the voice acting is great, the house looks amazing and you are truly immersed in the 90s enviroment.
Where Gone Home falls short is that it's expensive (I got it on sale, so I don't mind the pricetag) for such a short game (3-4 hours for me) and not much replay value unless you like exploring and the story is not what you'd consider a story designed for games. It's not a game for everybody since it's technically more of a story than a game :)
All in all, I like Gone Home and can relate it to an evolved version of games like Dear Esther. It's a unique experience.

After playing this, I noticed that many of the reviews here were negative, and I felt that I needed to stand up for it.
This game seems to be causing a lot of controversy within the gaming community. I've mostly heard positive remarks from critics, but it seems that actual gamers are less enamored by this game.
I'll cut to the chase: Put it on your wishlist and wait for a sale.
The less you know about the story, the better. In case you haven't heard anything about it, this isn't a "video game" in the traditional sense. There are no enemies, no shooting, no puzzles - you need literally no reflexes or skill to enjoy this game. It consists entirely of story.
When you do play it - and you should - don't rush. Take it slow. Soak in your surroundings. Pay attention to detail, because the details are what make this game fantastic. Many of the people who dislike it seem to have rushed through it, completing it in nearly an hour or less. I suspect that there is a correlation - either their haste caused them not to enjoy it, or because they weren't enjoying it, they rushed through it. Personally, it took me 2.7 hours to complete the game, and I wish I had slowed down even more to pay attention. The "main story", I think, is fantastic, and is by far the best love story in any video game I have played. But if you slow down, and pay attention, you'll be exposed to other stories - more complex, and in some ways more interesting. The only game I've played in the last year that had characterization and voice acting that were anywhere near comparable to Gone Home was The Last of Us.
This is one of the best games I have played, and it pushes the boundaries of the medium farther than any other game I know of. Unfortunately, I can't suggest that anybody pay $20 for, at best, 3.5-4 hours of entertainment, regardless of how incredible it is. Put it on your wish list, and wait for a sale. I'd purchase it at any price below $15.

Okay, I'll elaborate.
I don't care if Gone Home is a "game" or not. Whether it's a game, movie, book, or whatever else, it provides a narrative that - despite some flaws - is ultimately worth your time. It suffers from Whedonesque overly-smarmy writing, at the cost of relatability to the characters at times, but it has some very smart ideas about its characters.
Gone Home is ultimately "about" homophobia, and the kinds of things that may inspire someone to have that kind of mindset. Sam's character arc is a mostly well-done but pretty boilerplate love story - what's interesting is exploring the homophobia of the other people in her life and discussing the events in their lives that cause them to hold this belief despite knowing and being so close to a homosexual person.
The ending is tonally unclear, but maybe it doesn't need to be specific - whether or not Sam's choices turn out the best for herself and the people around her are probably best left to interpretation. It's not the herald of a new age of ♥♥♥♥♥eo shames, and it's not even the best-written "walking simulator" game (that honor goes to The Stanley Parable) but it's an interesting experience that's ultimately well-written.

Deciding whether or not to recommend this game was difficult, because part of me liked the game and wants to recommend it. But I have a lot of critiques.

It didn't really bother me, but I can see it bothering some.
One thing I did like was the music; it didn't play often, but when it did, it was nice, and it fit the mood of the game.
If you're not a patient person (I actually am a patient person so I'm just guessing here), I'd say this isn't the game for you. You really have to stop and read/examine EVERYTHING, and there are a lot of things to stop and read/examine.
For me to recommend this game, it would have to be a bit longer, and the ending would have to resolve things somehow. An inconclusive ending in any game is enough to ruin the game for me.
If you really want to get Gone Home, I'd recommend waiting until it goes on sale, because it's not worth the full price.

FAIR WARNING TO ANYONE READING THIS WHO'S THINKING OF BUYING VERDUN:
The game is a WW1 Trench FPS Shooter.
That mean's it's a MEAT GRINDER.
Expect to die ALOT and OFTEN!!!
DO NOT get mad if you die often, because EVERYONE dies at least 30 times a match when they start playing!
The game is near impossible to play in the usual run-n-gun style of more modern fps's, as it is about cover and strategic  co-op with your teammates.
Keep in mind that the entire game is made to be as real as possible to WW1; this means single-shot kills, little cover outside of the trenches, no kill cams, and other variables like gun sway when aiming and breathing.
Once you have played for a while, you will begin to understand the do's and don't's of trench warfare, and the game will get easier. (provided your teammates aren't afk)
Remember, DO NOT GIVE UP AND QUIT. This game is made to be tough, but once you get the hang of playing Verdun, it will be one of the best games you've ever played.

Do you have an interest in historical battles? A love for FPS action? All of this mixed with complex strategic play and authenticity in your weapons? Then look now further, as Verdun is the game for you!
Prepare to go over the top, in an intense mixture of offense, defence, strategy and furious FPS action, Verdun is a must buy for fps lovers with a passion for history. Squadplay in which your role and teamwork is of paramount importance in a fun-packed FPS where working with your teammates, using your unique equipment and abillities and playing the objective tactically coincided with an authentic, realistic depiction of one of the bloodiest and darkest wars in history.
Particularly, the structure of the squad system gives a strong degree of progression and customisation to the game, ranging from authentic uniform upgrades to subclasses utillising different passive and active abillities. The three squad types (infantry section, reconnaissance teams and assault troops) each operate differently, and adopt a different nationality or branch of the army of it's respective faction, including French Poilus and Chasseurs, British Tommies, Canadians, German Landsers, Stosstruppen and Alpenjagers, and the upcoming American Doughboys along with many more to come. The authenticity and description of each fighting force adds a further degree of immersion and realism, alongside the strong pre-game squad forming system where you and your friends can link up, choose a squad type, assign roles and then go over the top together.
The dynamic, active attack-defence, trench warfare game mode of "frontlines" is a breath of fresh air from your standard FPS match, but if a more chaotic, traditional type gamemode is preferred, "rifle deathmatch" will still be able to bring the immense authenticity Verdun has to offer into a more farmiliar setting.
Still, Verdun does have its downsides, such as the annoyance of swift death following and unvoluntary squad-spawn or the tedious nature of the balancing/ player approach to certain maps. For example, many players will gravitate away from maps such as Flanders or Artois, causing games to become unbalanced or near-empty. However, the game does have efforts made to balance the game without forcefully imposing team switches upon its players.
Despite these flaws, Verdun is definitely a very enjoyable experience. But one must be in the correct mindset to enjoy to its fullest potential. Heading into it with the typical approach/attitude to fps's will invite swift death and probably frustration, this could cause many to become fed up with the game fairly quickly, but it is important to remember that Verdun (at least in it's more popular Frontlines mode) Is not designed for quickly accumilating a large number of kills as a lone wolf. Verdun is a game of teamwork and slow, methodical strategy. A game in which patience and the willingness to learn from heavy early failure will reward the user significantly, the immersion factor does definitely help to suppress possible frustration caused from the brutal, unforgiving nature of Verdun, but to be able to prosper you must really put yourself in the moment and understand the do's and dont's of trench warfare to survive.
Overall, verdun is a blast. If your new to fps's or a hardened veteran, a history nut or simply wanting to know more, little compares to the sheer adrenaline rush of clearing trenches alongside your comarades, pushing forward along realistic depictions of the savage trenches of the first world war.

Critics appraised Gone Home for its incredible story which causes one to reflect on the weight of human lives, these critics were quite incorrect. I won't be spoiling the game rest assured; but the *clears throat* great story I was promised (which is the only thing this game has going for it) was mediocre at best and I've actually read many stories like this. It has been done to death in novels and movies. I like to do a small challenge with myself to see how few words I can sum up the story with. So far I'm at five, immersive rich story eh? Also for the price of the game the length simply isn't justified, one hour and eleven minutes is all it took for me to complete the story with all the diary entries. Now I know some people will be crying out to me saying "You fool, the story wasn't just about Sam - there's much more to it with the parents and such." And yeah there was, by the time I'd read four letters it was pretty obvious what was happening. This is a "realistic story" and it hits the realism to the point where it's generic, I guarantee you there are many teenagers who could write a better story than this. I know I'm not giving Gone Home any grace but frankly, I don't think it deserves any. As a game all you do is walk around, pop some secrets panels/doorways and enter two combinations for a locker and a safe. As a story, it's drab and doesn't end with a bang or a whimper - it ends with letting off a balloon in your lounge as it produces farting noises and lands in a crumpled heap with a plop. My advice? Buy The Novelist, it incorporates good enough game play and a much more interactive story.

For years WW2 shooters were all the rage in video games, Call of Duty, Medal of Honor, Battlefield 1942, Brothers in Arms, Red Orchestra, etc, but I always wanted to see a WW1 shooter and now there finally is one. Imagine extreme trench warfare, mustard gas, tons of different bolt action rifles, lugers, mortar fire, running from cover to cover in no man's land, mowing down enemies with the heavy machine gun! This is a lot of fun, it encourages teamwork even though there's limited VOIP, what I and many others will do is relay the enemies' position in team chat, such as "LEFT SIDE" if the enemy has breached our position on the left side of the trench, or is about to. One may view the lack of VOIP as a negative, but on the plus side you're less likely to hear any screaming squeakers on the mic and go through the effort of going in the menu and muting them. If you play as the officer class you can call in mustard gas strikes, mortar strikes or air recon (depending on the type of squad you're in) by holding Q and right clicking. The game is somewhat realistic, it only takes one shot from a bolt action rifle to kill someone and you need to use cover, but there's no friendly fire and there are crosshairs. If you like realistic, yet fun shooters, like Insurgency, you're gonna like Verdun. Like Insurgency, the developers keep adding content in free updates (they've added 2 new maps since I've owned Verdun), so I highly recommend this unique shooter as it gives you far more bang for your buck than your typical AAA shooter that charges $50 for a season pass.
EDIT: I just found out that they recently added VOIP, but it's limited to your squad only. The developers are adding free expansions that will include gore, new maps, the trench gun, flamethrowers and new squads, including the Americans and Belgians and in future expansions they'll add more fronts, such as the Eastern front between Russia, Germany and Austria-Hungary and many more. I normally do not write reviews. However sometimes I see that the overwhelming amount of reviews that are out are so startlingly in the wrong that I need to throw in my own coins. Because I swear to god every other reviewer has totally missed the point.
Gone Home is not a creepy/horror game. It has creepy elements to it but the main purpose of the game is not to scare you, it is to immarse into the (brilliant) story. If anything it is an interactive novel. That point is to tell the story.
As a game it is simple, true, but extremely immersive. That feeling that something is off that you get wandering any empty house in the real world is very much present. You KNOW that there isn't a dead body or ghoul or devil-monster at the end of the dark hallway but that doesn't stop your gut instinct from going into paranoia mode. The creak of the house settling or the wind rattling the house get to you as you wander this unfamiliar (to both you and the character) building is almost palpable. And, if you have a working brain and heart, the story as it unfolds wil rips at your heart and repairs it and drags you in until you know that you need to know how it ends.
At first the Greenbriar family looks to be the perfect family with the park ranger mom and the novelist dad with the wanderlust older child and the younger child who tugs at the binds that hold her to her lot in life just a bit. Cookie-cutter and plain, until you start to peel away the layers and find out the truth about the parents marriage and love life and the father's novels and that the younger sibling isn't so much as tugging as she is ripping at the binds.
That is what the story is about, A family and people in the purest form. You are not some amazing hero set to save the world or battling cosmic entities or leading a revolution or exploring magical places with magical people. You are a  girl, come home from an extended time overseas, trying to piece together what has happened to you family in the intervening year you have been gone. The core of this game is the story, and if you cannot understand or appreciate it then you have missed the point.
Is this game overpriced for it's short playtime? Maybe, I am no expert in these matters. Does it have no replay value? It has a lot of replay value (but then my stance has always been why buy a game you will never replay? It's like a buying a DVD so you can only rewatch the movie once). Is it a simple and easy game? Yes, because of the focus and purpose of the game.
Shoould you buy this game? A very emphatic yes.

This was done beautifully. I had no idea what this game was about when I bought it, I actually thought it was a horror game. Or going to be spooky. Although it seemed so at first, it becomes quite apparent the game is quite different than I imagined.
From the lightning and pouring rain, to the flickering light that are mostly off, to the fact that NO ONE IS HOME, I thought something bad had happened. Especially with such an eerie note left on the front door. (Not a spoiler if it's the first 5 seconds).
However, as you play and experience the game, you nitpick the house, and thus the life, of your family. You learn about your mother, father, and sister. Their lives, secrets, interests, etc. You become strangely close with them. This isn't a game about you. not really, at least. This is a game about them, and unraveling their lives.
Never has media more accurately portrayed how I felt in High School. How I felt as my body grew, and I had so many questions that I couldn't ask. The feelings I had for people, and the awkwardness of dating. This, packed with all sorts of 90's references made me completely immerse myself in the game's setting. I grew with the game. By the end, I was almost crying. It is beautiful. (Or maybe it's because it's 3 in the morning)
I must admit, it's kind of short, depending on how well you are with puzzles. I finished in one night. Although it's rather linear. The narration is done well, and I almost feel as though I know this sister that I never had before. Despite the game's brevity, it is a very touching piece. Anyone who has gone through adolescence will find sympathy for the characters. Especially if you have siblings, or have moved, or lived in the 90's. (All the X-File references were a plus too!)
Honestly, I give it a 9/10. Definitely worth playing.

Gone Home is not a horror game, nor is it an action game. It's not a strategy game, it's not a simulator. No, it's a slightly adventuristic, story driven, exploration game. You play throughout the entire game, exploring a mansion that belongs to your parents. You arrive home early from going to school abroad to find out that nobody is home. You must go through all the rooms, looking at all the artifacts and knick knacks. While doing so, you stumble upon journal entries that tell you more information about what had happened while you were gone abroad. The story is wonderful, and it has kept me interested completely.
I know that from the way the environment looks, the game should feel like a horror game, but don't let that fool you. It's a wonderfully done story game, with slight interactivity.

If we look at Verdun in the standards of modern gaming, it fails miserably.
Compared to triple A games and large developers, Verdun and it's developers fails in almost every aspect of game making.
No first day DLC save final updates.
No microtransactions.
No "pay to win" mentality.
No unrealistic twitch shooting.
No dodgy business practices.
No massive failures on day one.
No insane advantage for high level gamers.
No false advertising.
By today's standards, verdun would fail on the table of EA, Bethesda, CA, SEGA, Nintendo, and just about every single gaming company that is larger than, say, CD Projekt Red.
These failures, however, make this game the best FPS on the market as of now.
These indie developers have crafted the most satisfying experience I have had in a first person shooter in a long damned time.
The game is perfectly digestable, the upgrades system is easy to get, the weapons are balanced and look and handle fantastically...
The list of amazing acheivements this game has accomplished could go on for pages of writing.
Verdun created it's own version of FPS gameplay, taking us to an era most companies find dull and drab.  The trench warfare turn based attack gameplay is insane, as you see first hand the horrors of the First World War, which, by the way, is now 100 years past.
I bought this game in eraly access and was satisfied with it.  Now I can't get enough of it!
I have been fed up with large companies coming out with garbage and selling DLC every five minutes.  Verdun's updates and new squards are being released free of charge over the next while, so this game will become even better and more varied than it is now.
Verdun is one of a special kind of game, one that requires teamwork to dominate the map.  While battlefield has become zany and unrealistic, Verdun forces you to play as a team, and unlike in battlefield, if you fail to do so, you will die again, and again, and again.
I cannot recommend this game more to anyone.  The learning curb is massive, but you have so many classes to play as that are open to even the newest players.
Honestly there is something satisfying about having to use bolt action rifles in a trench that is captivating in and of itself.  It is insanly addicitive and the squad based gameplay is incredible.
Verdun is by far the best FPS I have ever played as I have put in so many hours of my life into it (roughly 10 hours alone in hte last few weeks).
I cannot recommend this game any more.
SO GO BUY IT.
And as for some advice, keep your head down.
This isn't Call of Duty.

Gone Home is an excellent example of environmental storytelling, features level design that really evokes the sense of a family home in the 90s, has a touching and well-written love story and does a nice job tapping into 90s nostalgia.  Oh, those cassette boxes almost made me swoon.
There isn't much in the way of complex mechanics - the player walks around, picks up and examines or reads things, and very occasionally uses objects in the environment or enters a code or something.  There is no physical conflict to speak of.  But the overall experience is atmospheric and engaging, the story is touching, and I think it's worth it for that alone.  If you go in looking for good environmental storytelling, a strong atmosphere and mood, and a good story, you'll not be disappointed.

Gone Home isn't so much a traditional game as it is a performance piece, the same as a play or a short story, except you control the pace and rhythm of said story. Interaction is mostly limited to only walking through the house and examining items strewn about. Don't think that, with that said, it offers nothing to the player.
What IS in Gone Home is a fantastic story of teen love and finding your own identity. The way it is told, spoonfed to you in small bits, is what makes it far more interesting than if it were simply read as prose.
Gone Home is an experience, and one I recommend to anyone. You will come out of it greater than you went in, provided you take your time and pay attention, of course. Think of it as a DVD. You watch it once, you probably won't watch it again immediately. But there will be some rainy day when the story has gotten a little fuzzy in your head, and you'll replay Gone Home to refresh it. And you'll enjoy it all over again.

So I picked this up because, everywhere I go online and otherwise, this game is getting huge buzz with Game of the Year on many lists and it's being touted as very unique and atmospheric. Mind you, a lot of this review is hard to get my point across without spoilers so I will not spoil much if anything at all.
Now, like I said, for one, I've read "unique" many times in reviews and I feel like the reviewers must be just playing main-stream stuff and not really hitting the fringe often but this game comes off as an uninspired Dear Esther which came out last year not to mention the other games trying to pass games as an art-form and story telling media.
The atmosphere is something to talk about in this review because it IS what's gonna drive you through this game. I feel like that is a great driving force in Gone Home but it leads you through an extremely quick game of seek and find that pulls it's climax from under your feet having you asking "what happened?" when you reach the credits. Not that the end is confusing or anything (if anything, it feels like it's attempting to preach about issues that're raging today), its just that there're clues to things that don't fully flesh out and leave most issues dangling.
In summary, the plot is unfinished and I feel it's getting credit because of the issues its pushing rather than the actual quality the game is built on. I beat this game in 45 min, taking my time, not rushing, and honestly stunned by its shortness. I think the developer can make a quality game, just gotta get that story and length worked on.

Overall pretty realistic, with the complex squad-based gameplay adding a twist of both unbalance and fun ( since squads composed of friends that are constantly playing togheter are overall higher leveled and get many bonuses that give them a considerable edge over their "non-leved" enemies, but playing in a squad and seeing it get stronger over levels is indeed really fun)
A fun thing is the "attack and defend" turn system, even thought I think the "foothold" and "enemy casualties" mechanics are needless. Also worth mentioning is the NCO system, which turns to be a great resource for quick trench take-overs if well used.
However, a bad mention goes to the guns. They're realistic anda authentic as expected,  but that's not the problem.  Indeed, I really like the hit-kill rifle mechanic and the high lethality of pistols, MP18 and Machine Guns, but some of them have really nice ironsights which make aiming and firing precise shots a quick task ( G98, for the rifles. To MGs, Chauchat and MG08/16 also, whilst the Lewis' iron sight is so lame) .
On the other hand, most weapons have some really nasty iron sights which front parts often get obscured of completely concealed. That gives some riflemen an astounding edge in scopeless sharpshooting and trench corner combat, whilst others must often resource to changing their loadout to a different rifle or even a sidearm, sacrificing a few resources in the process. The French and German machine gunners as well get a far superior speed and accuracy in identifying and shooting advancing enemy soldiers, whilst the British are sniped off  by the first target they find and kill.
Last thing I have to complain about is the lack of a South America server, which just ♥♥♥♥s me off with  100-200 ping against highly skilled riflemen with 10-30 ping. But, I can understand that there are probably very few Verdun players down South America, so maybe just the option to make dedicated servers would be good enough.
All in all, a pretty fun game which makes justice to what it promises. I didn't regret playing it.

Gone Home is one of those rare creations. It's cursed to be marginalized by a closed minded and insensitive chapter of the consuming public because it dares to call itself something like a video game, but that doesn't make it any less special, any less pure. It stands defiantly in the face of all that criticism. It holds its head up because, whatever labels you choose to put on it, it's going to make you feel more--more than anything else you've played this week, more than any Hollywood movie you've seen in the last ten years.
What it offers is simplicity, subtlety, and the essential ingredients of compelling narrative. True, it's a short ride, but if what you're looking to get out of your money is quantity, what you're probably not getting quality. Gone Home is a three hour exploration oriented adventure that makes every second of its brief span count.
It is an exercise in the haunting experience of ordinary things. It is theater specializing in the drama of real life. To step into Katie's shoes and explore her family's empty house, and the sundry relics of their lives, is to be swept away on a rockslide of sympathy, of tenderness, of intimacy, and compelling self discovery. It could be said that you're role in this story is that of a supporting character, but that doesn't mean that what you discover along the way will be any less cathartic for you.
If you are capable of empathy, if what you crave is an experience true to life that offers real emotion, then you can do no wrong by spending time in this beautifully crafted world.

This game is probably the best interactive story game I've ever experienced.  You play as Katie, the big sister to the main character of the story, Sam. Throughout the game, you interact with items around the house and find different peices and parts to your sister's Journal, each subtly reveiling a little bit more about Sam and her life while you were gone on vacation.
The atmosphere of the game really sucks you into it, rendering you almost unable to comprehend what's happening around you in the real world. I believe the weather and the creepy aspect to the house have a big role to play in this. With the impression that ghosts are all around you, it's really hard not to be pulled it, and this did a great job for developing the story and grabbing your emotional attention.
The story seems simple at the base, but as time moves on, it grows more complex. You're following the life of someone who's complexities are infinite, and you just find yourself wanting to hear more and learn more about her. This especially had a huge impact on me because I make a big connection with Sam on a personal level, for many different aspects. And I suspect that if you find yourself to be anything like her, this will really impact you as well.
I found myself trying to hold back my tears for the whole latter half of the game. The story is just so moving and I could help but feel what Sam was conveying throughout the game. Every implication just kind of clicks, strongly. As the credits rolled at the end, I was sobbing almost uncontrollably as everything kind of sank in. I was happy and sad at the same time. It's definitely something I can see myself replaying in the future, kind of like re-reading a good book. I love this story and highly recomend it to those with an open mind and an open heart.

'Gone Home' is one of those games that people seem to either really like, or really dislike. It's not a typical game, and I would even hesitate to call it a game. It's more of an interactive story, really. There are no battles or puzzles to solve--it's just you clicking around a creepy, empty house while you learn about the people that lived there. That's it.
While I did enjoy this game, I will concede that it is not for everyone. It is a bit pricy for the length of gameplay (about 2 hours, depending on how thorough you are), and occasionally buggy (I had trouble getting doors to open, even after obtaining the proper key--the only workaround being to restart the game with the option to have all doors unlocked enabled). Still, I enjoyed the 90s nostalgia and the cute love story.

Verdun is a game that (I think) you will either love or hate. You will die. A lot. You will fight over and over for the same stretch of land, again and again. Did I say you will die a lot? You will. A lot.
Being a veteran of the Red Orchestra 2 and Rising Storm games, dying a lot is not necessarily a bad thing to me. If I take a bullet, that means that one of my squadmates didn’t. Maybe one of them was my squad leader. Now I can spawn closer to the enemy trench! I love dying in the mud of no man’s land.
There are two game modes, but you will most likely only play Frontlines. In this mode, you fight over a small section of the Western Front where the goal is to advance and capture sectors, or defend those sectors from being captured. If an attack loses momentum, melts away in machine gun fire as it were, the roles are reversed and the defending team goes on the attack. Sometimes a team keeps on advancing, but mostly the teams go back and forth over the same stretch of bloody mud until the match is over.
The game is at its best with a full server. The maps are fairly small, and the fights are intense. It’s probably not that realistic, but it’s gritty. On of the best (and scariest) moment so far was when I had just fallen back from a failed attack and was back in my trench. I got up on the firing step and aimed my SMLE at a green cloud of bromide gas. Out of the cloud came three gray-clad Landsers in gas masks, rushing my position. I managed to take one down, but the others jumped into the trench and shot me in the back. Damn.
Are you on the fence about this game? I can’t tell you if you will like this game, I can just tell you that I love this game. Have you played Red Orchestra 2 and/or Rising Storm and liked those games? If yes, then you’d probably love this game.

Verdun 1914-18 has been on my radar for over a year.  I opted out of the early-release after reading the forums and watching whatever video reviews were available.  Based on various posts, videos, and word of mouth, it simply wasn't polished enough then.  Although it still held some promise.  I decided to wait until the official release to see if the game studio would iron out the major bugs/flaws/issues/etc.
I had high-hopes for this game, but was strongly let down because of a few critical factors:
1.) There is absolutely no single player mode in this game.  No ability whatsoever.  No provision to fight AI/bots, no sandbox mode for new players to tinker with loadouts/builds, or work on attack routes.  No way to feel the game out before you jump into some multiplayer frenzy (more on that later).  The closest you get is the ability to make your own private server.  This forces you to be 100% always online with this game, and the game also sends/syncs in-game performance info to the devs.  So if you want to experiement and end up blowing yourself up, the devs get that info and probably label you with trisomy.  Furthermore, while in this mode you can't exactly experiment or test much (like flanking routes) as there isn't even an option for some dummy AI to spam shoot guns or simulate bullets/shells your way.  If you cant stand the game enough to unlock additional items via the f-fest that is multiplayer, then you basically run around with a pistol doing and learning absolutely noting beyond sampling the basic trench layout.
2.) The online component can be unplayable.  The servers are often laggy, with noregs and desync issues.  They also seem to spread the online population throughout relatively low populated shards.  A total of ~200 players were online across all the US servers during "primetime gaming hours" today.  I've gathered several data points like this.  During another session, no one could log on.  This point could become moot, and I do sincerely hope conditions improve.
3.) The matchmaking is either non-existent, glitched, or hasn't (or can't) reached a kind of steady-state.  Basically, you have a bunch of WWI fanbois who've been spamming 24/7 nolife hours into this particular game (probably because the competition in other FPS titles is too much).  These keeners exploit the overpowered luger pistol making shots that are basically hack-worthy, and have levelled/formed/gelled rock-solid groups and basically dominate entire matches.  Its not uncommon to see obscure lobsidded k/d ratios (like 74-2) as people with 1+ years of "pre release" experience tea-off on a fresh stream of nubs just logging in for the first time.  The barrier to entry wouldn't be so bad if the game actually had a lot of people at diverse skill levels spread out into medium populated servers.  Unfortunately, all you get are completely barren empty servers (3v3) or full wait in line to join 32v32 battles, the later I have no doubt will become epic once the game matures somewhat.  That said, I don't see there being enough carrying capacity to support enough squads wanting to "go pro" for proper tournaments or any long-term sustainability.
4.)  The community is naive, biased, pretentious, etc.  Try telling someone this game is "meh" and you'll be labeled toxic, flamed, and told to gtfo.  You can discover this for yourself on the forums, but as I alluded to -- the clout/influence about the game is propped up by a small group (maybe 20-30 ppl).  These makeup an inner circle of die-hard players who get first crack at the devs ears, upvoting/downvoting reviews to keep the game looking sharp, and helping to sway design decisions and telling people everything is a-ok.  You should see how these players suck up to the devs on stream/forums/in-game/etc.
In general, the game still has some potential but obviously not as anything too serious.  Its a basic FPS concept embedded into WWI ambiance that probably isn't worth the $20 at this point.  If I had my time back, I would get my nostalgia/fix for WWI content through other vectors.  You can catch glimpses of this game on youtube, twitch, etc.  Unfortunately, those previews don't show the fact that this game has two options -- press a button to jump into a trench-fight server, or press the button to quit.  Without an offline mode, proper matchmaking, polished (net)code, and biased "community", I'll be looking for an uninstall button after I grind through 5 more hours to bring it to around $2/hour of wasted time.

There's a lot of controversy about this one.  It occupies the same categorical space as Dear Esther and shares the same discussions on what defines games, art, and the lines between them.  What you're getting here is a story in an interactive setpiece.  It's voyeuristic in a way, and absolutely heartfelt.  For the best experience, take the time to play through in one sitting.
It's certainly not for everyone.  If you're looking for action or horror beyond the creeping thrill of exploring a dark and unfamiliar house, you're in the wrong place.  Finding enjoyment is reading is a definite requirement as well.  Mind you, the price point is fairly steep at $20. You’ll be a default weapon and armor wearing commando for 99% of your experience. And don’t let those other players deceive you as they jump up and down trying to convince people that they do “just fine” without all that fancy equipment in PVP or PVE. What they won’t tell you is 75% of the time they’re being outclassed by super sprinters, super sliders, armor regenerators and people who can tank claymore mines with particular armor load outs. Long ago my review for Warface was rather positive, but man how times have changed. It all started going down hill during the previous Ice Breaker patch and the introduction of Crytek's new publisher
. The first problem was the new publisher introduced a brand new account login system that forced players to convert their old accounts over to this new one. For many others the instructions on how to convert one's old account over to the new account was not explained clearly enough for many. Also the info that mandatory account conversion had to be done by XX deadline or lose your account was not announced enough. I myself converted my account quickly and smoothly to the new format without any hiccups whatsoever. Heck for a moment I thought all was well when
& Crytek offered to give old players of the game complimentary Earth Shaker weapon sets for free when converting their old accounts. In hindsight I wish I saw the long con coming. They basically did something nice for you (The player) so that they could get away with doing terrible things to the player base later down the road.
Ironically the previous Ice Breaker patch broke the game for many players and forced even more players out of the game altogether. For starters they decided to cut the payout rewards of PVE, PVP and Spec Ops all by 50% which is devastating. Grinding in this game is quite the task in itself on the higher difficulty levels so knowing that I would have to grind twice or even three times as much was just frustrating to hear. There’s a difference between reasonable grinding in a game vs unreasonable grinding in a game. Sadly these changes are definitely the latter. Next they viciously cranked up the repair cost after every mission by 50% meaning whatever reward money you did get would be more times than not get wiped out by the repair cost. Also depending on the level of the gear you are using, you can now more easily go into debt and drop into the negatives money wise if you’re not careful. Luckily I was saving up for an expensive weapon before all this madness took place so I’m slightly ahead of the curb in that regard.
To quote the developers off of an old Q&A session they stated "The repair bills will be higher than those some of you have gotten used to, yet this change is vital to ensure there is no currency inflation" And I thought to myself boy oh boy looks like I won't be able afford anything decent anymore. Either that or the boat load of permanent weapons I already acquired can't be used anymore. Well scratch that last statement because I just discovered the weapon system has gone from permanent weapons to a horrible rental system. Later on in another review I read the developers also mentioned and I quote “The repair cost is more than manageable and they’re an additional difficulty level to the game. Seriously!? Trumped-up repair costs are now being justified as an additional difficulty factor? Sorry I’m not buying that as an explanation or an excuse. You know what else that can be an additional difficulty factor? Smarter A.I, Increased enemy accuracy, increased enemy damage and better map design.
The problem with
taking over is that the direction of the game has pretty much been made into a hardcore FREEMIUM game. If you want to cover your repair cost without the painful and unreasonable levels of grinding, you gotta cough up real cash for those VIP Boosters. Meaning if you want to make ANY kind of MEANINGFUL progress in this game at a REASONABLE length of time, MONEY IS MANDATORY in that regard. And to all those other people on the other side shouting, “Get out!” “So what?!” will be the same people months down the road complaining that are not enough players on “XX” server or that queue times for games are taking too long. So even if you’re one of those players who doesn’t care about the other players walking away or those forced to walk away from this game they used to enjoy know this, at the end of the day Warface will still need a player base to remain relevant so shunning the concerns of a large majority of the veteran players of the game will not benefit you in the long run...

Verdun is, for my money, the most interesting FPS currently available on Steam. I use the term "interesting" quite deliberately. It's not the prettiest, it's not the most fast-paced, action-packed, explosion-filled... actually scratch that last part. There are plenty of explosions, and they're pretty devastating. The point is, there is something to this game that will keep bringing you back for more.
If you're a history buff, you can't beat it for an air of authenticity - right down to the grainy, cheesy period music playing on the gramophone in the start menu; gas warfare, waves of inexperienced troops (yourself included) being mowed down by artillery and machine gun fire, drowning in a flooded shell hole in Flanders becuase you're too scared to stick your head out to look for the sniper who has you pinned down... I'd call that immersive.
If you're an FPS afficionado, this game will present you with an interesting challenge you won't find elsewhere, and not just because bolt action rifles take some getting used to after years of CoD and Halo. Face down a heavy machine gun armed only with five hand-grenades and a shovel, I freaking dare you. Maybe you're just plain sick of playing the same game modes in everything you play (capture-point, capture the flag, deathmatch,  slight variations on any of the above...). Then the frontlines game mode will probably be the most intriging thing here for you. Take the enemy's first line of defence, hold it against the immediate counter-attack. If you succeed, then take a crack at their second line. Nevermind the third, or the fourth after that. But if they take it back, you start from scratch - assuming you manage to halt their advance, of course.
Been playing for over a year now, and it's amazing how far it's come in that time. Expect this one to keep getting better, but it's already pretty damn good. 9.5/10

I am only going to review the game's gameplay, since I'm a firm believer that good graphics are non-essential to a game's ( non commercial ) success, and I'm playing on low settings. If the core game is at least very good, the rest ( graphics, voice acting, technical issues.. ) can be fixed or even totally ignored.
Where to start? First, I would like to say that this is the best shooter I have played in an extremely long time, easily the best since COD4 ( it's even better than that game ). The game is also the most balanced video game I have ever played, it's ALWAYS your fault when you get killed, and when your team loses it means that you have been completely outplayed by the other team, not by one individual player like COD.
You will probably notice that the game's most salient feature is its emphasis on realism and teamwork. You simply cannot capture basis or lift the whole team on your own, and trying to blindly rush the enemy will get you absolutely obliterated. Guns have sway and recoil, in addition to ballistics, meaning that using them is much more than simply aiming at an enemy troop and firing; You have to patiently take your shots to mitigate the recoil and sway effects, which in turn makes the game significantly more tactical and detail-oriented. Often, the only difference between losing or winning a sniping duel is taking your shot a bit too early, and thus ruining your accuracy due to recoil or sway.Also, mobile targets require you to lead your target to compensate for their movement and distance, a feature that is increasingly being done away with in modern shooters.
The maps in this game have a very unique design unseen in other shooters: they are large and open ended, but with many trenches scattered accross the landscape. This means that they tend to favour long range combat when the enemy hasn't yet come to capture your base, and close range fighting when your base ( or frontline ) is infiltrated by enemies. Of course, the maps being designed that way means that taking cover and carefully choosing when to fire and whom to fire at is more crucial than in any other game out there, and being out in the open for any extended period of time is next to impossible - the only other game I know of where taking cover is also vital is Medal of Honor 2010 - . The large size of the maps do lend themselves to camping and sniping from long distances, which isn't a bad thing once you realize that these players are a liability to their team in this objective based game and can be taken down if you pull out your rifle and very patiently hunt them down. In any case, it's better than the corner camping garbage that plagues other popular shooters ( usually a direct consequence of very poor map design ).
The aforementioned points ( maps, teamwork, guns and realism..) have several ramifications upon how the game is supposed to be played and how it is approached by the community. You will notice a more ordered and structered gameplay with very little random chaos and unexpected events, like constantly being shot in the back due to poor spawns or map design in other games, or appearing to be winning only to be baffled that you're acually on the losing team. Battles have a flow to them, you can notice on the spot without looking at the scoreboard which team has the momentum and which team is being dominant, which is proof of the underlying excellence of the game's mechanics and overall design. If you are on the receiving end of some serious beating, it will be very palpable. The extreme dichotomy between being on top and mercilessly exterminating the opposition, and being pinned down and ripped to shreds has rarely been nailed down so well in the gaming industry.
To sum it all up: the game is extemely fun, very well balanced and, because most guns kill in a single shot, quite brutal ( but in a completely fair and great way). You can't help but appreciate the hardcore feel of the game and the guns in it. It is also a throw back to the old days ( pre killstreaks and health regen ) when shooters actually required skill and were among the most lovable games, and a healthy escape from the low levels the genre has stooped to since then.  If you want a new take on the FPS genre, a uniqely different experience, this is one of the very few games that can provide you with that, and much more.

Gone Home captures the essence of nostalgia. The player has not seen the Greenbriar household, but the feeling of coming home after a long time remains universal. Exploring the house feels like skimming through a scrapbook or thumbing pages in a photo album. Every note, object, or clue grazes an emotional touchstone. Gone Home is more than a video game. It is a love a story. It breaks the boundary between the real and the virtual by exposing emotions we all recognize. It is powerful evidence that video games are as flexible a creative form as any other.

After going through Gone Home on New Year's Eve and finishing it off on New Year's Day, I can't think of a better title to embody the spirit of this holiday. Gone Home is the preemminent example of the wave of indie non-games, such as Stanley Parable and Dear Esther. The story focuses on the home-coming of a daughter and sister from a European sojourn. When she arrives the house is empty and you are set to explore it, discovering the lives of the Greenbriar family.
This may be among the best written stories I've every gone through. It's moving in the way that all good art accomplishes. I sat in my seat after it all ended to take in what happend, piecing together the family history and thinking about what comes next for them. There is hope, saddness, strife (personal and interpersonal) and humor all told through items, letters and drawings.
If you've noticed, I haven't called Gone Home a game. Because it isn't. Unfortunately, we haven't come up with a better term than "Interactive Media", and while that's a catchy term, maybe something that doesn't take seven syllables will come along soon. There is no proper goal, maybe once or twice you know you have to find smething, but that's it. That said, it doesn have some common elements of games: immersion, an inventory and a map. But while it often communicates in the language of games, you can be assured this is a very different creature.
Gone Home has the length of a movie, about 2 hours, and is worth taking some time and going through it in one sitting. In the first 10-15 minutes you'll know if this is your kind of thing or not. I hope it is though. Gone Home is the most likely "game" to motivate pure cinephiles and classic art types to enjoy the medium. I have no doubt that it represents a milestone in the history of the medium. Try it out. Please.

I'm normaly alot more open to such things as the "Early starting snikkets" that effect all gamers as they load up a new game with idea of grandue. However, I found Verdun in my short time playing the game a complete bloodbath (and not the good kind).
With little to no intruction other than "Stay close to your Squad" You are thrown into a very realistic (Wonderful job by the way) state of first World War warfare with nothing but a rifle and a few odds and ends.
i found myself having infomation and statistics poured down my gullet with little to no idea of what they were. How what i persume was a global map of players all fighting for something... All stuggeling to gain something... all killing in the name of something...
However, that is just my critisim of the pre-game screens and nonsence you work your way through to get to the action. Action that in all sence of the word, was chaotic. The moment you dare to leave the safty of some cover, you are blow away in the most lazy of ragdoll effect %20 gravity animated way possible by some invisible german or "Tommy" rifleman who is just as confused and scared as you are.
I persume that bonuses are given for staying near your squad of four players, although i dont know what those bonuses are, nor how they effect your gameplay and/or account, simply because its too diffucult to stay alive long enought to even consider working towards them.
All this said, as an Englishman... I completely know where the Devs stand. Their creativity and historical accuracy is next to none. our great great gandfathers felt helpless, scared and confused, as much as we were. They felt the same terror and reluctence to claw their way over the muddy walls of the trenches, just as you will when you play this bad...yet remarkably beautiful game.
if you do play this game, then please remember them, and all they sacrificed for us.

While this game does lack some polish (not graphically intensive at all, animations look somewhat old and a bit stiff), It's a good FPS with a unique setting (Think back, how many other WWI FPS's have you seen or played in the past?). The fighting is intense, and varies from long range, trench-to-trench fighting, mid range firing to and from no-mans-land, and then finally close quarters in the trenches.
Gameplay functions in a manner such as this: At the start of the round one team is attacking while the other defends, if the attacking team fails to take a foothold or outright capture the trench in the time allotted to them they must retreat and brace for an attack from the enemy. Once a team succeeds in capturing a trench the enemy is given one last chance to counter-attack before it's lost, if they fail they fall back to the next line and the cycle begins again.
Maps are varied enough that even though it's all trench warfare, it never feels stale, this is done through different trench layouts and sizes, terrain that ranges from mostly flat open fields to hilly bombed out areas covered in craters.
Players pick squads and classes to play, each squad type represents a different nation (most nations have multiple squad types), and each squad type has a different set of classes with unique loadouts to fill different roles. Each match is made up of 4 squads of 4 per team, totaling 16v16/32 total.
I'd say to give it a play if you like realistic FPS, and maybe want a change in setting or are interested in playing a different setting that isn't often used.

Gone Home is a story adventure that unfortunately falls flat.
I love a good mystery and thought this would be right up my alley. A college-aged girl comes home, circa 1995, from traveling abroad and finds the entire home empty when she arrives late on a stormy night. The family had just moved into what some in town call the "psycho house". Lights flicker, thunder booms and you hear the sound of your footsteps in the old house.
That sounds like the beginning of great, spooky adventure. But it soon becomes clear that the only background narrative you get is from your sister, Sam, who is 17. You hear bits of an audio journal after examining key clues. You do find bits and pieces out on other family members through the notes and items they leave around, but Sam is the only voice over.
What you soon find is Gone Home is more of a coming of age (and coming out) story within a spooky setting. (Trust me, I'm not giving anything away here.) While you can pick up a lot of things and open drawers and such, almost none of the things you find, save notes and letters, are useful. You can only keep a few items, like keys, that you will need to unlock certain areas. And, although at the very start, Sam warns you not to poke around, she certainly doesn't act like that was the intent throughout the rest of story.
There is some indie band music (on cassette tapes, of course) that you can pop in a player and listen to. Personally, I thought it sounded terrible--unless you like death metal women bands who scream their lyrics. I was hoping they'd have some clues on tape or that you would be able to pop in a VHS into the player for some visual clues. Oh well....
There are no real puzzles save finding keys to unlock doors and combinations that unlock other items. It's a very short game--only a few hours. The graphics are good, the voice acting is done well, but unless you find this type of storyline appealing, you'll probably be disappointed.

Warface is an okay first person shooter game. Its free, so you don't lose anything if you download it and don't like it. One of the main pros is the interaction with objects and other players. For example, for higher objects that one player cannot climb alone, two players can help one player climb up it. The graphics are also great, you can adjust them to be amazing. There are two main game modes, co-op missions and versus (or online games). Co-op missions have a variety of difficulties, some are easy, some are challenging yet fun. In versus mode, there are 24 maps, but most are small or tiny so snipers are rendered useless in most maps in this game. There are game modes inside of versus mode like team deathmatch, plant the bomb, which is almost identical to Search and Destroy from the Call of Duty games, and many more. The weapons have a lot of customization too, but it is pretty much pay to win upgrading in the weapon store. At times, the game can be laggy or very laggy, almost unplayable. Also, there are 4 classes you can choose from, Rifleman, Engineer, Medic, and Sniper. I wish there was made a few more, like 2-3 more, maybe including a Heavy or Grenadier. I didn't notice an unbalanced gun which everyone used that was really overpowered. One thing I really hated, spawns online. In almost EVERY game online, the amount of spawn camping is RIDICULOUS, I mean you can get trapped in your spawn along with your whole team for 1-2 minutes+. Lots of people dropshot too. Another thing; in Warface, teamwork is the most important aspect of online, so if your teammates are bad, then you can't win, especially with spawn trapping. Finally, the game is okay in my opinion, but its a fish in a school of 100, in that there are tons of first person shooter games that are good. Warface can sort of compete especially for a free FPS game, but most small FPS games get drowned out by the main games like Call of Duty, Counter-Strike, Arma, and maybe even Team Fortress 2 and Half-Life 2. Overall, this is an okay game with its respective pros and cons. My rating is 6/10. This game can get very boring very quickly also. Give the game a try and see if you like it.
