Well , i was wrong . I was so very wrong.
The game focuses on straight infantry combat. You start the game and jump right in the tutorial with no explanation about what is going on . Some female voice tells you everything that you need to know about classes , movement mechanics , weapons etc. After you finish the tutorial you get a weapon which only lasts a week ( I will talk about this MAJOR problem later on ) . You get to choose whether you want to jump in a game through matchmaking or through dedicated servers. I truly recommend dedicated servers because you can find a game faster and you skip the 20 minutes wait time until you find a server that is empty in matchmaking.

The gameplay itself has some next-gen elements in it , such as : helping a teammate climb a higher structure by boosting him up , reviving ( not really next-gen but oh well ) and also
. I said SLIDING in bold text because i want to point out that it is OP ( OverPowered )  , meaning that when you slide , you can also shoot. This makes it so that when you see a dude , slide and shoot towards him and he's dead. No matter his skill , level etc , he will not notice you and you will get an easy kill. It was slightly nerfed since i first played this game in the closed beta , but it is still OP.
The game also has classes , which are primitive and remind me of Battlefield 4 . You get the same generic classes you see in every shooter ( medic , sniper , engineer , and rifleman ) . The one that somehow stands out is the rifleman , which is somehow a support from Battlefield , but with the ability to give himself ammo without droping it .
Anyway , you've probably played other shooters and you know how they handle.
The gunplay is very unbalanced. You start out with some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ weapons which are actually waterguns because all their stats are set to 1 ( out of 100 ) , and all of your enemies are higher levels with weapons that seem like very small miniguns combined with Counter Strike AWP's . In other words , you will lose every single battle if you don't have proper cover.
The maps are very small . Actually , they are smaller than Nuketown in Call of Duty . No need for more words here
Yes , you will be swarmed in little ads with weapons or clothing that doesn't do anything . These items will continue to appear on the screen until you buy them . And the worst part ? You will struggle to kill and kill and kill for money , money , money , and when you have enough money to buy another ♥♥♥♥♥♥ item with all the stats 2 , you will rage and throw your PC out the window when you will notice that it will only be available for one week . Of course , until you buy a Premium account that will cost extra money ( real money )
Overall , i DO NOT recommend this game. Don't let the screenshots and trailers fool you. It's not worth it. It will never be , because this is what the corporations do to the developers: They make them create unfinished games like this one

Gone Home is an unconventional story exploration adventure game
The story takes place in 1995. You play as Kaitlin, a student returning home from world travels to see her family, but nobody is at home. You walk around your empty home, in first-person exploration style and you have to find objects that uncover bits of your family's past.
The actual gameplay consists mainly of exploring an environment and checking out every item available. The game is also very short, it can be finished under 3 hours.
The graphics are not the greatest, though they get the job done.
Gone Home takes place in 1995 and the sound reflects that. Strewn around the house are cassettes with typical mid-nineties rock on them. Taking into account the main topic of the game, the selected song are very appropriate. There are also some ambient tunes which are there to highlight certain events and plot points. A nicely done effect is that the ever present thunderstorm raging on outside constantly accompanies the game's protagonist throughout the house, sounding louder or softer depending on her location. Gone Home also features some good voice acting.
I can not recommend Gone Home, the story is not interesting, it is too short and it is also boring. The sound is the only enjoyable thing in the game.
If you are searching for good story exploration games, you should take a look at Dear Esther or The Stanley Parable.

Gone Home is a rare title that transcends gaming into territory that is meaningful and heartfelt. There is no action, no flashy set pieces, little puzzle solving, and no level up system. The entire game consists of a simple premise that asks the player to simply explore and solve a mystery by moving at their own pace. When the game starts, it uses some mystery cliches to lead the player into thinking the story is heading into one direction while heading in a completely different direction when the true nature of the story unfolds. The more you explore, the more the story is unveiled to the player. By the game's end, I was presented with a very personal, thought-provoking narrative that accomplishes what many games do not -- actually making me feel something. This is a very short, but memorable game that actually uses objects within the environment to hook you in and make you care about what is happening. I played through the whole thing in one sitting and refused to stop until I got answers. Highly recommended.

Bonus points awarded for those who recycle all the pop cans!

The game is amazing. The amount of thought and care the developers put into this game is admirable. They have a weekly blog where they communicate with fans, and are a breath of fresh air when it comes to video game dev's. Since I started playing the game has gone through many changes, most recently the Horrors of War expansion pack, which nearly doubled the amount of content in the game for  no cost at all.
Gameplay:
The game works by having 2 teams of 16, separated into 4 squads of 4. Each squad member has a specific role and a choice of 3 loadouts that contour to those roles with a unique type of offmap support for each of the NCOs to use.. There are a few kinds of Squads as well: Theres the basic infantry squad consisting of an NCO, Marksman, Machinegunner and Grenadier. These squads are the British Tommies, French Poilus, American Doughboys, and German Lansers. Theres also Raider squads, Reconnaissance squads, Heavy Defending squads and Specialist squads. The Raiders are the Canadians and Stosstruppen who use Gas attacks, Recons are the French Chausseurs Alpin and the German Alpenjaeger who use Air support. Defending squads are the Belgians and german Schutze who use precision heavy mortars. the Specialists are the USMC who use 30-06 French Chauchats and the M1897 Trench Gun, and the German Pioneers who use the Flamethrower and both call in Smokescreens and White Phosphorous attacks.
Game modes:
the Frontlines gamemode where the above mentioned set up is in play, and each team starts either defending a trenchline or going over the top to the enemy  trench line and the objective is to take or hold the trench, and if captured to defend against counter attacks.
Rifle Deathmatch is a free for all mode where you choose a rifle and attachments and just play free for all.
Attrition is a TDM that uses the squad system.
And squad Coop  is when you enlist in a pals battalion with you and your friends and hold a trenchline against waves of attackers.
I could go on even more than already on this game. I highly reccommend it especially for history buffs. The game definitely deserves 10/10

Gone Home is a more of an interactive story than a game. Similar to A Stanley Parable and Dear Esther, it is demonstrating that a game can be used as a way to tell a story and nothing more.
In this case, the game doesn't deserve a lengthy review, and if anyone is looking for a game in this genre, then the two games mentioned above, would be the best ones to play.
The environment is very well done, and you really feel a connection with the characters due to all the little details scattered around, but the entire time you're expecting something big, or you feel like you're getting closer to where the story really starts, or the climax, but instead the story ends before anything really starts.
It felt more like a concept/prototype and is definitely not worth the full purchase price. At maybe $5, it may be worth your time, but even then there are 1000s of indie titles that you haven't played yet, I'm sure.

You spawn in the middle of a rough, dirt-covered trench, with the sound of distant artillery and shots.
The whistle blows and you climb over the top and charge for your life at the direction of the machine gun's rattle; through puddles, barbed wire and your dead friends.
You jump in a shell hole a few metres from the enemy trench, you are so close that you can hear their voices so you pop your head out to see.
You are quickly reminded to get down by sand and rocks that have splashed in your face from the bullet that hit the earth just in front of your nose.
You get a grenade and chuck it over, then you wait... and jump over as soon as the scream of the dying enemy reaches your ears.
You suddenly feel very lonely as you realise that you are the only one that has managed to make it this far, and out of nowhere a gas shell explodes and you rush to get your gas mask.
Through the mist you find that there is an enemy right in front of you, ready to pull the trigger of his long rifle.
You stab through his throat with your bayonet and carry on.
As you pass the corner you hear a bullet going into your chest as you look into the eyes of another enemy soldier.
You soon respawn and do the same again, and again, and again.
Most thrilling shooter ever.

A defining game in the interactive adventure genre that pushes it forward to new heights. With an incredible attention to detail, engrossing story, and approriate length; this game captures you and doesn't let go until its wrung out every last bit of emotion. The narrative is grounded, yet potent and realizes itself like a puzzle, a method of storytelling that truly captures the spirit of the medium, despite an apparent lack of gameplay investment.
The game does become steadily more linear as you progress, but that does not make the journey of finishing the puzzle any less fufilling and is only a source of encouragement to find where those last few pieces fit. This is not a game for those looking for involved gameplay or the kind of storytelling you expect from a movie or triple A title.
Best of all, the story doesn't fall prey to storytelling tropes or the worn out conventions that have plagued the industry in recent years. Gone Home isn't perfect, but it's a unique experience that everyone should at least be aware of.

Absolutely love this game.  I have played many FPS games, but this one is definitely unique.  As far as I know this is the only fully fledged WW1 first person shooter.  I have played the WW1 mod for BF1942 which was great, but nothing like this.    Verdun does remind me of Red Orchestra, but I actually enjoy this game more.  I have recently become more interested in everything WWI thanks to a podcast I listen to called Hardcore History by Dan Carlan.  So a couple months back I looked to see if there was a good WWI game that would represent the war well.  This game certainly does.  The trench warfare mode is fantastic and really replicates the fierce battles that those men had to endure.  The mechanics of the game are great.  There is a slight bullet drop, but nothing too noticeable. It is really more realistic than the bullet drop you would experience in Battlefield Bad Company 2.  The maps are fantastic and replicate the uniqueness of the war.  I hope that someday the battles will be increased to 48 or 64 players.  Problem is the server populations are pretty small right now.  Hopefully with the official release of the game more people will play.  This game is pretty difficult.  You will not be able to run and gun like you can in Call of Duty.  If you play Red Orchestra or Battlefield you may be able to not mind the long wait period to respawn.  Successfully capturing a trench will require patience and teamwork. Critics contend 'Gone Home' isn't actually a game, but rather a poorly-written, angst-ridden, glorified walking simulator shamelessly pandering to third-wave feminists. Suffice it to say, these critics are indeed correct―overwhelmingly so.
Ignoring common sense and logic, I purchased this game in the offshoot chance that I’d experience, at the very least, a reverberation of emotion.
(Spoilers ahead.)
The player controls Kaitlin 'Katie' Greenbriar, who incidentally returns from her overseas trip in Amsterdam to an abandoned château in rural Oregon. A presumably Methodist household, you are also introduced through various letters and business cards, your parents, Terrence and Janice Greenbriar. Terry is a failed author dabbling in mediocre political thrillers about JFK. He opts instead to write album reviews for a Home Theater aficionado magazine. Jan is a senior conservationist working at the local Forestry service. Her dedication to her career leads to estrangement from her family, leading her and Terry to leave that week for counseling.
Katie also has a younger sister, Samantha, a fiery, sharp-tongued teenage writer who sends you on an 'adventure' to see where she’s inexplicably waddled off to. Wonderful.
What follows is a menial tour of a well-designed dollhouse. Expect opening and closing doors, turning on lamps and other fixtures, searching over and under floorboards in an attempt to discover― a plot. Immersion is a touted feature by many reviewers, but not once have I felt immersed in the nostalgia-filled world of '95. All the proclivities and details in these rooms are offset by their distractingly mindboggling placements. (Tell me, who in their right mind would leave private letters randomly scattered all around their house?)
The plot revolves around your sister and her acceptance of being hopelessly in love with Lonnie, an army brat and oddly enough, a rebellious punk rocker. They go to costume parties and riot grrl concerts, dye their hair, and protest patriarchy in all forms. Eventually, they kiss and thus sets the stage for their ill-fated Shakespearean tragedy. This not-so-subtle progression of sappy lesbian love is doled out over a painful length of an hour and a half.
Then the game just ends. Lonnie elopes with Sam, abandoning her duties as a servicewoman and wanders listlessly throughout the New English coast. A misplaced hodgepodge of saccharine, sentimentalist music swells over the credits to provide a supposed, illusionary feeling of a heartfelt and revelatory experience.
If you’re going to make a narrative-driven 'game' about the characters, make sure we actually get to know them first. Not through what we’re told about them, but through actual experiences that the character, as well as you and I, experience. Real emotional connections are possible in games, but not through the use of force or tedium. This trend of masturbatory, preachy kitsch (Dear Esther, BioShock Infinite, Dream) should be quickly stamped out and be replaced with games of genuine heart and depth. Don't give these hacks your hard-earned money.

Want to see your assumptions and expectations of a game subverted right before your very eyes? Do you want to experience a shimmering beacon of hope when it comes to storytelling in video games? Get this. It's a ~3 hour experience, give or take, but that entire 3 hours is... Just simply incredible.

You spawn in the middle of a rough, dirt-covered trench, with the sound of distant artillery and shots.
The whistle blows and you climb over the top and charge for your life at the direction of the machine gun's rattle; through puddles, barbed wire and your dead friends.
You jump in a shell hole a few metres from the enemy trench, you are so close that you can hear their voices so you pop your head out to see.
You are quickly reminded to get down by sand and rocks that have splashed in your face from the bullet that hit the earth just in front of your nose.
You get a grenade and chuck it over, then you wait... and jump over as soon as the scream of the dying enemy reaches your ears.
You suddenly feel very lonely as you realise that you are the only one that has managed to make it this far, and out of nowhere a gas shell explodes and you rush to get your gas mask.
Through the mist you find that there is an enemy right in front of you, ready to pull the trigger of his long rifle.
You stab through his throat with your bayonet and carry on.
As you pass the corner you hear a bullet going into your chest as you look into the eyes of another enemy soldier.
You soon respawn and do the same again, and again, and again.
Most thrilling shooter ever.

I have recently become more interested in everything WWI thanks to a podcast I listen to called Hardcore History by Dan Carlan.  So a couple months back I looked to see if there was a good WWI game that would represent the war well.  This game certainly does.  The trench warfare mode is fantastic and really replicates the fierce battles that those men had to endure.  The mechanics of the game are great.  There is a slight bullet drop, but nothing too noticeable. It is really more realistic than the bullet drop you would experience in Battlefield Bad Company 2.  The maps are fantastic and replicate the uniqueness of the war.  I hope that someday the battles will be increased to 48 or 64 players.  Problem is the server populations are pretty small right now.  Hopefully with the official release of the game more people will play.  This game is pretty difficult.  You will not be able to run and gun like you can in Call of Duty.  If you play Red Orchestra or Battlefield you may be able to not mind the long wait period to respawn.  Successfully capturing a trench will require patience and teamwork.  Gas and artillery strikes will be essential to pull this off in most battles, but this adds to the fun for me.  Highly recommend this game.

It's hard for me to recommend this game, because it entirely depends on your taste. Do you enjoy mediocre indie bands from Portland? Do you like to have your story spoon-fed to you in a conveniently laid-out trail? What are your thoughts on being entirely and unnecessarily spooked out for 2 hours? Do you get off on being more pretentious than your friends? Or do you simply need a quick go-to example when someone questions your progressiveness? Then this may be the game for you!
That being said, I did actually enjoy the experience of stepping into someone else's mundane shoes for a while and exploring a beautifully crafted and detailed space. It's clear a lot of hard work and love went into this project, The story was so-so, but heartfelt, and despite its practically linear spoon-fed layout, it still managed to keep my interest for the two or so hours it took me to complete the game. I wanted to find out more about my virtual home and family. It really wasn't all that bad, in fact.
If you want an interactive experience that's a little different from the norm, and you've already played The Stanley Parable, and Gone Home happens to be on sale for less than the price of a matinee movie ticket, you could do a lot worse.

Touching.

The newer people will be impatient or naive, and crawl along on the dirt thinking they are hidden or charge gloriously with their comrades, only to be machine gunned down.
After that, you'll will get a feel for the battle, seeing the shadows of enemy movements in enemy trenches, watching out for the flash of a rifle, knowing that the bullet sound that sounded a little 'too close' was indeed too close and that you should start crawling down for a different approach. Survival is important, leave forlorn hope to those who want it, you want to live right?
And then whatever idea of self preservation will be thrown out a window
Your brothers in arms will start to swarm in, the enemy line reduced, dying by dozens trying to take one tiny foothold in the trenches. You'll see a teamate charge next to you and get sniped, and still, you'll get up and charge in, praying that the next bullet doesn't hit you. Because that trench has to be captured, even if you know it'll be hell. You'll hear the explosion roaring around you. You might see it happen in front of you, killing your squadmates.
Bodies will be sprawled across the trenches, move cautiously to clear it out, The moment you take the trench, there is no reprive, only onslaughts of mortars and toxic gas, you can't see anything, you can't tell friend from ally. Shoot shots blindly into the gas, you could've sworn you saw something moving.
Reload- no, he's in front of you now, charge him! Stab him!
Hold the trench, you move next to an ally, popping shots at the krauts or tommies that are charging to quickly retake your position. Then a small clink, a bounce at your feet, and a spring in your foot would be an understatement of what happens to you and your friend.
If you allow yourself the experience, you will receive it, every charge through no man's land, every euphoria of a shot knowing the enemy never knew what hit him, protecting your CO, even above your own life. Every moment of the WWI experience is here in Verdun, it is breath taking and glorious.

I got the game on sale for $6.79.   I have played the game for two and a half hours, although I believe half of that hour was idle while I was chowing down on some delicious ham.   I will tell you this...if I paid 20 bucks for it, I'd probably be upset.  Being that it was under 10, I was more than entertained.  It was fantastic.
The premise is that you are a girl that returns to a large, spooky home after an overseas trip where you studied abroad.  No one is home.  It's a dark and stormy night. You hear cracks of thunder.  Occasionally a lightbulb might go out on you. And you are aaaaaall alone.  Except for bits and pieces of journey entries you get from your sister Susan who is voice acted.
There are rumors that the house is haunted.  And so the premise builds that something wrong happened to your family.
But did it?
And that's the whole gist of the story.  You playing inspector detector to try to gain insight on what happened while you were gone. Oh and it takes place in the 90s.  Which oddly enough...I grew up in the 90s so I remembered a crap ton of the references.
This game is not a Slender Man game. You're not running around with your heart pounding afraid of what might jump and gobble you up from behind. It's a story about discovery and understanding. It tugs on the emotional heart strings.  It's not going to be a game for everyone.  But it's fascinating in that it focuses on story and that is literally all there is.  And a few minor puzzles.
Game gets my two thumbs up for making me feel something and entertaining me.

I've done enough hours to now provide an honest review. In a nutshell -well worth the money even though it's currently in Beta. There is a small developer team that are active and constantly improving  the gameplay. The community in this game is supportive and constructive as a whole. Having come directly from Rising Storm / Heroes of Stalingrad there are similarities; differences are evident in the weapon dynamics,hit location, movement and tactics. There are no tanks to help  storm through defences , disrupt and draw enemy fire. Verdun is a meat grinder where every trench held or taken is often paid for in lives.
The battlefield terrain for each map is well researched, each map is a challenge in it's own right. The graphics now are more detailed especially in ultra settings. Rag doll physics lead to some interesting positions for the dead. Animations will likely need to be improved especially those poor devils hit by artillery. Currently they fly through the air intact.
Each match is a battle of frontal assault in attack and defence with high casualty figures reaped from the attackers due to the channelling effect of wire, small arms, grenades,machine guns, artillery and gas.
Weapons are deadly in their own right and it is easy to see why the Mauser and .303 SMLE were retained and improved. As you progress in the game in points you get weapon and ability unlocks according to the role you choose in each team you join. There are some very good players in the game and these may tend to pack together as team unlocks are much faster. Beginners can level these masters with one shot, team dynamics, positioning  and player ability are the deciders in both holding and taking trenches.
The question is can you survive the fire get through  and make a breach in the defence? Once you are in the enemy trench start to clear it - exploit the enemy backs with your trusty weapon bayonet / melee weapon team while they face and shoot your side. Reducing the firepower at your team. As a defender can you drive the enemy away within your field of fire, do you need to move and protect another section of trench? All the while remaining situationally aware of a potential enemy invading your trench.
In game smoke shells or poison gas plays a deadly role in masking both attackers and defenders adding to the claustrophobic condition of the trench interiors and no mans land where you must adjust to the fighting in a gas mask.There are some very good players in the game and these may tend to pack together as team unlocks are much faster.
Achievement hunters and badge collectors will get plenty of mileage from the game. So far no hackers detected apart from a bug glitch / exploit that has now been corrected.
My experience of game server activity when I have been on - the US  is by far the most active; Australian / Asia Pacific servers improve in the afternoons and Europe is fairly quiet due to the time difference (gamers are sleeping). I can say you will always get a game with the ping issues not too bad. Personally I have always done well either with low or high ping when the end game scores come in.
Look forward to seeing you in game.

Being a dude who likes to play games that push the medium as a form of art,  I decided I would give this incredibly hyped game a chance. Hearing folks I  really respect such as Adam Sessler gush over how amazing it was, I had high hopes.
Boy was I disappointed.
This "amazingly written storyline" is an ever so slight tweak of the old "forbidden teen love" story that has been told for hundreds of years, and has been told much better too. Now, the subplot surrounding the parent's lives were more interesting, but not too much better, and not as fleshed out as the main story. So, yeah, story doesn't meet the hype.
Graphics were pretty good. I'm starting to see more Unity based games really explore what all the engine can do.
The sound design and overall atmosphere was definitely my favorite part of the game. Now, I might have a problem with some of the decisions on how certain sights and sounds were played out (in relation to the story), but the lighting and environmental sounds (especially while wearing headphones) made the experience  pretty engrossing.
Overall, I’d say I wouldn’t recommend anyone buy this game, unless they really want to see what everyone has been talking about. And if you decide you want to buy it, PLEASE wait for a sale. This game is in no way worth $20.
And one last bit of advice to those about to play: forget what everyone has said about it, and just try to play the game without outside influences coloring your experience.
(PS. The Linux port is good, as most Unity games are.)

If you're unfamiliar with the gameplay of Counter-Strike, it's a round-based team elimination first-person shooter with slightly asymetrical objectives.  The most common mode has the terrorists trying to plant a bomb, and the counter-terrorists trying to defuse it if that happens.  Another popular mode requires the counter-terrorists to rescue hostages that the terrorists are guarding.  Frequently, the two teams will simply fight each other until only one is left standing.  There's an in-game money system that allows you to buy better equipment if you survive and do well, but many servers give free money at the start; this allows everyone to pick whatever guns they want.
Why choose Source instead of Global Offensive?  Well, as new generations of gamers have moved on to CS:GO or Call of Duty, CS:S has retained a generally more adult crowd and relaxed atmosphere.  It's like hanging out in a pub after work, except you're all shooting at each other.  Another advantage of playing a game that was top-of-the-line 9 years ago is that it still looks alright today, but it will run buttery smooth on just about any hardware.

Alright, so it's time to review this highly critically acclaimed game. First of all I'm gonna say that I would probably neither give the game a thumbs up or a thumbs down but more like something in between. Since I can't do that it's gonna be a thumbs up. Im gonna give the game props for telling a sweet little love story that hits close to home, without the use of cutscenes or dialogue but through interaction with the environment. The kind of metamorphosis between gameplay and narrative that I really would like to see in more games - You can tell the inspiration these guys took from BioShock after they left 2KGames. The detail put into the game; The 90s pop cultural references to famous rock bands, tv shows, movies and books alike did well for the immersion. I'm a big fan of games like Gone Home that encourages exploration in order to provide further exposition to the overarching plot. There are so many items you can interact with in the environment and visually it looks beautiful. This is what I'd like to see in more adventures games, and horror games, alike. Bigger emphasis on exploration and interaction with the environment that made up for the game's rather short length, which ended up being almost 5 hours of game time for me. This is what drags the game down for me. It was incredibly short for an adventure game, but the developing team was small in size, nontheless, and it felt more like an experiment for something greater - Because Gone Home could be so much more! The exploration is pretty much all there is to this game, combined with the short length, it's not worth the high price it originally was set to before it went on sale. I ended up paying only 6 euros, which was fair enough for me. It was 6 euros worth my time. I hope to see more from these guys in the future.

Verdun is Amazing Upcoming Trench Warfare game. It is game that any Gamer who enjoys Classic World War 1 game must obtain! It feels like a Classic WW1 shooter right off the bat, Reminding me of Call of Duty 1 and Medal of Honor Allied assault with the Different Squads based on real squads from the Verdun war.  The game runs on the Beautiful Unity 2 engine which is used for Cross-Platform gaming and also features the ability to play on Mac and Linux! The Graphics are stellar and I extremely enjoy it since I've been waiting for a Next-Gen World War 1 game for years now.  There is a basic System unlock tier for all weapons and different types of attachments. The controls simple and easy to play with, It's just like any other FPS game.  The server system is very unique, Where you select a gametype on a Big Board and then select a Map to play on as opposed to a specific server, making it much easier to play with Friends. My favorite part of any FPS game is a statistics counter, Which Verdun has! It keeps track of all your kills, Melees, Deaths, Stats for specific gamemodes etc. It even has achievements and medalss within it!  Verdun is absolutely a must have for the current price of $22.99. M2H and BlackMill games are hard at work developing it and making it better with each passing day!

While immersive, coupled with wonderful voice acting and an ominious atmosphere driven to lure the player into questioning as to whether the game will deviate into the survival horror realm, it falls short in providing a satisfying storyline. Throughout the game, the story builds at a good pace but ends prematurely, which left me thinking, "Wait, that's it?" The main plot was predictable, but the voice acting compensated for its lack of a surprise element and kept me engaged. I just felt that the developers had ample opportunity to create a more interesting and original storyline on par with the detailed, interactive elements placed around the house; they could have delved further into the sub-plots surrounding the family and their issues, which I found very intriguing, and tied it in better with the main story. However, lots of the items around the house did not contribute to the story line or any puzzle elements (not that the game truly had any at all, anyways) whatsover, and seemed to be there only to keep the player clicking longer (e.g., shot glasses, soda cans, toothpaste).
In conclusion, the game is filled with potential but ultimately fails to reach it. For a price of $20, it is not worth the purchase whatsoever. Only consider purchasing on sale, but even the price there seems steep at $6-$10 for only an hour or two of gameplay with a highly cliched storyline with no replay value. However, if you're big on ambience, it is well worth it. Even though description stated that the gameplay is non-violent, there were numerous times where I felt extremely on edge or tense from the thunder, creaks, lighting, and darkness after finding several items in the game that seemed to suggest horror elements.

Gone Home is another one of those videogames-as-an-art form projects which promises to deliver a unique experience to the player. The concept of this game ticks all the right boxes. You are returning from a year long trip to find the house seemingly empty and leaving you as the player free to investigate and interact as you solve the mystery at your own pace.
From here, the game fails in practically every way. The atmosphere is completely at odds with the story the game ends up telling. Interaction with the environment is extremely basic considering it is such a integral part of the game. The house itself is utterly generic; it could easily be house #103 you walk through on the way to the next level in any other game.
The games only strong point is the story is the one it does end up telling. The strongly narrated monologue that plays when you find the next piece of the puzzle keeps you playing till the end. This story will better resonate with some players and give these players a much richer experience.
For me, this is a game of failed promises. This game tells a strong story but, with the atmosphere the game creates; it may be the wrong one.

Gone Home seems like a propaganda piece for LGBT.  It's a cleverly wrapped package, complete with a compelling mystery and a highly interactive world.  A lot of attention to detail went into this, but I can't get past the message, which is to make a seemingly innocent "love" story into something natural and normal, when it's not.  It's a shame that the game only has one recurring theme.  The game world had potential for so much more... and without the unnecessary LGBT message.  The game can be completed in an hour or so, if you take your time and check out everything in every room.  Really, it's not a game, but an interactive story telling.  Even though the interface and design is perfect, as is the execution, I can't recommend this to anyone because it goes against my moral convictions and what I believe to be the natural order of things.

Verdun, just like WW 1, welcomes you to the great stalemate.
If you start off on defense, be ready. It will not be long until you see waves of enemies coming right at you, sprinting like mad while you try your best to lead them, call down mortars or gas, or lob grenades accurately. All the while, for every enemy soldier you see, you know deep down that there are three you don't. Where are they? Do THEY see YOU? Do you risk popping your head up to blow the pulp out of an enemy, unsure whether or not your enemy is waiting the blow the pulp out of you? Do you go out to the juts and extensions out of your trench; you will see the enemy better, but those juts out are fire magnets, is it truly worth it? Either way, you cannot stop them all. Enemy officers WILL call down artillery and gas, soldiers will hide or kill defenders fast enough, and soon you will begin to see them sweep down your trench like a raging river. Trenches become hallways of death; officers ordar shells dropped on their own lines while rienforcements from both sides pile in and add to the body count. Grenadiers go wild and the rifleman quickly falls to the pistoleer...usually.
When the time comes to attack, things are just as bleak. Though the surge of the charge and the squeal of the officer's whistle flow through your blood like fire, the splendor soon wears off as you begin to see--and hear--your comrades slump over, dead. Those craters only seem inviting until you see another of your soldiers die before your eyes; do you risk it and run like hell through the crater in search of better hiding spots, or do you stay where you are and hope you're not next? Some stay back to try and offer aid; officers call down arty and gas in a pathetic attempt to clear an opening. One will be found, but how many must die first? Now comes the truly hard part: holding the trench. No easy task as grenades are thrown out like candy at a holiday parade. Was that "clatter-clatter" a friendly grenade? Worry still, as enemy mortars drop right on top of you as  they pound their own trench with reckless abandon. Machine gunners charge down the trenches in both directions spraying fire they cannot control, and quite frankly do not need to.
The winners are the ones who lost slightly fewer soldiers.

I went home not knowing what to expect, at all, I just read reviews online (not steam reviews) and heard it was up for GOTY so thought i'd give it a go in the steam sale. I just knew it was a 1st person exploration game in a house.
It throws a lot of things at you, the game really plays with your expectations, which could be frustrating to some players I guess, I mean, there are a lot of things available to explore, you're not sure what to make of the situation. But quickly it becomes apparent this is a very personal story about the members of the household, and it was to me anyway very touching. I may not be anything like the caracters at all, but that doesn't stop from relating to them and wanting to know all the details, the fact it is set in the mid 90s probably helped too. The sound design is fantastic, both the voicework and the noises in the house create a totally believable world.
It's a short experience (barely 2 hours), but the fact this story is told through a game enhances it. Sure, you could write the story in a couple of lines if you want, but here you find all the pieces of the puzzle yourself, you really feel for the characters as you walk through the house and go through their stuff. So if you're open to a different sort of game, go on ahead. I can understand that the full price tag is probably not worth it for a lot of people because of all this, but on a 66% or higher discout, you can't go wrong. So go ahead, it's an important game that deserves some recognition for daring something different and telling a story you don't usually see in this media. It may be short, but it left a real lasting impression, one i'll remember more than most games I can think of.

Gone Home... Either you like it, or you don't - I liked it. Gone Home is not long (about 2 hours in my case), not complex and is only playable once, since the story is always the same. The regular price is definitely too much, even with 66% of (Steam Sale) the cost-benefit ratio is still pretty bad. As much as I liked the game, I still wouldn't buy it for 19€ (the regular price), that's not worth it in my opinion. But let's get into the game:  I didn't know what to expect before buying it: "Does it have difficult puzzles to solve? Does it have elements of a horror game?..." - there are many questions you might ask yourselves before and also while playing. The atmosphere is absolutely great. It's dark, you hear rain and thunder outside, flickering lights in the house, sounds from above... the game gives you the feeling that every minute there could be a sudden screamer. The knowledge (you will soon get) that the house your family owns and you are currently walking through is known as the "Psycho house" doesn't exactly ease these fears, nor do the secret passages behind walls (in which you can find such things as a crucifix) or the books and reports of your sister about ghosts and other supernatural beings.
While walking through the house, you find out many things about your family, especially by reading documents and letters that are lying around. However, the career and life of your mother and father are only "told" as a side note. The game focuses on the story of your sister Sam(antha): Goint to a new school, not having any friends in the beginning, getting to know and love Lonnie (who is a girl as well)... I don't want to take it any further since I would spoil the story. Everytime you find and important note about Sam (and Lonnie) you hear short diary entries by Sam (amazing voice acting!) that tell you about all the important things. The further you play the game, you better you get to know everybody, including yourself, Katie. After the story of Sam continues and takes a turn for the worse, you, intensified by the atmosphere of the house and Sam's personal feelings, expect the worst. "Did Sam kill herself? Did she do something stupid?" - The game wants you to think so. I don't want to tell too much, but I can tell you this much: The story (including the end) is not the usual story you'd expect, at some parts of the game, it even makes fun of the repetitive stories of many games.
"Gone Home" is an experience. If you need action, this is not for you. But if you like games that focus on a good story and a interesting and good way to tell them, not action etc., you should definitely consider buying "Gone Home".

Gone Home is built upon quite an amazing, emersive and incredibly atmospherical environment.  Although it only took me the best of 63 minutes to finish, I would confidently say that those 63 minutes may rank among the greatest and most fun hour of gaming moments of my entire gaming life.  "Return from a holiday to find that no one is home".  Gone Home's story plot may sound like the most simple of any game to be released yet, however upon digging deeper into the game you will realise that this is not the case.  Such a basic and simple idea may sound fit for more of a horror or murder mystery novel, but Gone Home is quite the opposite.  I felt on edge the whole way through, expecting a jumpscare or shadowy figure to be looming at the end of the hallway which I was entering, and each time this didn't happen I only felt more on edge.  The developers have gone to an incredible effort to create the most detailed and rememorable setting for a story telling game which I have ever seen.  This setting will no doubt stick with me for weeks to come, and I have the feeling I may even revisit the Gone Home universe, if nothing more than to try uncover more of the games fantastic little secrets.  Follow the protagonist, Katie, as she returns home from a trip around Europe to discover that no one is home, and help her find the secrets that lead up to an unexpected conclusion, uncovering many of the house's secrets along the way.
I would highly recommend Gone Home to puzzle fanatics and story telling fans alike.  It was a fabulous experience and I would love to see and would eagerly buy a follow up game.
9.5/10 for story depth, plot, environment and setting
3/10 for value for money
Easily a 8/10 for overall enjoyability, however I would not recommend paying more than the Steam Sale's $6.

The game is doing well, I definetely recommend this. It does the Trench warfare of WW1 really well.
What the game has -
- A really realistic frontlines mode where you have to push in waves to the enemies last trench. Its really fun as you think your winning and then they manage to push you all the way back as if nothing had happened.
- Really cool maps
- Great squad system (your in squads of 4 and each have an individual class with their own weapons and abilities e.g. Corporals lead the squad and call in mortar strikes, Riflemen push into the trenches, Machine gunners offer support the advance and kill enemies whilst on the defensive, and well, depending on the nation there are multiple 4th classes like grenadiers)
- Great weapons that are historically accurate.
What it doesnt have-
-It needs more maps, although the current ones are good, after a while, they get repetative
- It needs the option to be artillery and fire from behind the trenches to support your guys at the front (We get mortar strikes but we dont actually play as the morter guys, it would be reaqlly cool if we could)
- It needs more gamemodes. There are only two which are frontlines and rifle deathmatch. We need something else.
-It would be cool if we got a little character creation. I dont expect much but at least allow us to change our face.
- It needs gore. WW1 was a gory war.
What needs fixing.-
-There arent animatioons for climbing ladders or climbing in/out of craters (In general we need more animations and make them good - ill explain more in my next point)
-The death animations are awkward (Its poorly designed ragdoll and like I said before, add GORE!)
Now the game is early access and so THERE WILL BE BUGS, dont rage when your like "Oh the games a buggy mess". For one its not that buggy for two, its early access, EXPECT BUGS.
Overall, its a great game and worth the price, I cant wait until we get the full release :D

I love playing Verdun.  It's frenetic, in your face, brutal, compelling, sounds amazing and genuinely makes me feel like my♥♥♥♥♥is on the line..  I'm a long time Battlefield 1942 / Vietnam player with the occasional Modern Warfare mod from years ago.. years of early Counter Strike AWP'ing around..  I played Battlefield 4 multiplayer very briefly and went back to Battlefield P4F - Call of Duty Advanced Warfare got all of 45 minutes before I said 'what is this cr*p' and went back to finding something interesting which is where I came across Chivalry Medieval Warfare and thoroughly enjoyed the 'oh.. he's going to hurt me' gritty close range fighting but always felt it a bit cliched, with Verdun it's got the intensity of Chivalry without the moment to look each other over.. if you stare into someones eyes in Verdun one of you is going to die and that happens a lot.
The maps?  Glorious.. some are wide and expansive rolling fields of carnage, some are watery graves of face crawling, all with layer upon layer of attack and riposte.
My only frustration is people seem to not acknowledge the game for what it is - a rolling to and fro of attack and defence - this means as the attack phase timer ticks down, 5 or 10 team mates will be laying prone, meters from the enemy trench seemingly frozen in space and time..  if the timer ticks out and you haven't got the trench, you loose your attack wave (and eventually the game)..  the historical trauma of WWI was the obscene body count due to hurling massive numbers against each other ..  as this is a WWI game, sitting on your♥♥♥♥♥meters from the objective does nothing except frustrate your team mates and amuse your enemy.  Get with the program - Take the trenches (and die trying).
It might be a worthwhile feature to have a 'ground covered / advanced' counter so everyone could see who was covering the most forward ground and potentially, that NCO's could execute those who refuse to attack.  You want to hide in a trench and not go forward when the whistle blows?  Bullet for you buddy.

Verdun is unlike anyother FPS in the market. Some buzzwords I like to use are "unforgiving, squad based, trench warfare, 1 shot 1 kill, slow-paced, rythmic, and back-and-forth".
Unlike MANY other FPS', squad synergy, tactical movement, and map awareness are truly important. There is no 360NOSCOPEMLGPRO nonsense in Verdun.
There are 3 classes of squads, Recon, Rifle, and Assault.  Recon squads are very fast, have high powered rifles, and can reveal enemies across the map. Rifle squads are well rounded, possessing great offensive and defensive abilities. Assault squads specialize in trench clearing, have lots of grenades, and can launch poison gas attacks to cover advances.
All are extremely important to have for each side in each match. Have too many assault squads? You will probably waste valuable time assaulting positions that are too heavily fortified? No recon squads? Good luck knowing where the best sector to attack is.
Each squad contains 4 soldiers, each specializes in a different area. To generalize you have the squad leader, fire support, rifleman, and assault, however depending on which faction you pick, each of these classes are different.
The Entante factions are Canadians (assault), Tommies (rifle), Poilus (rifle), and Chasseurs (recon). For the less educated, thats 1 Canadian, 1 British, and 2 French.
For the Central Powers, the factions are all German. This is very disappointing because I was really hoping to see Austria-Hungary. Hopefully in an update we will see Ottomans, Italians, Americans, Russians and others.
I highly recommend picking up this game if you are willing to experience a steep learning curve and die alot. But if you are not 12 years old and using your parents credit card, be an adult and pick up this game.

Less of a game and more of a story that you play, Gone Home is interesting (and terribly atmospheric) experience. The story is simple and short, you can easily finish it in less than two hours, but when the price is that of owning a movie of the same length (and the movie is wholly less interactive) Gone Home is definitely worth it.
The gameplay, such that it is, is that of adventure games. Open things, turn lights on and off, read scraps of papers and uncover journal entries. You'll encounter a whole bunch of locked doors and things that actually make sense as to how to open it instead of rubbing random items on doors to get them to open.
The thing that is incredibly interesting is the atmosphere. It is 1am, there is a thunderstorm, all the lights are off, no one is home, and there is no sound. What got me was the references to the house as "psycho house" and your sister's obsession with the X-Files (as the numerous recorded tapes testify to) and Ouija boards. The ending was truly heartpounding, for me at least, because my mind was making leaps in logic (because of how games have done in the past): dark empty houses, thunderstorms, creepy basement trap doors, suspected hauntings, I was expecting something truly terrifying. And in the end the free form way you uncover Gone Home's story allows you to, potentially, get that very same dread. Or not. It depends on your experience when you play. Which is all of the fun.

As someone who started out playing alone, and now plays in one of the "competitive" clans (it's a beta, there's only so much we can do, but vet players know who's who), I've had most of the experiences you can have in Verdun.  It starts out difficult, absolutely, and a lot of the bad reviews you see are there for two reasons:
1) They only played a few maps, couldn't get over the learning curve in that amount of time, and quit
2)They forgot it's EARLY ACCESS, yes, it has bugs, it says that in the pop up right when the game starts
Now then, the learning curve can be extremely steep.  Expect to die, and expect to die often.  You will be killed on occasion the moment that you spawn due to spawning on the NCO into enemy fire or unlucky spawns into grenades/mortars/artillery fire/etc.
This game is about playing smart.  Going rambo/gung-ho as you would in CoD/Halo/etc rarely works.  You want to move up, use plentiful covering fire, watching for movement, and don't fire from the same place too many times.  If you stick it out and learn to play, and especially if you can find a good group to play with (feel free to add me, I'm happy to help new folks), then this game can be extremely rewarding.
Updates are fairly frequent, so the devs are hard at work.
It also has the buff of being a rather accurate WW1 game, which we know is uncommon compared to WWII.  So, give it a try, expect to die, and learn the game.  The community is pretty solid for the most part, and we're happy to help new players and answer their questions.
10/10 - Would recommend if you have the patience to handle a learning curve and occasional bugs.

Verdun is a very good game, although it is still in development.
I had been hoping for some years for a World War One game to be made, but did not really expect that one would actually appear, as there seems to be little interest in that period (World War Two gets a far wider coverage); so I was pleasantly surprised when Verdun was released.
It has a great feel to it, with all of the ambience of trench warfare. There are maps for Argonne, Artois, Flanders, and Picardie. Loved that they did a limited Christmas truce scenario in December; let's hope that they repeat that one.
It can be quite hard fighting in some maps. If you have two good teams, games can end in a draw, but it makes for great gameplay.
You have to get used to the bolt-action rifles (most of us being used to the semi-automatic and fully automatic weapons in the games of WW2 and later).
I found directing the mortars a bit hard to get used to, but I guess I will get better with time. I do know that it can be really bad being on the receiving end of a well-placed mortar barrage; it can wipe out your entire squad. But it cuts both ways. As in real life, barrages can be quite useful for clearing out a section of trenches prior to an attack.
You upgrade weapons as you get more experience. Having a rifle with a scope can be a great advantage (I'm not exactly clear on how to get one, but - then again - I haven't really looked into it).
The use of mustard gas adds a different element to the game (not one that I expected, but it gives yet more historical  accuracy). It can be quite hard to fight with a gas mask on (for both sides); it adds another tactical option to a charge. Just don't do as I have done, and take off your mask when you think all the gas has dissipated, as to do so can have fatal consequences.
The only major criticism of the game I have is that it does not have team balancing. I wouldn't be too concerned about a little bit of team imbalance, but I have been in games where one side has had more than double the players of the other side for the entire game (players can switch sides, but often people don't want to leave a winning team).
Now for my "wish list". If the developers brought out a Gallipoli map, that would be great. Something from the Russian front would add a bit of variety, and maybe a map from the often-ignored Italian front as well. Actually, the Battle of Beersheba would be an interesting one too. But, then again, Verdun was on the Western front, so if they did add maps from other theatres, they might have to change the name of the game (although, the name "Verdun" is fine by me, even if they add maps far beyond that area). It would be great to have such maps added. I know that the makers of Verdun can't do everything asked of them; but I'll ask anyway, just in case they agree to follow up on those ideas.
As a final word, all I can say is:
If you have an interest in World War One history, then I would highly recommend this game to you!

This game has a ton of potential.
This a great squad based first-person tactical shooter that punishes you again and again for the decisions you make (and don't). This game is not for the lone wolves out there. You assuredly will die by a K98 or SMLE fire and your corpse will jiggle on the barbed wire.
You will die following your buddies breaching trenches too. A stray bullet whizzes past your comrades into your heart. Your last breath is a 3rd person view of your comrades awkwardly running into the trench avenging your death!  How glorious.
You will die by artillery. You will spawn again in 20 seconds and be killed by artillery. You will be an NCO and call artillery on the enemy positions. You will not kill anyone with your artillery.
Sometimes, though, sometimes you don't die. Sometimes you get the drop on your target. Sometimes your artillery lands and nets 5 kills. Sometimes your charge following your artillery barrage means you caught the enemy by surprise and 5 types of blood wet your bayonet or trench shovel.
The game is just so much fun. Be patient, be cooperative, and press shift to hold your breath for accurate fire!
The real mastery of the game comes in how you play each class. NCOs should stay back and provide themselves as support/safe spawn to keep attacks fresh. Machine gunners should find perfect vantage points and fire down on reinforcements...
Great game.

It's hard to say whether or not I would recommend this game.  I did enjoy playing through it and picking up the story from bits and pieces left here and there.  It was a fairly enjoyable experience, but now that I've played through it (in less than two hours btw) I don't think I'll ever play it again. Toward the end, I was plowing into dark rooms without any fear because I knew there wouldn't be anything to really scare me.
To be fair, I feel that Gone Home does a hell of a good job conveying the story the Fullbright Company wanted to tell.  I hope to see more games like this in the future as long as they capitalize on their strengths and/or give the player more incentive to revisit the game once they've completed it..
Anyway, since its hard to sum up I'll make a pro/con list.
Pro
-Good story with lots of subtext.
-Unique/Fresh Premise.
-Stress Free Gameplay.
-It is fun to piece the story together.
-Easy to immerse self in game world.
Con
-Minimalistic Puzzles.
-Fairly linear.
-Creates a suspenseful atmosphere but doesn't use it.
-Short play time with little incentive to replay.
I guess in the end, my love of storytelling wins out.  If you can pick it up cheap from a Steam sale, get it.

First, I want to address the large quantity of negative reviews this game has received. Most of them seem to have expected the wrong thing from this game. This is not a horror game. This is not a puzzle game. This game is not about making decisions. This game is an experience that has very little "gameplay". This game is actually not a game.
Now, let's talk about what this game does right. The atmosphere is amazing, the attention to detail is incredible. The setting is mid 90's Oregon, and it captures the spirit of the 90's really well.
This game is less of a game, it's more of a story. This is an experience. Your experience is relayed by the belongings and notes strewn throughout the abandoned house. While the story itself is fairly predictable, the manner in which it is conveyed is as engrossing as you let it become.
Personally, the story resonates very strongly with me, with several parallels to my own life present. But as I said earlier, remember that you are getting a short, linear experience and not a game. If you can get this cheaply, it's an experience as worthwhile as you want it to be.

Spoiler free, but in my mind it's best to play through it blind. I'll start by saying Gone Home is a very interesting 'game'. It's a form of interactive narration, more akin to going to see contemporary art. Unlike other kinds of media, video games offer a very unique position of interactivity that can be brought onto any kind of spectrum, like the next level from movies, or from novels - kind of a mix of both. You have the intriguing, thought-provoking movies or books, and then there's the ones aimed at more earthly entertainment. I'm not going to say 'artistic' in this instance because one way or another, every piece of art is, as a friend once said, a commodity, one that can be consumed by others, and one that can be a message or expression of the creator. See, Antichamber.
That said, Gone Home was like visiting a very interesting art museum in the sense that it does amazing work in provoking thoughts and feelings in the player. When you enter the empty, dark house as Katie who had never been into this new place on a stormy night, you're a stranger in a new land - similar to Katie herself. At the same time, unlike Katie you know nothing about her. And yet, as you traverse through the home and piece together pieces of random furniture, goods and notes strewn about in the house belonging to the 4-member family, you get to know who Katie is, who her family is, and who, most importantly, her sister Samantha is as well as the people they're interacting with. By the end, you'll feel like you were 'home'.
That said though, this is still a narrative, despite the exploratory and 'stranger in big expanse' elements that the game exudes. There is a 'linear' path that the players are guided through - almost like an amusement park ride. It's almost like a roller coaster because you go through some of the more important clues and hints in a somewhat organized manner, and each key step where you learn some important thing about Katie's family you feel and think certain things in the way it's carefully laid out, where it'll change by the next key note or letter. Most of these are actually optional, but the way its done is to make it so that you'll go in a roughly defined path the first time you go through it blind.
Overall, by the end, I think I felt that I might be feeling the same as Katie was. I was quite satisfied at the marvellous experience, and the way the entire thing was laid out so expertly for people visiting the mansion. Definitely worth playing.

This game received a lot of love from critics when it came out, initially resulting in an over 90% metascore. Most critics praised it for being unconventional, experimental, emotional and unique. While some gamers agreed, a large part of the user community didn’t seem quite as excited about Gone Home, calling it “boring”, “not even a game”, “too short and still a waste of time” or simply “too expensive for the content you get”. Gone Home apparently is one of those love-it-or-hate-it games.
I’m also having a hard time calling narrative-driven games actual “games”, since there is hardly any gameplay or challenge to be found. All you can do is walk around, click on objects and crouch while you figure out the story. That’s why I also understand people who call it boring, because there is just not much happening on the screen. And yes, it is short; very short. Even searching the whole house and reading every letter and scrap hardly got me two hours of gameplay with a replay value close to zero. So yes, its standard price is way too expensive for the content you get, so I waited until it was on sale. And I didn’t regret the purchase.
At first I just really enjoyed that good old 90s nostalgia which made me immediately miss my own good old times. The overall atmosphere is pretty decent, although it might come along as to horror-y for a game that has absolutely no horror in it. Sometimes it gave me the impression to get jumpscared any minute, which just felt a little out of place for a love story. Since I want my review to be free of spoilers, I won’t give you too many details about the story itself. Let’s just say I found the story wasn’t as original or daring (when it comes to the topic of homosexuality) as some people said it would be. It’s just another love story in my opinion and love stories are not my cup of tea by any means. However, I still found it very touching at some moments. The monologues are very well written and the voice actress reading them with a beautiful voice and the fitting amount of emotion does a fantastic job in helping you imagine how things developed for the characters. Creating such an immersion without much actually happening on screen is something not many games can pull off.
I enjoyed this game a lot and I’ll probably think about it for quite some time, but I still have to say that 20 € is just too much for two hours of gameplay. Gone Home might probably have prevented a lot of the hate it got if the price wasn’t so high in the first place.
So wait until it’s on sale and have a good time if:
-	You enjoy exploring an environment and unwrapping a story
-	You enjoy (love story related) emotions in a story
-	You enjoy reading and listening to monologues in a game
-	You don’t mind the lack of actual gameplay or challenges
-	You don’t mind a game being short

Where to begin?
You will experience the First World War in all its mud and blood soaked glory.  You will be shredded by machine-gun fire from all angles, grenades will fall on your head, and expert marksmen will pick you off just as you go over the top.  If you don't enjoy dying, this probably isn't for you.
Now, if you do enjoy a relatively realistic tactical shooter but also demand some classic rifles, then this is the game for you.  Gewehr 98, Enfield Mk. III, and Lebel 1888 rule the battlefield by delivering death across no man's land.  If you like getting stuck in, then your feldspaten and trench clubs are there to help you batter you enemy at close range.  A variety of classic pistols round out the weapon choices for rapid firepower in the close-quarters of the trenches.
In terms of gameplay, Verdun uses a simple attak/defend model.  One team attacks while the other defends, and the roles switch.  It is so simple, yet so brilliant. It keep the game moving and the players busy.  The map sizes also make sure that the player does not have to walk a mile to the combat zone, but instead spawns in a jumping off trench or a reserve trench close to the action.
The squad based team system, or rather section based since it is only four man teams, allows for specialization of roles ranging from support based Landser and Tommy squads to assault type Stosstruppen and Chasseurs Alpins.  Each squad role is different and they have different unlockable weapons, although all have a common rifle loadout.  Each squad has a different uniform, especially in the early game, so they are easy to tell apart at a distance.  The shako on Alpenjaeger, the feldmutze on the Stosstruppen, and the pickelhaube on the Landsers make it easy to identify which German team is attacking/supporting you.  Kepis and berets distinguish the Poilu from the Chasseur.  Of course, in the late game, everyone wheres a steel helmet so the distinction is not as easy.
The uniforms for me are one of the best features of the game.  All players start the round in the bright and pretty 1914 uniforms, complete with decorative piping and for the French, bright red pants.  As the squad levels up by working together to take objectives and take down enemy units, the uniforms change.  The french change to their characteristic sky blue uniforms and eventually get Adrian helmets.  The British eventually trade in their caps for Brodies while the German pickelhaube gains a field gray cover and loses its spike before being replaced entirely by the stahlhelm.  As a plus, the uniforms seem to get a bit grimy in the later levels.  A really nice touch, even though I am partial to the 1914 uniforms.
The dev team has really put effort into making this game work, even cleaning off some bits to make the gameplay smoother and simpler.  The recent move to the Unity 5 engine has also broguht with it some nice new graphics.  Hit detection has been greatly improved, although there is still some ways to go on it.   Upoming melee fixes should be nice to encourage more melee in the trenches rather than tactical pistol clearing with grenades.
One aspect the devs can not hope to control is the community.  Rarely have I found a community in a game that is friendly, helpful, and polite.  I can happily say that every time I have played Verdun, I have found my allies and opponents all to be quite helpful and friendly.  As a game gains popularity, inevitably the community declines, but hopefully Verdun with its nice little niche community remains the kind and pleasant place on which I can sacrifice hundreds of young soldiers on the battlefields of the Great War.
Forgive my long-winded review, but to sum it all up in a few short sentences would have been difficult.

If you like a good WWI game, don't mind dying, and can be polite when you have 30 deaths and not a single kill, then this is a game for you.

When I see this game, the first thing i think of is potencial. Verdun has been around for awhile now, and it that time has been updated and improved. I played Verdun when it was on google chrome for free, and it was pretty bad. But the new Verdun has gotten so much better!
I've played Verdun for several houres and all the classes and i can say that it works well. There are minor issues in the game, but overall it's a very solid early game. The class dynamics work well, with each being able to counter another. One thing i have to mention is the supression. After playing many games with supression i can clearly say that they nailed supression on the head. It's literly done perfectly.
There are 2 modes currently in the game, TDM and Trench Assult (i think it's called but you get the point). I've never played TDM becuase only brainless zombies would randomly kill people with no purpose. Verdun is a game about WW1 so Trench Assult is definatly the mode to play. In Trench assult, each team takes turns defending and assulting. as a defender you have to protect your trench from wave after wave of silly peasents trying to take your trench. As a assulter, you assult the defenders by throwing your meaty bodies at their guns. It's as simple as that!
Five main classes make up Verdun. There are a few countrys in the game, but they're versions of the classes are generaly the same. There's a Heavy Machinegunner, Sniper, Trench raider/bomber, Squad leader, Riflemen, and submachine gun/running LMg class. These are not the names of the classes as they arent consistent, but i figure you would know by their weapons. Each "class" also has "perks" which can be advantages or disadvantages such as longer reaload or more points when near a squad leader. I wont be going into the classes in this review, but maybe in a guid. All you need to know is that they work togther well. I will mention that squad leaders have a area around them called a NCO zone (or something like that) where you will be given extra points for doing stuff in that area. This creates team work.
This game is a game of moment i like to say. Kinda like Dayz or Arma, but more action. Some times you will spend all of 10 minutes running in the open and getting mowed down. these are the boring and fustrating moments of the game which some times i admit lead to a rage quite, but there are amazing moment to.
There are times where your charging into enemy gun fire, bullits whizzing past you. you look to your left and see your fellow soldier die as mortors explode shaking the earth. When the dust settles you realize that the once large group you bravly charged with, now lies dead behind you. It's moments like this where i silntly giggle to my self, becuase it's soooo cool. Some times you rush into trenches, suppress enemy postations allowing your troops to move in a kill the defenders, and it feels so great doing that.
There are sadly bad moments to. Some maps are so flat between trenches that once you spawn, you can be shot from 200+ yards. Most people tend to stat away from these maps. Besides a single bad map, there are some bugs and annoyinces aswell. The game feels "laggy" even though i manage to stay around 60FPs the game still feels "wibbly woobly" if you know what i mean. People stutter some times and even your own movement doesn't feel right. There is also a audio and graphics bug that i got when i started the game for maybe the first 3 times. People would look metalic, like tin robots. Gun shots would play REALY loud and cut out at times. But this all seemed to go away after I started the game up a bit more.
Overall this game is SO fun. You cannot get moments that happen in this game in any other. I would reccomend you play Verdun as it has passionate developers and such potencial. I have made a video on my impressions of Verdun which you can watch here:
Thanks for reading my review of Verdun. <3

Over the past few years, the narrative value of video games has been explored and expanded upon. No longer just a medium of just action, scifi, and fantasy, video games have evolved to adapt themselves to any genre for storytelling. Dear Esther, Ana, and countless others have paved the way for a new kind of game.
Gone Home takes that endeavor and drives it home. Like a scalpel in the hands of a veteran surgeon, it cuts deep into the player, and leaves a permanent impression. The ambience of the game is magnetic, drawing you in to a world that is not defined by dragons or laser guns, but by the kind of human interaction that defines us as individuals, the kind of interaction that creates a story that does not seek to thrill or shock, but simply to touch the heart.
If you can finish this game without crying, you have no soul.

It's always interesting to see a game that has been so wildly regarded by critic's falling under such divisive opinion by the gaming community.  It's a testament to a game such as this which falls under certain genre criteria but goes its own way in various means of implementation.  Given that and the hype surrounding this title its little wonder that a game such as this will be met with the rumination of some members of the gaming community.  Gone Home is not a typical game in many traditional sense.  Though it takes the form of many familiar staples of the industry.  It flies in the face of these traditional moulds in so many directions that its no wonder it has fallen under the scrutiny of those who don't seem to understand it. Perhaps most pervasive of these complaints is the price tag.  Which is agreeable that given the content of this game 19.99 may be a little high for most. Not really a better way of describing Gone Home than a story exploration game.  The game's like if you took the ambient storytelling of Bioshock and removed the enemies and horror elements.  It's a game of exploration, discovery, and rifling through trash cans to learn about the family history.  It's exploratory storytelling in its purest form, and that's not for everyone.
If it is your thing, Gone Home delivers.  It's legitimately one of the most touching games I've played.  The story itself is a fairly cliche 90s indie movie-type thing, sure, but it's all about the execution.  The loneliness of the setting brings home the loneliness of the characters, and slowly discovering what's going makes the reveal all the better.  I smiled at points and I got a lump in my throat a points, the game does a very strong job of summoning up involvement and emotions.
It's interactive storytelling that actually uses interaction to its advantage, and you should play it if that's up your alley.  Play it now.

Definatly worth playing. Definatly not worth the price (unless its like two or three bucks).

I want to like this game. I mean, I really do. I love Dear Esther, it's probably one of my favorite games, and it often comes under fire for not being a game. So, this isn't one of those, "Isn't actually a game, sucks because of this!" reviews. I truly believe that a strong narrative can hold up a game that lacks what we've come to expect in games. However, for this to work, the narrative has to  be built upon the fact that it is a game, not just being a strong narrative. The reason Dear Esther is one of my favorite games is because it uses a mechanic that only games can do to finish it's story. This game... does not. This game could have easily been a movie, novel, shorty story or it's best incarnation would have been graphic novel... However, this isn't even why I truly don't like it. I could have given it a pass were it truly an amazing story, as gaming often lacks these. This story was bland in my eyes. Before you go "Gay Hate!," I feel that by saying this story is good just because it has a lesbian love story is what's wrong with our approach. Imagine this story being re-told but with a straight couple. It might still be a sweet story, but it definitely wouldn't be deep, or as deep as people claim this game is. Am I saying that we shouldn't have gay love stories? No, we need more. What we don't need is gay love stories for the sake of gay love stories, and if we do do this, we don't need to proclaim them as deep, cause they wouldn't be. They would simply be another love story, nothing more.
TL:DR... wasn't great, found story rather boring, and totally misses the point of being a narrative driven game.

Needs a lot of work. Very light on content, clunky and unrealistic feel, and not worth $23. If it was $5 I would be satisfied. Here is what's wrong:
- Game is painfully repetitive. But hey its WW1 trench warfare so a bit to be expected
- Weak on content. Weapon selection is poor. No useable props - cannons just sit there as scenery, as do tanks. Trenches and fotifications not that impressive.
- Realism problem 1. No heavy machine gun emplacements. Which is totally unrealistic being that this was the primary trench defence in the war. Same for mortars and artillery nothing interactive.
- Realism problem 2. Rifles are not realistic. The sight pictures on those rifles don't look like that (I know I have a real Enfield). Holdover at 100m would not have been nessesary with those rifles, and the scope has outrageous zoom compared to the 2x and 4x scopes of the era.
- Ragdoll physics for bodies is horrible. 15 years behind. And graphics for weapons and characters almost as bad.
- A little splatter and gore? This is WW1 people, the most horrible experience of the century. The bodies just collapse when they get shot and do the herky jerk with the bad ragdoll physics. It feels lame, fake, and sanitary. Another hit on the realism.
- The whole thing is not convincing at all, and feels like a 3rd rate FPS, and does not give the feeling of trench warfare. I feel like I am playing a very early version of COD, or the 1st Battlefield (without the cool vehicles). It just isn't immersive.
On the good side, the landscapes look ok. And the walking around and climbing physics isn't horrible.

So I headed into this thinking it would be another artsy-deep indie creation. I'm glad to be mostly wrong.
The game puts you in the shoes of Katie, who has just arrived home from Europe. The family's new house is empty, you don't know what's going on, so all you can do is look for clues of the events that lead to this situation.
Most of the time you'll be reading notes and listening to journals. It might sound boring, but it is anything but. Even though this  story will last only a few hours, the characters are interesting, the atmosphere is immersive and the whole thing is packaged tight enough not to feel like a drag.
As I mentioned, Gone Home is all about exploration and going through the numerous tidbits of information you can find. There are no real puzzles or challenges. If you find yourself stuck, you should probably just check to see if you have missed a few rooms to rummage through. I don't feel like I can call this a game, an interactive experience seems more accurate. Likewise, I don't feel it is worth the current full price (20 usd), but it is totally worth it when on sale.
