Without a doubt the most emotional experience I've had in a video game. Few movies, TV shows or books have able to touch me the way this story did.
On beginning the game, it immediately hooked me with an intriguing mystery that motivated me to explore every nook and cranny of the house. I felt strangely uncomfortable at times, like I was invading their privacy as I rummaged through their very personal and private belongings. But as I examined the various Items I found, I learned so much about the family, including their relationships with each other and events of their past, It made me think about the things in my own home and what they say about me. By exploring a family's home, you learn of their struggles, the happy moments they treasure, the unhappy moments they try to bury, and their hopes and dreams. We all have these little items in our home that tell the story of our past.
In Gone Home we learn about a father whose career is struggling and a marriage that's lost it's spark. At the heart of the story is their 17yo daughter Sam. Much of her story is told through the superb performance of the audio narration of her journal. To call it a coming of age story would hardly be doing it justice. We learn of her difficulties starting a new school, and her childhood friend from whom she's drifted apart. We find bits of school work that show she's bright and talented, yet rebelious. She's grown distant from her parents, who love her but are finding it difficult to connect with her. Most importantly of all, we discover the compelling story of her falling in love.
What makes the story so powerful is how authentic it is. The characters, Sam in particular, truly feel like real people. You understand them. We've all experienced moments like these growing up. The desire to fit in, sneaking out, your first concert, the nervousness as you get close to someone for the first time, and the feeling that your parents wont accept your choices. Sometimes all we get from the game is just suttle hints, and your imagination infers the rest, because it all makes sense.
Towards the end of the game, I cared so much about Sam that I felt genuine fear for her wellbeing. When I finally reached the conclusion, I was overcome with emotion, and haven't stopped thinking about it since. Not only about the game, but reflecting on my own life, my own possessions, my home, my family, and my past.
An unforgettable experience. And my game of the year.

You're a young American girl (well, woman) coming home from a lenghty trip to Europe. It's middle of a stormy night when you arrive at a mansion your family moved into while you were gone. There's some cryptic message pinned on the door from your younger sister apologizing for not being there to see you and urging you not to dig around trying to figure out what happened. There's noone home. What do you do?
Obviously, you do start digging around, exploring the mansion, rummaging through the belongings of your family members, reading random notes, letters, tickets, books left here and there, piecing their life stories together. The focus is on your sister's story, but you also get juicy tidbits about your mom and dad, and mansion's former owner.
This is this type of non-game game, a virtual art installation. You are pretty passive, sure maybe there's some key or two to find, but it's not that complicated. It's just what I already said, exploring the mansion and examining every piece of memorabilia or just plain trash you can find. Though its shortness may irk the conventional gamers, "Gone Home" effectively and poignantly presents the history of a family, their growing up, their work, their loves and relationships, and a few skeletons in the closets.  And it does so without showing anything on the screen other than primarily the personal artifacts of the family.  You see children's drawings and writings, greeting cards, personal letters, newspaper clippings, legal documents, manuscripts, and even receipts, concert posters, and cassette tapes that offer glimpses to this family's life.
Some of the reviewers here are far too basic in their thinking.  They want great stories, without realizing good storytelling doesn't necessarily have to do with good stories.  The film classic "Meet Me in St. Louis" does not have a definite story either, and is basically a series of vignettes of family life.  And this is what "Gone Home" is like: it is primarily a series of events in this family being looked at retrospectively by the player, letting you feel the hopes, dreams, and disappointments of what seem to be a fairly straight-laced modern family that is going through some crises.  You cannot go into this game expecting a conventional adventure game, the same way you cannot go to see a film like "Picnic at Hanging Rock" (which is also very light on conventional storytelling) expecting a conventional plot.  "Gone Home" pushes the envelope in both the art of gaming and the art of storytelling and that is why it is getting all the praises.

All in all to not make this too long, Verdun is a great WW1 shooter. WW1 shooter are seen rarely and if there is one game like this, it does not capture the trench warfare, gas warfare and the psychotic warfare as nearly as Verdun!

Know as little about this game as possible before you start playing, don't read anything, just play. This is a gaming experience in its infancy, and hopefully one of the instigators of a revolution in game storytelling.
Without giving too much away, Gone Home is a game that inevitably draws parallels with Dear Esther, but lacks much of the pretentiousness brought about wondering aimlessly listening to a melancholic audiobook on a remote island in the Scottish highlands. Instead, a much more relatable storyline is provided in Gone Home, based upon the life of Sam, teenage girl in 1995. Her life over a year is documented, through a journal written for the player-character, her sister Katie, whileshe  explores family's new house.
The main strand of the story is one often visited in other media, but a relative unknown for gaming. Despite this, the themes of (spoilers)
, which adding to the perfect juxtaposition of an atmosphere akin to that of Amnesia: The Dark Decent, give one of the most meaningful gaming experiences I have ever felt.
Ultimately, I don't think this game lives up to the hype many people have pushed upon it, a lot of the praise being a result of the complete saturation of 90's nostalgia throughout. However, the game in and of itself, is a beautiful, thought-provoking way of spending two hours. (These feelings going far enough as to compel me to write this!)

It's been over 15 hours since I finished Gone Home, and I haven't been able to stop thinking about it since.
Gone Home is a small indie title published earlier this year by the Fullbright Company, but no-one has really discovered it until about a week ago. That's when everyone started buying it, playing it, and loving it.
But, firstly, let me talk about the fact that you either love this game, or you hate it. It all depends on what kind of person you are. If you are one of those guys who religiously plays Call of Duty for ten hours every single day, and only thinks a game is good if it has blood, explosions and swearing, and sex; you probably won't enjoy this game. At all. People like these can be described as "Action Junkies". Now, I'm not saying that all Call of Duty players are Action Junkies; not at all. But, there are some of those people out there, and the majority of them do play Call of Duty.
However, I'm going to call these people Action Junkies simply because most of them don't appreciate games that don't focus on killing♥♥♥♥♥♥ but focus on telling a more emotional story, or focus on telling a story that's designed to make the player think.
All of the Action Junkies can stop reading right now, because Gone Home has none of that. It has no gore, no blood, no shooting, swearing, explosions, ect, but It's still one of my favorite games of this year. Let me explain why.
Gone Home is a beautiful indie game that has conveyed the most believable and incredible emotional experience I have ever had. It blends story with design in a way that I simply can't describe. It tells a story that feels real, and true. And it all takes place in a little house for about two hours.
In Gone Home, you play a young college girl called Katie who has returned home after a year abroad. However, your family has moved while you were away, and you find yourself in a brand new house. However, when you arrive, the house is empty, and riddled with clues and secrets to uncover. This is genius. Because your Katie's family has moved, Katie has never been in this house before, and the character that you're playing is just as unfamiliar with the house as the player. But, even if you're unfamiliar with the house, you're still familiar with the characters, and you still feel part of the story, because you are the other main character's sister.
As gamers, we have these instincts and assumptions about games that we don't even realize. Gone Home takes all that and flips it upside-down. For example, near the beginning of the game, you walk down a dark corridor. Bam. I instantly thought that something was going to leap out at me from the shadows... But it never did. This game is NOT a horror game. However, it still has this keen sense of nervousness and uncomfort to it. Just the feeling of walking around a house, at night, while a storm rages outside, when no-one else is home, kept me on the edge the entire way through the game, especially when I had headphones on. Gone Home also places brilliant hints to scenarios, and you instantly suspect things are something they're not. For example, you eventually come across a bathtub stained with blood. However, as you explore the room a little more, you find out that it's actually not blood, but red hair dye. That then triggers an audio diary that explains the situation. It's a great way to tell a story, and I fear that it's some thing that we, as gamers, are seeing less and less of these days.
As you walk through the house, you find secrets and pick up clues (Key story clues/secrets are accompanied by brilliant audio diarys). And as everything starts to add up, as everything starts to piece together, and as you start to understand what happenned in that house, you finally understand what an amazing and beautiful story has taken place while you were gone, and you finally understand what a brilliant design feat that this game is.
If you ever get the chance to play Gone Home, trust me. Do it. You'll come out of it with a completely different mindset and outlook on life, and you won't get it's beautiful story out of your head for weeks. Playing Gone Home is like watching the most sad/tragic/emotional/uplifting movie ever made, but you're part of it. You are in the same place, where the other characters once were, discovering everything that has taken place in that little house.
I just hope that when people play Gone Home, they play it with the right mindset and attitude. Like I said, If you play it with an attitude of an Action Junkie, you probably won't even spend the time to finish the game. But if you jump into Gone Home ready for a great story, great design, and a great game, you won't be disappointed.

For the time it takes to complete (around 2 hours), it's not worth 20$, but at 10$ or lower, it might be ok. This is more of an interactive story than a game per say. There is no combat, no puzzles, no conversations. You basically explore the big house of your family in 1995 that seemingly seems abandonned. There's a storm outside, all the lights are turned off. Gameplay consists mostly of turning on those lights, opening whatever can be opened (drawers, cabinets, etc), picking up stuff to examine it (3d object you can move) and reading various writings. It seems boring, but it isn't really. It's all done through a decent-looking first-person 3d engine.
The fact it's dark until you find the switch in each room, the storm raging, outside and the weird, yet could be normal, sounds of the old house makes for a creepy experience. I was even kind of scared by moments, but it's not an horror game per say. The story is told through writings and from "audio" diaries by your younger sister popping up from time to time. Those are acted very convincingly and even though the game is short, you'll learn to like her and care about her potential fate. Overall, it felt like breaking, entering and exploring a 1995 house. It's atmospheric and a very good story told indirectly.

My initial review was pretty sparse on details, plus the game has been updated and added to so much since that I decided to re-review.
Verdun is a realistic World War I multi-player first-person shooter trench-warfare simulator (Whew!). You either play as Entente Powers (French, English, Highlanders, Canadian, Belgian, and American) or as Central Powers (German).
As of this review, there are four game modes:
Free for all, rifles only, no teams. New players start here, as all weapons except for one rifle are locked at the beginning of your Verdun career. You have to earn career points to unlock weapons, and you earn career points by doing well in matches.
Play on a team as either the Entente or Central powers. Choose a primary & secondary weapon from a variety of authentic weapons used at the Western Front. It's important to note that these weapons are locked to new players. Again, you use career points to unlock weapons.
Basically a practice mode for Frontlines. Play in a squad of one to four players against endless waves of AI bots. You can still gain XP, medals, and unlock weapons and achievements in this mode.
The most complex game mode. I recommend getting experienced in all other modes before even attempting this one. Play in a squad of up to four players as either the Entente or Central powers against other squads. Capture trenchlines and defend trechlines. Teamwork and communication are very important when playing Frontlines.

-
One shot, one kill with rifles. Bullet drop at long ranges. You have to lead moving targets, especially at distance. There are suppression/shellshock effects (vision and hearing partially goes out, and you can hear your heart pounding).
-
Gas, trench melee weapons, flame throwers, artillery barrages, and of course machine guns to name a few.
-
There are nine total maps at the time of this review: Vauquois (only available in Rifle DM and Attrition), Vosges, Douaumont, Argonne, Champagne (Night), Aisne, Picardie, Artois, and Flanders.
-
A gore option was added in the last major update (which is off by default). Burnt bodies, limbs blown off, caved-in heads, lotsa blood, etc.
-
Great sound effects, making the game all the more immersive. Sometimes when a player is killed, he'll lay there screaming and writhing in agony for what seems like minutes. Quite demoralizing! (Gore mode must be on).
-
Compared to other multi-player games I've played, Verdun has a really good community. Most experienced players are friendly and will offer advice to new players if asked.
-
Devs are constantly improving, tweaking, adding to, etc.
-
"Currently" because I just found out that Battlefield 1 is set in WWI, and will be coming out soon. I don't count NecroVision because, well, if you've played it or even seen the store page, you'd understand.
-
For such an otherwise realistic game, this is something that really needs to be added.
-
You'll save yourself a lot of aggravation if you modify your keyboard/mouse layout for at least melee before playing. Also, you may want to change the crouch and prone keys.
-
There isn't an in-game tutorial, but there are helpful guides and gameplay videos, as well as a spectator mode in-game.
-
There are definitely some issues, rarely something happens that breaks a match. I have had to exit and restart the game a few times due to glitches though.
-
This game is really built for multi-player. If the devs did make a single-player campaign, it would probably be similar to Red Orchestra 2 single-player - separate from the multi-player game, and not much fun.
-
Weekends are the best times to play on the US server. Any other time, & all you'll be able to play is Frontlines and Squad Defence.
I highly recommend Verdun. It's a frustrating learning experience at first, but stick with it. When you get good at this game, it's a lot of fun! See you in the trenches!

For a game that was highly recommended to me, and having seen it rated as ‘Indie Game of the Year’, I thought I couldn't go wrong by getting it. Unfortunately, I was sorely disappointed by it. It’s a shame because I did actually quite enjoy the game – up until it ended (much too soon), and I was left feeling dissatisfied.
It’s unfortunate because the rooms in the house were beautifully made, and it really did make you feel like you were exploring a real family’s house, with lots of backstory and substance. There were some cool mechanics (like ‘put back’), and the sound and interaction did really immerse you. But the actual story felt severely lacking and, frankly, quite mediocre. All of the atmosphere that had been built up lead nowhere, and I was left with many unanswered questions and devoid of any accomplishment by the end.
It took me a mere 70 minutes to complete, and I didn’t feel that I was rushing through it. Fortunately, I had purchased the game for just $4.99 on Humble Bundle, but if I had paid the full price of £14.99, I would feel really ripped off.
I went into this game with absolutely no prior knowledge, and I guess I didn’t really know what to expect from it, but I was expecting something more, and it never delivered.

It's June 7th, 1995. Kaitlin has come home after a year long trip in Europe. There's no one to greet her other than a note taped on the front door. The note is from Sam and tells Kaitlin not to go digging around to find out where he or she or it has gone. As you enter the house, the lights flicker on. The house appears to be deserted. Welcome to Gone Home.
Gone Home is an exploration adventure game that tasks the player to wander around a house piecing together clues of what happened to its' occupants. There are hundreds of objects littered throughout the game that could be picked up and viewed in greater detail. The in-game objects are rendered with such high fidelity that the words on a piece of paper can be read. In fact, every object in the game was crafted and placed in deliberate areas so it feels like an actual home in the 90's. As you pick up certain items, Sam will narrate how that item is relevant to him/her/it and as the game goes along reveal to the player Sam's innermost secrets.
The game is fairly simple. There are no points to gain, achievements to unlock or things to shoot. All the player can do is walk around and look at objects. The setting is mundane and grounded in reality which is incredibly refreshing. There are too many games nowadays that aim to be bombastic and epic with over-the-top special effects, cut scenes and FMVs to tell the story. Gone Home plays it straight and respects the player's intelligence to be able to piece the story together without blatantly telling it to the player.
Gone Home is still “gamey” at times. The player is corralled into taking a certain route with other rooms being locked or inaccessible until the player finds the right key or code. Gone Home lacks a navigation marker or main objective which makes it frustrating to know where to go next once all the rooms have been unlocked. Miss an object and you'll end up wandering throughout the house looking at every crevice, picking up everything just hoping that it will contain some kind of clue of where to go next.
The game has some technical hiccups. The in-game engine feels horribly unoptimized with frame rate issues even on lower settings. My PC rig can run triple A titles like Mass Effect and Batman fine on high settings but seems to struggle with Gone Home even though it isn't as graphically impressive. Objects have a tendency to glitch out or clip through other objects if they are placed somewhere else. The music can also mask Sam's narration especially when the thunder strikes or when near certain environmental objects like a refrigerator.
This game is not worth the $20. It takes around 2 hours to finish the game but as of October 2013, a commentary mode has been added, similar to how Valve does its' commentary modes which doubles the game's length to 4 hours. My suggestion is to wait for a Steam sale or Humble Bundle Sale to knock it down to $5 or less.
Gone Home is still a game that should be played when you get the chance to. It's approach to story telling respects the player's intelligence in that it doesn't explicitly tell the player what's going on. It's a game that doesn't feel overly pretentious and hip or trying to show a point just because it's an indie game. It's a game with a memorable, relatable and believable story that would have never worked in a book or movie.

Gone Home is a unique work of art and game design that bravely pushes the medium to branch out further. It defies gaming conventions and shatters expectations as it delivers compelling insight into a relatively ordinary American family coping with various real life situations.
Gone Home is set in 1995 in Oregon and you take over the role of Katie Greenbriar who returns to her family after a year spent traveling across Europe. The Greenbriars have recently moved into a new house which Katie has yet to see. The game starts with Katie standing on the porch with her backpack right next to her. But there’s no one home. The only thing to do is head inside and try to find out where is everyone.
For the most part Katie is an empty vessel occupied by the player although there are some interesting tidbits that you’ll find out about her as you explore the house. The main narrative revolves around Katie’s younger teenage sister Sam who left a series of letters for Katie to find. While this is the main story structure, there are many other sources all around the house that will provide further insight not only about Sam, but also the two sisters’ parents Jan and Terry. There are actually little side stories about the whole family that I personally found even more compelling than the main narrative. However, the key thing here is that almost every little snippet of information paints an increasingly intimate picture about all the various relationships within the household and also outside of it. And as you find out more and more information, you will become more and more interested in the Greenbriars.
When it comes to the actual game design, The Fullbright Company has taken a bold route in the complete opposite direction of what most players expect. Whereas most developers constantly try to expand their game worlds, Gone Home features an incredibly small yet extremely focused and believable world. A house. And it’s not even a particularly large house. Yet it conveys so much. So many little details that you should discover on your own.
However, there is still plenty of room to grow. Both on the design and storytelling fronts. However, it is impossible for me to delve into this any further without completely spoiling the entire story.
Gone Home is not a grand novel, it is a short story. A refreshing game about real people dealing with real everyday problems and situations. A new direction that confirms that this medium’s conventions are far from set in stone. Gone Home is worth your time not only because of what it is, but what it represents.

This game is frustrating and wonderful. It is not COD, and it shouldn't be. Every battle begins variously with charging at the enemy and definitely getting gunned down or gunning down the enemy who is charging at you in a near hopeless, but sometimes fruitful attempt to get into the ruddy trench you are in. That's just the experience of the game, but there is far more.
Want to shoot a machine gun? You'll have to work for it. No-one starts this game with machineguns or SMGs, they either end up with a pistol and a bundle of grenades or with one of the bolt-action rifles each of the various entente and central powers sent their boys out with. You'll ask questions like: Why the hell did the French design a rifle with only three rounds that could not be reloaded in between? Why? Then you'll realize the beauty of the Lee Enfield and the utilitarian vigor of the G98. The choice of weapon is decided based on which power your squad is with, the role in the quad you get, and how well you have fought in that role to garner various specializations. It's a nice system, and I have enjoyed the fun of trying to level up every specialty. It's a good way of promoting experiementation which I appreciate.
What about Beta?
This game has some obvious bugs which can screw up the sky and ground, but for the most part, the game still needs development in it's matchmaking capabilities. Too often, players are sent into battles without enough other players, and the game doesn't seem to send new players where they are needed, because you stick with your squad into the net battle. That design has its pros, but the con is that empty games, while uncommon, occur too frequently for a good release.
Oftentimes, the servers time out and you get dropped from a game, or your squad doesn't get a position in a battle, and you therefore have to retry making your squad.
The friend function in the game is skeletal. The developers obviously have the buttons there to make everything else functional, but there is no easy way of connecting players with their steam accounts and getting steam friends into games can sometimes be difficult. There are great examples of how to make this system function, and I think the developers will do it justice.
The community on the game has been largely understanding of the beta status, as well, and in in-game chat, I've seen the regular amount of trolling and criticism, but it seems that most of the players are pretty into the game with all its drawbacks, and would rather have a good game and some fun, than ruin the experience for anyone else.

Counter-Strike: Source, or CSS for short, is very tactical, team-based first-person shooter. CSS could be called anything, from fast-paced to slow, tight control or too easy to use, and things all across the board. However, those comments have a certain context to them, in that people have played either CS 1.6, the game to predate CSS, or CS: Global Offensive, the game to succeed CSS. This game can be compared to either of those games, and have a variety of things said about it. Some consistent, and some that are different. Either way, what can be said about this game is that it is
.
CSS is the only Counter Strike I have played, and will not be the only one. This is the "sequel" to a genre-defining game that has set standards across the board, so expectations from those who have played CS 1.6 could have been let-down, met, or surpassed. That is all dependent on who you ask. If you ask me, this game can satisfy a very serious gamer, but at the same time far fewer servers than CS:GO, and be a little outdated in the graphics department.
What makes CSS a good game is that it is fairly simplistic, yet CS:GO has been said to be a viable option to those new to the franchise. While I myself have yet to experience the game, CS:GO certainly has the more populated servers, the more higher-end graphics, and a simple enough system that a newcomer won't be "complete frag bait". Buying this game at full price has left me yearning for a more competitive scene, which apparently exists almost completely on CS:GO.
If this was too long, and you didn't read it...
,
. If you really just want to have fun with a more varied assortment of gamemodes on fewer servers than CS:GO, than that also validates purchasing CSS. This is a worthy use of the Source engine, in my opinion, so if you do get this awesome game to use in GMod, don't forget you can actually play this by itself for an excellent, team-based FPS experience with some friends.

Gameplay:
I won't lie the gameplay is more or less generic shooter, the gunplay definitly is. Sure bolt-action rifles are uncommon in FPS but by no means completely new. The Squad mechanic is a nice little feature, it actually makes you bond a bit with the people you play, IF you or them don't leave the squad after a few minutes, which is why I'm not sure whether or not the join-in-progress mechanic was a good idea. Verdun lacks the depth of a Red Orchestra concerning health and wounds and the movement system is a bit clunky compared to RO, this shows especially when you try to make your way through No-Mans-Land and get hit because you didn't crouch as fast as you wanted.
Even though this does sound rather harsh I don't mean to discredit the game. If you have any experience with shooters you won't find this game to be very different, apart from the obvious fact that the weapons aren't full auto of course. It's real strength (for now) isn't the gameplay but the setting. Also I have faith that the Devs know about these 'issues' and will address them in the future.
Setting and Environment:
Like I said this is what makes this game unique: the World War 1 setting. The Equipment is highly detailed and fairly accurate, and so are the uniforms. The maps are ugly, muddy wastelands, full of craters, wire and tranches which really sells the setting. The maps are also rather diverse, ranging from true trench-riddled wastelands, where lurking over the top will get you killed in a few seconds, to rather open maps which feature a little less deadly razor-wire and a bit more nature.
This game only features the western front, where most of the gruesome trench warfare took place. One can play as either different German squads as well as French, English and Canadians. The Voice-acting is rather good, with all sides featuring good, propably even native, and diverse voice actors. This may not seem like a big deal, but nothing helps me more to create immersion than an angry british NCO yelling to 'get my♥♥♥♥♥over the top and smoke out the bloody jerries'
Graphic:
While I don't care too much for good graphics, this game looks rather nice but is has really bad optimisation, be warned.
I would also like to add that this games has one of the best main-menu screens I ever encountered, but you'll see what I mean by that.

Amazing game to say the least. I love the gametypes, both the Deathmatch and normal Trench Warefare. It's a game that I never get tired of playing.
Although the same maps appear over and over, the fact that the outcome of every battle is different, the amount of time spent hiding in a trench and trying to cover literally every angle and time spent attacking the enemy trenches -- Trying different strategies, etc.
Usually in conquest type matches in other games, the tactics are always the same; capture a flag, capture another, go back and capture the first one again, etc.
But here, you can find yourself in a situation where you just started attacking and all of a sudden, your team loses it's foothold and you have a limited amount of time to retreat -- which isn't always an option... You might end up with a bullet in the back.
There're of course some bugs and network issues, but I can't complain. It's to be expected in a Beta. Better have it lag during the Beta and not after release... *cough* *cough* Battlefield *cough*.
Once you get used to your gun... How much lead to put on your target, adjust for bullet drop, etc - it's a non-issue.
I find myself in matches all the time where people are whining constantly about lag, when I'm sitting here with a crappy ADSL modem which is probably a lot slower than a dial-up connection, and getting 4-5KDR.
A truly amazing experience, and I can't wait for the release!

Probably one of the best shooters since the first couple CODs, but nothing like them. Not really a true tactical game either. It's early access and a hair buggy, but has more content and playability than a good chunk of the "finished" steam games in my library.
Not that I was there, but this game does a great job of capturing what I think WW1 was actually about. You die alot, and gas is scary the first time you hit it, and there is tension in the silence when you're waiting for a counter attack. And in the end, even if you win, it was pointless - you gained really nothing, and even in the game itself your team might have only made one solid gain. It's hard to describe, but this was a war where people were still trying to see eachother as people while killing them with death machines like MGs and gas attacks and where a single dude could take 100 prisoners with an empty rifle because no one wanted to get hurt, and while the game can really only provide so much atmosphere in this regard, the community fills in the rest.
Don't get me wrong - it doesn't feel pointless playing this, at least any more than any other game. When you die 20 times with only a few kills, it's somehow kind of ok because you died rushing the trench, and that's life. And when you don't die, and you and a handful of guys sweep through a trench by yourselves, you actually get that "My God boys, we've done it!" feeling.
All and all, this is a really good, unique game. It does run at a much slower pace than most shooters, but there's plenty of action to be had.

It's very unusual to find a competitive multiplayer game that gives a great sense of immersion. This game is one of those rare examples, where you will soon find that the best tactics go hand-in-hand with many of the real tactics one would see in World War One. Running and gunning or explosive spamming are virtually impossible, whereas players will be rewarded most for assisting their teams in defending a trench through coordination or performing group charges with the aid of mortar shots, while ducking and weaving behind the cover of hills, blasted terrain and fallen trees. Does this game have a few kinks? Yes, as it is in beta, but with the presence of solid, accuracy-rewarding gameplay, a great squad system (better with friends!) and an authentic First World War vibe from the realistic weapons and scenarios, it is definitely worth looking into.

It is hard to call this great piece of interactive fiction a game, but it is an experience well worth the two hours or so it takes to play through. A lazy criticism would be that it is "too linear", since there is pretty much only one path to progress, but you can spend as much time as you want exploring the empty house and all of its cultural artifacts. Beyond the primary plot of an adolescent love story, these are what make the game great - there are tons of '90s nostalgia references (though I was unaware of riot grrl as a genre/movement until very recently). I also find myself wanting to read the father's trashy sci-fi thriller novel series. I would strongly recommend exploring every item in every room.
The setting is slightly spooky, which helped make the development of the plot unexpected at a few points. I also played with a self-imposed rule where I turned off the lights and closed the doors as I left each room.
There is some talk of Gone Home winning "Game of the Year" awards, and I could support that. If you had any doubt that games are art, this should change your mind.

I would like to start by crushing any arguments of "but it's in early access" with the fact that this is a paid product, and calling it "early access" is an excuse to squeeze money out of people without finishing the game.
Even with the consideration that this is in alpha, it's terrible.
-Graphical issues appear everywhere. Looking up causes graphical errors, water causes graphical errors, sometimes the screen just turns black and you can only see your arms and gun.
-Enemies that know where the spawn locations are abuse spawn points.  You will sometimes be given a moments glimmer of life as you spawn in, before a bullet removes your only chance of playing.  When this does happen, leave the server because it will continue to happen until they push your team to the next objective or the match ends in your loss.
-Tactical HUD visuals lag behind.  Names lag behind team-mates as they run along.  Objectives drag around across your screen...the floaty symbols give you a headache after 10 minutes.
-For a game about extreme realism, they sure keep all the good weapons and attachments for higher levels.  Meaning not only a learning curve from realism, but a leveling curve.  Vast open fields are extremely difficult to see enemies across.  Too bad you don't get a scope until a higher level.  So a team with higher level players usually wins because they have the necessary gear to play properly.
I have more problems than fun.  There is so little in this game...it may be a neat idea, but it is not worth the $30 price tag.  Stay away from this game until it is finished.  You will regret the purchase.

Let's start off by saying... Wow.
I came into this game not sure what to expect, a little bit of horror, a little bit of adventure. What I got was something I could not have possibly imagined. The events are set in motion for you: Katie Greenbriar to be returning home from a trip over seas, only to find that no one is home. The events are filled with horror, love, and coming of age. The game is rather short, clocking in at around an hour and a half if you dont go afk at all, so you may want to grab it on sale. However: the narration, the ability to move at your own pace, and discover the whole story for yourself is one of the most rewarding thing I've had the pleasure of going through.

Gone Home is simply a phenomenal story. I've noticed some reviews saying that they "saw the twist coming a mile away." But this isn't a story that hinges on one twist. It's just about people. People who you come to love and care about. People who disappoint you, betray you, make you laugh, and make you care deeply about them. By the end, I felt like I had grown up with this family. Like I was the character. Honestly, Gone Home is a roleplaying game in its own odd way.
If you would like a story to make you laugh, cry, and experience the full breadth of human feeling (yes really) then get this.
I read a comment on a Let's Play video of GH that said, "I beat it in 10 minutes, game sux." You can't "beat" Gone Home any more than you can "beat" Pride and Prejudice or something. Arguments about whether GH is a game or not are neither here nor there. It doesn't matter what the crap it is, as long as it's good. $20 does seem steep, but on the other hand the writing (in terms of quality and quantity) is pretty amazing. This is definitely at least worth picking up and trying during a sale, though.
Also, this game is amazing if you like Riot Grrrl music. I had so much fun headbanging to the cassettes.
TLDR: get Gone Home if you have a functioning human soul. I don't care if you play games to blow stuff up. Believe it or not, you're actually allowed to play more than one kind of game! :O

I am at odds with this game. I went into this, not knowing what it was about really. On the one hand, it challenged my gaming expectations, the conventions in games that I have become accustomed to. It led me to believe something horrific would occur at one moment or another and sent chills down my spine as I expected a physical oppossing force to stand in my way. If I'm to be honest, I feel this would be more suited to the medium of cinema than videgames as it's story turns out to be (SPOILER ALERT) a coming-of-age tale about the main character's (the player's) sister who discovers her sexuality. I found it's story somewhat pretentious and cheesy at times, feeling contrived and almost adolescent in it's attempts to tell a "deep" story. Once the finale reveals all, I had mixed feelings. I felt somewhat relieved, knowing that Sam (the main character's sister) was alive, I felt slighlty frustrated realising the implied JFK time-travel angle was nothing more than a writer's ideas and that the paronormal element would never be explored despite supernatural occurences being firmly implied and their aftermath shown in parts of the game.
This is a game that felt far too pasive to be considered a videogame (by the scientific definition) and what I find worse still, is how everything you investigate throughout the 2 hour experience is all retrospective, there is never an impactful action by your character. That is to say, you never ever have any bearing on the story, as you are merely discovering what has already transpired. I felt relieved that this was not a horror game. I was intrigued with how it toyed with what I, as a gamer, am used to experiencing and expecting (generally negative things, like bad guy will show up or a ghost will attack etc.) but somewhat frustrated by it's pretention, trying to be a game deeper than a game.
If you want a deep story in a videogame (that is actually a videogame as opposed to an interactive museum), play a "Metal Gear Solid", "Red Dead Redemption", "Heavy Rain" or "The Last of Us". If you want a far more fun "game" that pokes holes at gaming conventions and points out how gamers think etc., go play "The Stanley Parable" which uses humour rather than pretentious misdirection to show just how predictable gamers expectations can be.
Such an awesome game to spend your time with!

Hell, it doesn't even resonate with me despite the fact that - once upon a time, back when dinosaurs still roamed the earth - I was a teenager.
Unfortunately, this rather trite tale of a lost girl's discovery of her own sexuality requires you to emphasize with her plight. I suppose it is all sort of touching in a way, but it is not a particularly riveting story, especially given her otherwise sheltered upbringing. And it certainly does not make for an interesting game, or whatever "Gone Home" is supposed to be. There's something to be said for the slow and methodical exploration of her (unrealistically spacious) home, but it also feels rather mechanical as you scour the rooms for clues. I suppose voyeurs might appreciate the ability to stick their fingers into every closet and crevice, but I don't even like looking in the medicine cabinets at my friend's house, much less poking through the virtual belongings of a strange family.
Much fuss has been made about how "accurately" the game represents mid-90s Americana, but that's not very hard to achieve. Keeping dates on a wall calendar or scribbling notes on scraps of paper are hardly long-lost arcana (I only tossed my mix-tapes a couple years ago). Heck, the lack of any computers in such a well-to-do household as presented in the game is actually an incongruity; by 1995, almost everyone I knew had a computer in their house already. I suppose for pre-teens the '90s may seem like some exotic far-away land, but for most gamers (average age: 36 and rising), waxing nostalgic about the 90s makes about as much sense as reminiscing about last Tuesday's lunch.
I get that "Gone Home" is intended to be more mood piece than game, more art than entertainment. It follows in the footsteps of games like "Anna" and "Dear Esther". And as an experiment intended to take virtual worlds in new directions, away from the ordinary run-n-gun format of our Call of Duty and Elder Scrolls games. But both as a story and an experience, the hour-long story of "Gone Home" fails to entertain and captivate, being a dry, lackluster and unrewarding adventure that neither inspired nor evoked any emotion other than yawning ennui.

I will recommend this game and attempt to acknowledge some of the criticisms others below me have brought up. Gone Home is a short game. It is atmospheric and story driven. If either of these things are unacceptable to you, then this is not your type of game. That said, I've never been so moved by something in this medium. Sure, I played to the moon, and I teared up, but this is another experience entirely. Some of the people commenting on the game below are upset because 'they saw the ending coming', well I would argue that's irrelevant. There are certainly suspenseful moments in the game and spooky atmospheric tidbits, but this game isn't solely about some big plot twist or jump scare or anything like that. This game provides a realistic emotional experience. You shouldn't feel cheated by having guessed what happens with Sam, but rather you should feel rewarded by having explored a story about love, oppression, and the awkward teenage years. I've played many great games that engage you in a universe entirely different from your own, but this is one of the rarer type that have strong implications for the very real world in which it made me cry like a child.
Give this game a try, it may not be like all the other FPS games, but this is a really fun game!

Never have I ever thought I wanted to be in the trenches of WWI so baddly.
I was hesitant about this game because whenever I see squad based combat, I expect a free for all frenzy of run and gunners like every other FPS game.
Boy was I wrong.
Pros: It REALLY is squad based. It gives you incentive to actually stick with your NCO, fufill your role, and not just one man show it. Because that doesnt work. Stick with your squad, sit tight, and move up when he tells you.
Speaking of roles, it has a finite amount. The map isnt filled with snipers or heavy MGs, each squad has a purpose and that makes each individual just as important as the next.
This game really makes use of the tug of war gameplay. Some people are complaining that theres really one game mode, and there is. But I have plenty of games that let me do whatever I want. WWI was a war fought in the trenches, with each side fighting in shifts, and this game really portrays that. It makes you really work to hold the line, and then when its your turn to advance, you head across no man lands like its nobodys buisness, and then you HOLD that trench. It punishes players who dont follow the game plan, and I like that. It gives the game order and purpose.
Adding to the fact this game is beautiful, and the weapons are nice to look at and it doesnt feel fake, like some other titles.
Cons: This is an Early Access game. Expect a few bugs every once in awhile. My biggest problem is the damage system, and the firing system. In WWI guns were not pinpoint accurate. They still arent today. They always were heavy, and had sway. This game lacks some of the more realistic parts of firing that, while challenging, I enjoy in a game. I like a kill thats earned, I dont want to shoot someone across the map in the hand and see them drop. Give the kills more depth, and you have people coming back to make more of them.
This is an amazing game with a HUGE potential to have a great cult following. It is a niche game, and isnt for everyone, but it is definitely worth the investment and time.

Even though there are a few keys and combinations you need to discover, every location in this deliciously detailed old mansion is open for you to explore, and in exploring, you are drawn into the complex interactions of a family, it's problems, and its past.

You know those quiet moments in, say, a Bioshock or a Fallout?  Where you get to take a break from the action and just walk around somebody's abandoned house, collecting audio diaries and figuring out what happened here?  The poingnat, sort of sad story of exctly WHY this house is abandoned and free to be rummaged through by the likes of you?  If I'm being honest, those moments are among my favorite, so one of the Bioshock devs going indie and making a game consisting of literally JUST that scratches a definite itch for me.  People tend to criticize this as a "non-game," and they're not completely incorrect.  If you rummage behind a bookcase, say, you won't find money or ammo, just a half-full bottle as a quiet indicator of how Dad is coping with his failed writing career.  It's short and on rails and there's not really anything you can do to change the outcome, but this game has so much heart and emotion going for it that I've got to recommend it.  The ending made me teary-eyed and, if it's the sort of thing you're into, it is absolutely chock-a-block with 90's nostalgia.  Get it on sale to avoid any buyer's remorse over the brevity, but do get it.

First, the good:  It starts off as a promising adventure game, very reminiscent of those made in the past, just with an updated engine.   Objectively, and without considering a large and very important part of the story, the game is a fantastic adventure/exploration experience.  It reminds me a bit of "Scratches" and similar titles.  The graphics are nice and the attention to detail is really quite breath-taking.  It was also nice to have a female lead for a change, that wasn't just an eye-candy dress-up to sell more copies.  The game runs well and its pace is just right.  You have an entire mansion to explore.  Think "the original Resident Evil, but without the zombies" and you'll get a pretty good idea of what kind of laid-back adventure this game is...  on the surface...
The Bad:  They took the great oppertunity they had to make a serious game with a female lead, and threw all of its credibility and likability into the furnace.  Because of the story, this game is nothing more than homosexual, feminist propaganda.  That's seriously it.  You play this game to uncover more story, and that's all the story is, thus, that's all the game is.  Now, I say this as an Agnostic who supports gay rights and has participated in marches and protests for the cause.  There is a love story (actually more than one if you really pay attention, though the additional story(s) show how terrible straight couples are at relationships) and it's a deep and caring one.  I enjoyed the story for what it was, but I also noticed how entirely preachy it was.  Make no mistake; this is a gay/fem struggle/rights message disguised as a video game.  You could tell me this game was created by Pu$$y Riot, and I'd believe you.  My gripe isn't entirely with the game itself, as some of it lies with the views of the development studio representatives.  Their decision to not exhibit at PAX due to a group panel that would be there who pinpointed a real issue in society today (quote from source: "Any titillation gets called out as sexist or misogynistic, and involve any antagonist race aside from Anglo-Saxon and you’re called a racist. It’s gone too far and when will it all end?") completely floored me, as it showed their blindness to such an issue.  The developers showed that they only care about their own interests and willfully turned a blind eye to an ever-growing fact of modern society (not just games) in the process.  You can't be liberal while only pushing for your own interests.  The goal is equality across the board (as opposed to punishing white males), and that panel was bringing up a valid point for discussion.  For a company to decide to cut loose and decide to not show up, simply because another viewpoint was being brought into the light, shows exactly how closed-minded they are.  At that point it's not about their principle, it's all about blind, uneducated stubbornness.  This is detrimental to gay rights and feminism as a whole, as it makes them look just as bigoted as those who would oppose them.  They’re essentially closing their eyes, plugging their ears, and yelling “la la la la.”
Again, the game is designed well, and really, the love story is quite good to an extent (albeit quite cliche and young-angst at parts).  It’s just far too preachy, and far too obvious, so much so that it gets to a point where you’ll find yourself rolling your eyes at every “journal entry.”  The story unfolds in a really interesting way as there’s actually multiple narratives going on.  For many, there will be a lot of guessing going on to the very end; for the more experienced adventure gamer (who pays very close attention to detail), you’ll have it figured out pretty quickly.
Final verdict:  If you’re a hardcore feminist lesbian who believes that your rights are the only ones that matter and every single white male on the planet owes you respect beyond words, this game will be #2 on your “top games of all time” list, just under "Castrate the White Privilage Patriarchy" (especially if you like “riot grrrl” music).  If you’re a seasoned adventure gamer with mild to strong supportive views on gay rights, you’ll be able to enjoy this game for what it is, while appreciating the modernist aspects it brings to the genre.  Additionally if you’re level-headed and not a complete libtard, you’ll be able to see its flaws and point them out accordingly.  If you’re an absolute conservative♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ you’ll most likely have an adrenaline rush by the end of the game and have an urge to go out and kill every homosexual you can find, especially if you’re Christian (yep they throw that at you too, subtly, so they think).  I liked the game, but I would have liked it more without the preachy aspect.  It is for this reason that I cannot recommend it.  I believe only a small minority of steam users would actually enjoy this game, preachyness included.  I believe the description of the game is left so vague for exactly these reasons, and it's going to catch quite a few gamers off guard.  It's to the point of being quite misleading.  Yes you do what's described in the write-up, but that's more of a mechanism for the game's actual story to vomit all over you.  For some, it will be good to take them out of their comfort zone, but to many (who can look at it, taking a step outside the box), it will appear as nothing more than dressed-up politics, and certainly not the kind of adventure they signed up for.
You may find that you like it and if so, please don't view this review as being against you.  Just try to step outside the box and look at this "game" with a clear head.  I can't recommend this game because I believe the majority of Steam users would not enjoy it.  While I enjoyed it for its atmosphere and classic adventure gameplay value, only a minority of gamers enjoy those kind of games, and fewer enjoy blatantly forced politics.

Thankfully, I knew absolutely nothing about
other than seeing it on a couple Game of the Year nomination lists.
I probably went into it with the frame of mind the developer intended... and that's by assuming it was an artsy horror game.
The game has you assembling all the clues and story fragments to piece together a seemingly scary timeline of events while you've been away in Europe.   Searching around the house, filling in the blanks was surprisingly engrossing.  The entire time, a raging storm, an old mansion, and a buckling electrical system conspire against you.
By the end it's clear that
is a
I also noticed there were plenty of people angry over the price vs. length of the game. They *might* have had a point. It's a very short game. I clocked in about 2 hours of entertainment... and I really scoured the house, going into every nook and cranny. A $9 or $12 price point probably would have gone over better.
Of course, there's complaints about the graphics, but honestly, for chrissakes, it looks fine. It's not some AAA budget hyper-detailed simulation. The graphics are decent enough for the story at hand. It's not without lots of little details and nice touches, though. The 90's vibe is very well done, though it's simply a setting. It's amazing how many kids couldn't get past that in review comments. "This means nothing to me because I was born last week." Good for you. Go gargle some Drano.
Then there's the big question: IS IT A GAME?
Yes. It's a game. In the loosest sense. It's an interactive story that leads the player through by giving them clues.
Just like
.
Just like
.
You move around. Click to use things.  Discover clues.  Move along.  If
isn't a game, then an entire chunk of the Sierra and Lucasarts library just got their Pluto on.  You may say that
games have puzzles. Great. This entire game is one big puzzle: finding the answer to the question of what happened. Hell, there's even an inventory.  What, do you need a little score in the corner to increase every time you find a piece of paper?
It really makes me sad to admit that

Your name is Kaitlin Greenbriar, and you've returned home after a year abroad (and a family move!) to an empty house.  Your task is to figure out just what happened while you were away, and where everybody is.  Pretty much every little detail in this game is devoted to making this seem like a real family.  Little touches, like letters between your author father and his publishers, add depth to characters and make you feel like you know them, even though you never technically meet anybody.
I will say that I came into this game all amped up after playing "The Screecher," and so every little creak and groan had me on edge, constantly checking corners and jumping at every lightbulb flicker.  That, uhh, may have been the wrong sort of priming.  Anyway, the game lasts about two hours if you compulsively search every surface of every room for interactivity like I do.  I got the game for five bucks at the Humble Store, and I must say it's worth every penny.  Be advised that there are no antagonists, though, so if an exploration-driven character drama with no direct conflict isn't your cup of tea, then you are not the intended audience for this game.  If that
your cup of tea, then yeah, it's pretty damn awesome.

Stability increased. Game came out from Early Access. So how it plays?
It's a son of Insurgency + Red Orchestra 2. Better then Insurgency but not so polished like RO2. U got no tanks here on the battlefield and only 32 players. Weapons are good, you feel them. Game has it's own atmosphere of trench's warfare. Frontline mode -- first you attack then you hold. Devs cut the nerve -- you really feel the insanity of war. You keep dying trying to reach trench, then you got to fall back and it's infinite. I read Remarque's book about WWI and it's really that feel.
But if you pass this period you will get E.Junger experience. You will start love that insanity. Trench's massacre, close quarters battle rage.
Also each map is different. In 1914 it's more about rifle shootings, in 1918 -- class quarters in trenches.
+ Weapons

+ Balance -- you need to teamplay
+ Frontline mode
+ Devs learn a lot about WW1
+ Speed Bolting

"Gone home" is initially enthralling, but it loses its grip on your interest very fast.
Just to be clear about something: This isn't the kind of video game you're used to, even if you are familiar with graphic adventures, this is more of an interactive story than it is a game, there are no gameplay aspects asides from walking and picking up notes, therefore, for the review, I will only concentrate on the story that the game tells.
The game is set in the 90s, you play as a girl who is returning home after a 1 year trip to Europe, however the house is new to you, since your family moved in while you were away.
When you get there, nobody is there to greet you, so you walk into the house and you find out that your sister has left you diaries scattered around the house to explain how things have been since you left.
During the first minutes of the game, there is a certain aspect about your sister that is hinted throughout the notes, this initially captivates you, it is a really interesting point to explore, but once this point is confirmed, it suddenly becomes bland and boring, you lose interest in the plot really fast.
The plot "plays" with you, makes you believe that things will go in a certain way, only to go in another one, which is good, since you can say that this is definitely not a predictable story at least.
There are also 3 subplots to explore, though they are a bit more ambiguous than the main one, since they don't concern your sister and the main plot is told from her POV, so in the end, the only thing you can do about these subplots is speculate, which is very sad, because they are really interesting.
The game's writing isn't a big deal, it's extremely basic. If you were to transcript all of the script, it would probably account to seven pages or less.
Given this, and the fact that the game is 2-3 hours long, with no replay value whatsoever (asides from Commentary mode, but that's not much of a reason to replay the game.), I would definitely recommend you to STAY AWAY from this game, even if it's at a cheap price. The game is a scam at 20 bucks, devs should feel ashamed to charge this much for this "game":
Really, dont waste your money on gone home. Critics were extremely light on this game for fear of being called "homophobic" or "non-progressive".

You come home at 1:15 AM after a year away to a new family house you do not recognize. Of the three family members you expect to see, you find none. Doors are closed and lights are off. You begin your cautious search of this alien place. Among your first pieces of evidence are journal entries from your sister: apparently, your family has moved into this town's "psycho house." Your mind races to dark fantasies of poltergeists and serial killers. All of the clichés apply; it is a dark and stormy night.
Gone Home gives us constant hints that, at any time, it's going to lay it on thick. However, The Fullbright Company's inaugural game is more interested in dismantling and repurposing these horror tropes than reveling in them. We expect a "video game," broad and sensational; what we get is an emotional drama, affecting, sensitive, and satisfying – not to mention quietly ground-breaking for the medium of video games.
Nestled within a familiar framework of extreme fiction is an intimate story focused instead on the dramatic of the everyday. You are Kaitlin Greenbriar, coming home from a year abroad to a house you find unfamiliar. Your family isn't there. Gone Home will have you asking, in the most common yet resonant sense, if they are OK.
Gone Home pushes aside the exaggerated in favor of the real. It is not a game of thrills or reflexes, but that doesn't make it any less of an engrossing story experience. You will only experience as much as you find, but that is not to say that the story is hidden away – most of your family's things and thoughts are left in plain sight, though puzzle adventure game instincts will drive you to eventually leave no corner unexplored. However, as your thoroughness uncovers more guarded secrets and insecurities, you may come to feel that your roving eyes are piling on multiple counts of casual voyeurism. You may also feel ever more unable to rein in your curiosity. The various feelings you find laid bare in each successive tidbit, from humor to heartbreak, spur you on to find the next. The stories and characters are the driving force here, falling into place in a way that is nothing short of impressive. If you think of yourself as particularly empathetic, these emotional beats might make you feel as if you were discovering your own family.
Throughout the game, you are never sure if you'll see another person in this empty house, but you will discover a full sense of the characters nevertheless. They are presences absent and missing from the house: not just "offscreen." You'll find your father's discarded drafts and the regular distractions he used to dispel his writer's block. You'll find your mother's attempts at artistic appreciation and creation that took her mind off of what she sees as a happy marriage becoming less so. But most of all, you'll find your sister – every aspect of her – as growing up a teenager tends to leave behind many rambling thoughts. It is clear that she questions who she is and what she's doing with her life, but amid the uncertainty is the core of a wonderful little sister who has grown a lot in the year you were away. Her mixtapes of cathartic and immediate riot grrrl singles are my absolute favorite of the family's artifacts.
Human connection comes at a premium. The disconnected lives of our average, nuclear, suburban family have led to the conception of many modern horror stories and the clichés they represent. In a medium so commonly used as a delivery system for escapist fiction, it means very much that this small game has opted instead to tell us a down-to-earth story of love and its byproducts. Gone Home is about connection over separation, and the wonderful contradiction that is extraordinary love from ordinary circumstances. One can only hope that there will be more such stories to follow.

I have no problem recommending this game, so long as you know and understand what to expect before purchasing:
1. There is no action. The game is story driven and revolves heavily around exploration.
2. This is not a scary game. However, there is an eerie charm to it and I found myself sporting goosebumps more often than not - mostly thanks to claps of thunder and squeaky floorboards.
3. This is a short game. There is an incredible amount of detail put into this game and tons of objects to interact with, but I bet it's possible to play through in around two or so hours.
4. Be prepared to think outside of the box. I wasted plenty of time tracing my steps trying to figure out why I couldn't advance only to discover the problem wasn't that I was missing anything, rather that I wasn't investigating things I never thought I'd have to.
That said, it's an entertaining (and at times, frustrating) game with an intriguing story and great character development. Highly recommend it you can grab it for under $5.

My fingers tremble slightly as I clutch my Logitech G9X, index finger hovering over left-click. I whipe the sweat from my brow and take a sip of iced water to calm my nerves, yes, you guessed it. I'm seconds away from starting what could conceivably be the greatest phenomenon ever to grace the universe with its presence, Gone Home. My whole body is nearly spasming in trepidation as the game opens to the most hauntingly visceral rendition of a lonely mansion in the forest of Oregon. After being forced to take a thirty-minute nap due to an uncontrollable feeling of euphoria and headiness, I took my first steps in the veritable utopia that is Gone Home. I felt the temperature in my room peak as my GTX 660 strained to shoulder the burden of the Unity game engine. Unfortunately in truth, I was disappointed to find that I could not run this enlightening work of art on max settings without notable stuttering.
However, I would be a fool to complain about any aspect of this masterpiece. The graphics of this game are rendered immaterial due to the uncomparably complex narrative that was delivered to me in a way that I can only liken to some form of divine message. Having taken but a few steps, I am forced to quickly double-check the control scheme for the game (to reduce the risk of it catching me off guard). This bona fide holy grail of gaming challenges pre-conceived notions of gameplay across the entire industry. I could at this point barely contain my joy at the love and attention that had gone into the four-directional movement mechanic and the ability to be able to pick up AND manipulate certain objects in a 360 degree rotation!
After exploring the entirety of 1 Arbor Hill, and experiencing the most exhilarating climax to this gospel of gaming I experienced a refreshing sense of belonging, not to mention an overwhelming sense of longing. I feel that this visionary production has put me at one with the universe, and has without question given my existance a sense of purpose. This game has changed me forever and I am forever grateful to its profound teachings for having made me a better homo sapien.
This is more than just a game, its a state of mind. An inconceivable experience. A fleeting glimpse at the pinacle of reality as we know it.
Game of the year every year.

Beautiful, exceptional, nostalgic, intriguing, gripping. I could use all of these words to describe Gone Home, yet they do nothing to describe how profound of an experience this piece of explorative media is.
Fans of Dear Esther, To the Moon, and Thomas Was Alone will adore Gone Home. And I daresay anyone with even the slightest appreciation for a well told story should consider paying for the chance to meander through this empty house.

Gone Home is a game oriented exclusively around a story that unravels as you explore your family's empty home. You play as Kaitlin Greenbriar, a girl who has been off in Europe traveling for quite a while. On the evening of your return, the worst storm of this season is occurring in your hometown of Portland, Oregon, and you're bound to your family's mansion in the forest as the rain falls. From there, you progress through the game by interacting with the various things lying around the house, unraveling the story in the process, learning more and more about the secret lives your relatives have lived in your absence.
The story Gone Home presents to the player is the powerful sort that even the most hardened authors have difficulty emulating. It evokes emotions that very few games, movies, shows, and other forms of art have the ability to, and leaves the player wanting nothing more than to find what happens next. I completed the game in one sitting, which, while a great testament to its value as a game, is also an unfortunately accurate reflection on the brevity of the game as a whole.
Ultimately, for the price of $20, as much as I hate to say it, I'd not purchase it. I do, however, encourage everyone to take advantage of any sale they find this game subject to, so long as it drops below $10. The game will be worth every penny.

text:
The best word to describe Verdun would be;
Brutal.
But in a very, very good way.
Overall opinion: Fantastic, historical, a damn good game and well worth the price! If it's on sale, it's a must!
Verdun one of the most historically acurrate games I've ever played, from being hit by gas attacks, to being shot mid stride and  watching your body slump down into the mud and battling it out in trench warfare on some of WWI most know battlegrounds. Most weapons are extremly satisfying to use, with most rifles downing a charging enemy or and entreched one in one shot, Pistols maybe taking 2 shots on average but having the advantage of being semi-automatic, making pistols extremly formidable even at long range.
This game will make you work, espically in the trench warfare mode, where this game comes into its own. You will push up to cover or the enemy trench, most likely die in the process but you know you'll do it again, because there is that chance you will make it into that cover or arrive into the enemy trench, bayonet at the ready. Verdun succeeds in creating a very tense atmosphere from merly lying in no-man's land waiting for your squad or slowly creeping through the enemy trench, knowing that your probably going to get shot from behind. You and your team will have to rtry and detremine which part of the enemy trench is the least defended or create a space for your team mates to enter. The teams I have played on, usually worked together I havent really noticed much toxicity which is a postive thing and I hope it stays that way.
Although it can be daunting for new players, as getting shot from seemingly no where can be frustrating and not hitting your mark on long shots because you werent compenstating for bullet drop and travel time can be slightly, Most players will pick things up like compesation and not standing straight up at the edge of your trench or in the middle of no-man's land.
Overall this is a history buffs wet dream and damn good shooter, very solid for an early access game although its missing a few minor things. I'd love to see them add more battlefields and more forces, like Gallipoli which would hopefully cause the Dev's to add the ANZAC forces to the game for which the Australian and New Zerland members of the community would be very grateful for, also the addition of more blood and gore would add to the already fantastic immersion. I'm sure the Dec's will continue to polish and improve this game and I cant wait to see what it becomes!

In a nutshell,  Verdun is very similar to Day of Defeat in respect to the capture the flag aspect.    The action is fast paced, with larger servers offering a true WW1 battle environment, and constant respawning.    There is a deathmatch mode, but with such large battlefields, its not as much fun.   Couple of pros and cons to round it out.
Pros...
+realistic weapons true to the time period (bolt actions galore)
+forced squads, with spawn on captain and various weapons.
+squad captains, can call in gas attacks, recon planes ect.
+rich environments, lots of places to hide, graphically beautiful.
+Capture the flag with each side getting forced into taking turns attacking or defending (sounds unappealing, until you realize how much it truly adds to a WW1 game)
+Snipers don't dominate, they have a limited effectiveness with the amount of cover, and can't compete in close combat.
+Class balance is superb at the moment.
Cons...
- Very much a beta,  some strange spawn glitches,  server issues, all things to be worked out in time.
- Wonky shot mechanics that favor high ping players (you shoot, a player jerks out of your aim, and kills you, its rare but it happens)
- Server selection process is confusing at times, menus aren't fleshed out.
- Hungry graphics,  even with a medium to high end GPU, you will be hard pressed to squeeze 30-40 fps out of this game with a few options disabled.
Overall...
Its a great game that has lots of potential to revive the WW1 genre.   The attack whistle blows, over the top,  charge through a hail of machine gun fire, hoping to live to see the enemy trench.   The game can be challenging, but everyone who is playing it is a good sport, friendly, and are having fun.   Join us!

: December 27th, 1916. France.
Weather has been most unkind during these days of fighting. The mud soaked ground during the day makes transversing the already no man's land of hell all the harder. Many bodies flop into large mud pits and swallowed whole into the earth. During the night, the cold nights make the ground as hard as rock and the bodies of us men brittle and broken. It's only during these nights that we get some slight comfort, hoping for a grenade to clear our trench and give us some slight warmth before a cold death but alas, none so.
As I sit here, writing to you, bullets buzz by overhead and many men that are defending during the assult of the enemy drop beside me in a pool of their own blood but as quickly as he falls, another poor soul takes his place. It's not always been like this. Sometimes, we manage to push through all the trenches and defend them till the enemy run back further to the battle line. Other times, we are pushes back and defeated. However, its mostly stallemates. Neither side wins but really...is there winning in war?
One of the commanders has been dropping gas down on the enemy's trenches for some time. Its a yellow cloud of death that only brave souls would dare run through. We've been gased many times but we have thanks to our gas mas for protecting us. Its hard to see through it, makes shooting all the more harder. The muffled sounds around you as you wear it gives some sort of peace though...
It seems the assult is over and we are going to counter attack as orders of the commander. I pray I will make it through this push and come back home. The sounds of our guns firing across the battlefield gives some comfort, knowing I have someone watching my back. All the better we have a crew of Light Machine Gunners to cover our advance but they have some as well. Deadly things those..LMGs...they can mow down a whole squad of men within a blink of an eye. The sound of the enemy gunner is quite terrorfiying. I've seen many men coward down in fox holes, begging to go home.
Now I must go, time for my squad to take charge. Please wait for me, for soon I'll be at your side.

Lovingly yours,
P.S. This game is damn good. Gameplay is a blast and the imersion of the world is fantastic. Graphics are good but can be better. Sounds are amazing. As any early acess, there is bugs. One bug will throw you off the server for a while while I have one that cause me to have each frame of my grenade throw to be shown like a matrix sort of thing. Other then that, great so far. 8/10 till they optimize the game and fix the bugs.

The idea of the art game or an interactive story turns many gamers off, and for good reason. The majority of these games limit a player's interaction so severely, you wonder why they didn't just make a movie. Many others are so abstract that they conjure the story of the Emperor's New Clothes. This is not one of those games.
All the elements that make up a good story are here. The writing and voice acting are spot on. The pacing is fantastic and the atmosphere is incredibly potent. The gameplay is much more involved than your standard "interactive story" and is a bit more reminiscent of point-and-click adventure puzzlers.
The issue most people seem to have with this game is the price point, and at $20 for two hours of runtime (at most) that is a legitimate concern. I would make the case that the money is not for the amount of time you can get out of the game, but rather the polish, attention to detail, strong story, voice acting, and atmosphere.
In summary, I love this game and I would recommend it to anyone even at full price, but you shouldn't have a hard time finding it on sale on Steam or the Humble Store.

The Fullbright Company created a story about a girl named Katie (You) who come home to an empty mansion, and you are left with no directions but to figure out where everyone is. It is a dark and stormy night, and you are running around turning on lights to prevent yourself from being too afraid. The atmosphere is very chilling, hearing only thunder and the sounds of floorboards, with the occasional thump. Y'know, everything in a horror movie.
This is not a horror game. Nothing will jump out at you, despite the fact you are anticipating it upon the opening of every door. This is a testiment to how good Fullbright was at creating a realistic atmosphere that you yourself would experience, had you been in Katie's shoes. If anyone were to walk into an unfamiliar mansion -- alone -- in the dark -- during a storm -- one would be afraid, regardless if there were any true reasons for being afraid.
Practically, the game consists of walking around and finding a bunch of notes left to you by your younger sister, Sam. Each note will give you clues on where to look next, and-so-on. If you are into indie games that like to think outside the box and run with their own ideas, this is a good game to experience. If you are someone who is looking for a lot of action and/or horror, this is not the game for you.
