Counter-Strike: Source is the epitome of the few games that have aged qute well since their release when we were just fledgling gamers. For some of us, Counter-Strike holds a special place in our hearts. We get a overwhelming sense of nostalgia that races through our concious when we reminisce about our moments in Counter-Strike. I was first introduced to Counter-Strike, or more specifically, CS:S, some time in 2009, through a YouTube video of the community made mod Zombie Escape. I knew immediately from that point on that I absolutely had to play this game. The propsect of pitting humans and zombies against one another enticed me, though at this time I had no real clue as to what the actual base gamemode of CS:S even entailed. Around the same time of this discovery of mine, I became so engrossed in other video games that I became sidetracked, only to start up my escapade in Counter Strike around late-2013. Ever since then, GFL (now GFLClan.ru) has been my main source of quality (and autistic) Zombie Escape. I have always loved the community, I have always loved the players, I have always loved the fond memories which I have accrued from my time on GFL, and most of all.. I have always loved soloing maps, only to make BOT Keith mad. If you could not tell, I have no regrets with my time playing Counter-Strike: Source. I am grateful for everything that GFL has stood for these past few years. My only hope now is to see GFLClan.ru live and prosper on, to spread it's wings and prosper so greatly that I can continue to make more friends and have so many more pleasant and humorous memories. As far as I can tell, for the foreseeable future GFLClan.ru and CS:S still have so much more time left to live.

Terrorists, Counter-Terrorists, headshot, bomb, defusal kit, pistol round, de_nuke, de_dust, de_dust 2, de_aztec, cs_compound, cs_italy, jumping, rushing, crawling, flash, frag!
Some of these basic element are the things that make Counter-Strike: Source (or Counter-Strike as a whole) one of the greatest multiplayer games ever created. Although many people consider basic things such as maps, movement, and physics as unimportant, these are the things that make Counter-Strike what it is today.
Counter-Strike: Source is truly an amazing games that casts an almost identical shadow to its older brother 1.6. The differences in Source are ones that only improve that game rather than take away from its originality. It improves the graphics, adds much better physics, and ragdolls. Although the Counter-Strike games have never really been to concerned about detail (gameplay is a exception) Source adds the much needed polish that 1.6 and Condition Zero failed to deliver.
The gameplay is identical with only minute differences that only a hardcore Counter-Strike fan would complain about. Graphically the game is very appealing to look at. The sound is good as well (especially when you crank the volume up really loud!).
The verdict: One of the best games ever created and personally MY MOST FAVORITE GAME IN THE WORLD.

Counter-Strike: Source is a second game in the Counter-Strike series, the first one being Counter-Strike: 1.6. Counter-Strike is a FPS (First Person Shooter) game series which was first released in 1999 (Counter-Strike: 1.6). The game has alot of gamemodes (though, they are not default in the game but are doable with mods) such as Normal (one life, respawn after the round is over), Deathmatch (respawn right after death, usualy you can get any weapon that you'd like), Zombie Mod (pretty self explanatory, one or more random playes on the server will be chosen as the infected one who must infect as many humans as possible while the humans have to survive and hold the zombies back for as long as possible, usualy includes some kind of point/money system which allows you do purchase different upgrades and perks) and many more. Overall, the game is a fun online multiplayer first person shooter game with alot of customization (with mods and skins) and it can also be played offline with bots (bots are players played by the computer), i'd suggest this game to anyone who is interested in FPS games and who would like to have abit of customization and fun in one of those types of games.
Overall rating - 8/10

Counter-Strike: Source is the remake of the original Counter-Strike on the Source Engine.
The games are similar yet vastly different, Counter-Strike: Source has dated graphics compared to newer games, especially CS:GO, yet the game retains it's charm and is still an amazing experience, CS:GO took the top of the CS games for popularity, but this one is still kicking, with many servers to play on at a whim. Lag issues are there, bugs aren't too common as the game is pretty polished with updates always coming up, lag issues usually are hosts or the player themselves.
Host private matches on Hamachi is tricky, very tricky at that. The times I tried I lost interest as I stopped playing the game a bit ago, I used to play 1 hour a day for several years, one hour being the minimum.
As for online, there is a steed learning curb now, as most players are extremely die hard players who refuse to let this game die, and they won't hesitate to headshot spam you, so online can be intimidating. There is also a few hackers here and there but that's to be expected.
This game is reccommended if you want to play Garry's Mod, another game I've reviewed. It comes in a money saving bundle.
CS:S gets a 9/10 in my book, simply because its a well balanced game, easy to run, and just plain on fun.

If you like challenge in your first person shooters, you'll definitely find it here. The hit detection is specially designed to make some of your shots miss if you just spam shots. This is probably one of the most challenging multiplayer shooter games of all time.
That aside, the gameplay itself is smooth and enjoyable. You usually either go all sneak, or all rush. Either way, you absolutely must have good reflexes to get anywhere on the scoreboard. All guns have a great balance to them, and it's good, like any other well-balanced game, to find which one suits your style. Like I mentioned before, it's not a good idea to spam with most of the guns. However, if you get a weapon like the P90 or the MP5 this isn't as true.
The graphics, considering the game's age, are excellent. Sharp textures and realistic shading weren't really a thing back then (and honestly still aren't now, but I digress) but the game definitely holds its own against other games from the time.
The sound quality is on the low end, but this is merely in homage to the original version of the game/mod, back in the late 90's. That said, it doesn't take much from the experience and adds a bonus nolstagia to players of the original game.
Like many older multiplayer shooters, there isn't much in terms of progression. If you like, for example, the ranking system from CoD or BF, you won't find anything of that sort here. It definitely is a possible negative for some.
Last but not least, this game still has a large community to this day. There are many, many custom maps, mods, etc. I personally stick with the base game most of the time, but if you get bored, you can escape to them. Anyways, the community consists mostly of players in their late teens and older. You won't find many children in this game. Beware, however. If you are a child yourself (under the age of 16 atleast) you may find many grumpy people who won't like you and especially your voice. You have been warned.
Overall, this is a wonderful game. I play it on and off, but I have no doubt that is indeed a classic.

text: Counter-Strike Source is a dinosaur, but the kind of dinosaur whose wisdom and refinement have made possible a plethora of first-person shooter titles over the better part of the last decade. Like its predecessors, this game is about finesse, not excess. It represents a minimalist yesteryear of shooters that are all but lost to today's explosive A-listers-- most of which owe a great debt to CS and CS:Source. Furthermore, Valve's open-minded handling of this game and its assets has led to an exceptionally-rich modding community that continues to produce creative content. In conclusion, I have a great deal of respect for this game, though I won't pretend that I find it as stimulating as I once did. I don't believe that this game is timeless, but I do believe that its legacy will be influential for many years to come.

Frankly, anybody coming to CS: Source afresh, hoping to pick up the multiplayer game all their friends rave about, is going to have their work just as cut out as ever as new player will have no idea why they’re missing all their shot.

Counter Strike: Source (CS:S) Is the game that made me love the franchise so much more than any of the prequels could have, not because how skill based it was, if I wanted that, I'd have gone to 1.6, no, I liked Source because of the community.
This is mostly a nostalgia review as I've not been playing CS:S peridically for over 4 years now, but this game still holds a special place on my top 10 games fo all time.
What made CS:S special to me, was the comunity servers that were up almost 24/7. The variety of different kinds of gamemodes was insane back then and the freedom to do whatever in those servers was great. One of my favorite things to do was to go on some random website that had animated files such as .gif or the like and use those animations as my spray ingame. Then there were also those guys who had some NSFW sprays haha, good times.
Source was for me, mostly played for fun. I did not have a good PC at the time, so I usually played maps with not much of textures and not too many people. That may have played a part in as to why I wasn't as competitive in CS:S, but nveretheless. I loved playing surf, deathrun, jail and of course Hoejhus! The best of the best.
In retrospect, now that CS:GO has gotten as big as it has these recent years. I feel like that on the competitive side of things CS:GO outranks CS:S, by a fair margin, but the community side of things has never gotten to the level of what Source was at back in its time and the fact people can't use sprays like they used to in Source, has ruined some of the old fun that was had back in Source. I believe that Source is the better game when it comes to entertainment value and just having a good time, whereas its successor CS:GO has got its competitive scene going, but not so much for its entertainment.
(10/10)

New users or ones afraid of competition will tend to stay away, point fingers and whine. I think that Counter Strike Source is probably one of the best FPS games out there.
It offer:
Simple gameplay - Meaning there aren't too many unnecessary features that can give you an unfair advantage just because you have played longer.
A lot of different game modes - This is one thing I love about CS:S if you would like to surf then there are a lot of servers with surf maps, if you want to play DM then there are a lot for that and so on.. Not directly from the developers but yea still a good thing.
Community made content - I know this isn't directly from the game developers but there is a lot of extra content you can use. Some examples: Maps, skins, huds and so on. You can personalize how it looks which is a great thing.
There may be some negative things about it alos such as there have come a lot more cheaters over the years but if you play on servers with active admins then there is a high chance that you can play with legit people.
The game has changed a lot over the years I played it and I have to admit I dislike some of the changes while I like some others. At some point I like how the game is now but sometimes I think that the game didn't had to change the way it did.
Nevertheless I can't say I haven't spent a lot of hours playing this game because I have. To me this was one of the games that I will always like to play once in a while even though I am not playing it much anymore.

Me being the Tf2 loving fanatic was hesitant to get into the FPS frenzy that is Counter Strike and the fact it didn't have hats to wear.  But what I saw was a beautiful game of no regenerating health, lack of any cover whatsoever, the mechanic of buying weapons, fun mods and maps, etc.  Counter strike is a great experience that shows how good valve is at making online FPS and how much better they are at it in comparison to companies like EA and Activision.  My complaints with the game is the learning curve, the mind boggleing accuracy of the lowest pistol to headshot you can get annoying, how intence the game can get, the lack of hats, and the less newbie friendly system of matchmaking.  But other than those complaints, CSS is a great online shooter expirience that feels smooth as silk with controls and gameplay in comparison to COD or Halo.   But I reccomend this title to anyone bored with TF2(that is insane to think that) or anyone wanting to challenge themselves at a new shooter.

It's Counter Strike and even though it is an aging product it still manages to capture the same great feeling of a really well tuned multiplayer shooter.  It still suffers from both the good and bad things about the Source engine - the cone of fire system is still inefficient but the Source engine graphics still hold up decently in the wake up more next-gen graphics.  The best part about the game is the perfect pace that no game sense has been able to master.

Counter-Strike Source has forever been known for it's lucrative history of updates and constant development through the seven year period it has been on steam.
The game was launched alongside Half-Life 2, fresh from a much talked about beta test yet riddled with glitches and lacking in content as to be expected of the progressive technology that powered it. Back then, I'd probably find difficulty in saying if the game was any worthwhile given how poorly it compared to Counter-Strike 1.6.
It has grown to be it's own game though. Counter-Strike Source may pose to be the successor to 1.6, as if a up-to-date recreation of the original game, but it's controls, weapon handling and pace are unique. It also holds up audaciously given Valve's support for the Source Engine, looking very impressive and able to run smoothly on most hardware - including intergrated chipsets.
Counter-Strike Source still has a rich community of players, custom content and achievements so I implore you to try it

This game spearheaded not just the modern military shooter, but competitive multiplayer FPS gaming into common public knowledge. Simple in design, and considered by many as a 'lucky' or 'freak' hit, this (originally) half life mod succeeded in one area: the direct and deterministic mapping from skill to score, with very low signal to noise ratio.
The clean design of the game, along with its finely tuned unforgiving gunplay made it a game which drew people in quickly, but kept them due to it's very high skill ceiling.
CS: Source is primarily an engine update, while there are purists still on CS "1.6" running the original half life mod. Like it or not, if you've never played CS, you've missed a grand moment in the history of the modern FPS.

The game has been expanded into a series since its original release, which currently includes Counter-Strike: Condition Zero, Counter-Strike: Source, Counter-Strike: Anthology and Counter-Strike on Xbox. Counter-Strike pits a team of counter-terrorists against a team of terrorists in a series of rounds. Each round is won by either completing the mission objective or eliminating the opposing force.

It's a perfectly balanced, skill based game. Encourages some tactics,  and your success is determind by how much you practice and the speed of your reflexes.
It's the polar opposite of Call of Duty. You can't play for 100 hours and have better guns and shinier icons than everyone else. You don't earn respect for being 7th prestige, but rather for topping the scoreboard and being accused of hacking.
It's a fantastic game, even if you find it difficult there are modified servers with "gun game", surfing, warcraft mods. All really unique stuff, infinite replayability, appeals to all levels of skill. This is the game that makes people love first-person shooters. If I was allowed to play like 5 games for the rest of my life, I'd probably choose this as one.

The best free game ever (I got it for free with HL2).

No other game comes close for team based play.  Playing 5 v 5 with a great team against a great team is one of my all time gaming pleasures.
Steam was the first to get 'friends' lists right, and CS was the first game to get voice chat right. It is so easy to drop into a game with your friends, and so easy to make friends in game. The game can be very social if you find the right servers.
If you are in any doubt about how much I love CS, look at the amount of hours I sunk into it. Then consider that gameplay data wasn't recorded until a few years after the game was originally release. I couldn't tell you how much I played in those first few years.
That's also the one potential negative to the game, of course - it can become a timesink if you let it.

A modern-era FPS with good graphics and gameplay.
Maybe you've played deathmatch before, maybe you've played team deathmatch before. Well, the difference is this one feels more real. It's less cartoony than games like the Unreal Tournament series. You can't jump twice as tall as you are, won't be breakdancing in the middle of a fight, and you certainly won't be flying across the map (not while your character is alive, anyway).
The weapons look more authentic than most FPS games, instead of weird make-believe projectile weapons, these are based on the real-life counterparts.
While it lacks some more recent game mechanics, like an explicit "cover" system, it makes up for that with the fluid, addictive team-oriented gameplay.
While teamwork is important for completing your objectives, you can also go solo and try to survive and get kills as much as possible. If you're good at it, it can actually help your team by reducing the amount of enemies, even if that isn't your main goal.

A MUST-Play .

It's Counter-Strike, if you've been on Steam for even a year or been in the PC gaming scene for just about any matter of time, you know what this game is. It really doesn't need a review so instead, this is gonna be my little send off. (Though I'll still continue to play it.)
This game was one of the first FPS games that really sparked my insane competitive nature. I played Unreal and Quake before it, even the original CS but nothing quite got me pumped more than CSS. While I only show 180+ hours, most of my time spent in this game was before the achievements and before Steam started clocking your time played. I met a lot of great people, played on a lot of great servers, Alt+F4'd out of a lot of 18+ servers when I heard the floor creak outside my room when I was a wee bit younger, got called a cheater a lot, questioned a lot of admins, got banned from quite a few servers for doing said questioning or just killing the admin too many times but every minute of it was great.
I'll be completely honest, I don't know why so many people play CSGO over CSS. To me there's just no contest, CSS was seemingly crafted by the Gods, CSGO is a micro-transaction infested game that WANTS to be CSS but it isn't quite CSS. It's not horrible but it's not CSS and I don't really consider it a worthy successor. Sadly though, CSS is on life support, most people have moved onto CSGO for the gloves, weapon skins and matchmaking and the people like me who don't care about that stuff are only moving on because there's not many people left in CSS. Gone are the days of those sweet community servers you favorited where everyone knew everyone and you always had a blast, even when it dwindled down to 2v2 or 1v3.
And to end this sappy review, Happy Birthday CSS, being 13 isn't easy, I wish you had a lot more players and I wish I had more time to play you these last few years.
I'll continue to play CSS every once in a while, I refuse to let it die. There are still some decent servers but a lot of them have gone offline, many of which included people I never added as friends but knew really well just from hanging out in the server and having fun. Like when you go to a bar and meet some really interesting fellas and crack a bunch of jokes but never get their numbers and it becomes a ritual but then the bar closes and you all go your separate ways.
See ya guys, hopefully we manage to cross paths again. Until then, AK/AWP + Deagle for life.

This is an interesting little game that starts out like a seemingly logical mystery adventure with Kathy investigating the death of her grandfather. It takes a while to get going before it slowly becomes surprisingly...eerie. Without giving too much away, all I'll say is that it's not exactly eerie in the Gabriel Knight way (even though Kathy Rain kinda resembles the famous New Orleans point 'n click protagonist with her hot bike and witty lines) but rather in the...Silent Hill/Lovecraft kinda way?! I've seen a lot of people throwing Twin Peaks around as a comparison, and even though I've never seen that show, it seems like an appropriate point of reference. In any case, be warned - there is a lot more here than the marketing is letting on.
Also be warned: the plot ends without answering half of the (VERY) weird questions that it provokes. It gets wrapped up in its own metaphors in the last hour and becomes one of those "MAKE YOUR OWN CONCLUSIONS!!!" kind of things, which I usually hate, but in this instance... I still felt oddly satisfied at the end of my 10 hours? I think it's because the writing is solid, the puzzles are mostly enjoyable (especially some clever ones involving a computer) and Kathy herself turns out to be a very endearing protagonist that I would like to see more of.
So, a tad rough around the edges, but if you're in the mood for a suspenseful adventure game and don't mind some ambiguity this is pretty good. Best enjoyed with black coffee, on a rainy day with cig breaks in between. I would buy a Kathy Rain 2.

6/10. Good for casual players, such as myself, but suffers from extremely repetitive gameplay structure and awful, barely servicable writing. If you don't care about the story and you're looking for something pretty and easy, this is it.
Rogue Wizards is a spiritual child of Diablo games and doesn't try to hide it even for a second. Similar animations, structure, camera, musical inspirations... However, it's not exactly a hack&slash game. It uses turn-based combat and because of it you can always think about the best strategy for every moment. You can easily switch between various playstyles and the character progression itself is quite forgiving.
But, you know, it gets boring. It offers not that many enemy types and since all the enemies level up with you, the game has exactly the same pacing through the entire game. All of the boss fights are identical, while randomly generated levels lack strategical depth and don't require much adapting from you. You don't need to rediscover the game and change your strategy - after a couple of hours you'll have everything figured out.
The coolest part of the game is the inventory managment, especially since your items level up with you (to a point). Unfortunately, it's strongly related to randomly generated items. You lack control over this process and keep seeing great items wasting their potential by boosting the stats you have no interested in.
The game introduces an unlimited grinding potential, so you can always look for something better, but you have to remember - Rogue Wizards is a game that moved into mobile platforms, and it's clear that mobile devices are its natural habitat. A game that keeps being the same, has repetitive plot that doesn't require you to remember anything, doesn't really punish you for dying and so on - it's a perfect tool to keep you entertained when you wait in front of the doctor's office or you ride a bus.
As long as you know what you're getting into and you don't have overhyped expectations, you will be fine.

There is one positive for this game:  the unit sprites are pretty.  Everything else is negative.
This game (cannot be called a war game) purports to provide the opportunity for the player to control either side in one of eighteen scenarios.  Each scenario is a battle from ancient times --  Cannae, Arbela, and Marathon are three examples.
The major fault is that the AI is non-existant.  Here are two examples:
Arbela.
Macedonians vs. Persians.  Macedonians vastly outnumbered.  Battle begins with both forces arranged in long lines with cavalry on the flanks.  Playing the Macedonians, shift much of my second tier light troops to my left flank, and then advance those units and my left flank cavalry.  I move no other units.  The Persians do not move any units until my flank movement nears their right flank.  They then send one or two units each turn from their flank to meet my advance, which crushes these piecemeal attacks.  No other units move.  My flank attack continues until the Persian right flank, 1/3 of their line, is obliterated.  All of these tuns, no Persian units other than the right flank move.  I continue to roll up the flank, with the only Persian units responding being those which I am attacking until I reach the center of their line and destroy their camp and kill King Darius (who never moved).  Total victory.  Playing the Persians, I decide to not move any units as did the AI when I played the Macedonians.  Turn after turn the Macedonians did not move either.   The AI was in a coma.
Cannae.Hannibal vs. Romans
Playing as Hannibal, I tried to duplicate his victory by moving my wings on the the high ground on the left and right sides of the valley and allowing my center to be pushed into the valley until the Romans were entrapped.  Only problem was that the Roman forces didn't move.  Playing as the Romans, I didn't move.  Hannibal attacked with his vastly inferior force.  Well, attacked in the sense that the AI sent one or two units at a time to charge into my line and be eaten up.
I cycled through a number of the other scenarios, playing both sides and not moving my units.  As expected my experience with Arbela and Cannae were repeated.
In summary, most of the time the AI does nothing.  When the AI does do anything, commits its unit piece meal in one on one attacks and never takes advantage of many on one attacks.
There is no multiplayer option thus the only way to actually fight the battles would be by hot-seating.  I can't even recommend this game to the neophyte wargamer as it would do more harm than good.

Ironically, what could be HexWar's best game for the PC has no reviews yet? That needs to be remedied. For those familiar with Matrix old Fields of Glory (FoG), this game is better in almost all respects. Graphics and animations do matter, and although I probably have 400+ custom FoG scenarios, the game just seems dull, even in multiplayer.
The biggest difference in this game, compared to say HexWar's "Nuts" or "Assault on Arnhem," is that it feels like a complete game system, not a puzzle game like Arnhem. That it doesn't have an editor like FoG is to be expected for the current price of $8.99. FoG and almost all the DLC I bought cost me a fortune back in the day! What this game does have is 18 varied battles. And, hold onto your hats, the ability to easily modify most of the text files. Certainly a first for HexWar, and the reason I have less time in-game than I should have by now.
I know most people simply won't do this, but simple cutting and pasting of unit names in the scenario file gives one complete freedom to replace any unit in the game system with any other. Unit strengths and weapon effects can also be easily modified. So for a tinkerer like myself, I can get a few months from the system.
Only overt oversight I've noticed so far is the Combat Analysis box is rather large (my native res is 1900x1200), so in some cases it gets partially cut off the screen. Also, in the Idivisto (16 A.D.) scenario, I expected the Germans to rush me like the crazy barbarians they are, but the AI was very slow to move its units forward, so I was able to deal with them piecemeal. But in the other two scenarios I've played, the AI wasn't bad and certainly as good or better than FoG. It may also be possible to modify AI behavior in the script files.
But unless you are an insane Ancients fan that can deal with the UI horror and micromanagement found in the HPS ancients series, this game has plenty of stats that should satisfy most "normal" players and includes a variety of charts to consult in-game. The aforementioned Combat Analysis box gives the average player a good feel for the potential attack, without all the bumbo jumbo that appears in FoG's detailed combat analysis function.
Amazingly, this is not just another cookie cutter HexWar game, and I need to check the game credits to see who designed this thing. So far, it actually seems worthy of future DLC and/or a scenario editor, which is typically not the HexWar way of thinking. Meaning, this game seems worthy of follow-up work, but that will only happen if people buy it. Forgive me, but forget HexWar's other ported games and just get this one. It looks good, plays smoothly, is moddable and quick to play. And the battle maps I've seen so far are satisfyingly large and etailed--much more so than FoG--and contain upwards of 50+ units per side (Idivisto is one, but I haven't counted).
Anyway, unlike the HPS epics, it is big enough to be satisfying and you've got a great shot at actually finishing the scenario in one sitting. For the price, I highly recommend it to novice on up to intermediate players. Even if you don't start modding the files, the 18 scenarios are more than worth the asking price.
EDIT: Sorry to say, but the next reviewer is right on regarding the AI. Did too much modding before playing and got a bit too enthusiastic. It can't be that hard for HexWar to just script the AI to move its troops into the attack. If there is a scenario where that happens, I haven't played it yet. Also, been unsuccessful in modding "defensive" AI orders to "Fanatical" or anything to get them to move.
My apologies for leading anyone astray on my overly optimistic review.

in it's bid to be that pure middleground between Shooter & MOBA with a 90s weekend-cartoonesque cast that certainly can provide appeal, but can be of two extremes.

Trino's capture mechanics are fun enough to justify its purchase.  I honestly enjoyed playing.
However, despite the ability to unlock each new level as a starting location, the linear level progression left me feeling cold.  In later levels, earlier enemies are replaced with vastly different opposition.  Meanwhile, unlocked player abilities can't be used in earlier chapters.  While having each level bring its own challenge may yield variety, I never felt like I mastered the skills.
Don't let the ascetics fool you into thinking Trino is a quick arcade fix of endless flow.  Instead, it is a long, defined set of varied, discrete, timed events.  While often satisfying, it may at times feel like a frustrating tutorial for a game that never begins.

Anyway, it starts off kinda fun, but the enemies in the later levels are too hard to capture, making it a frustrating experience. Sounds are also very poor, basically same as the original game from 15 years ago. And the icing on the cake, the game begins to crawl to  a halt once you have big armies engaging each other (+2000 soldiers), which was not the case in the old game, which was really low on resources and you could have huge, realistic battles.
A PRO thing: the campaigns, quite fun and engaging, so basically it's worth buying for that aspect, but only if it's on sale for like 8$ like I got it. Still thumbing up, because if you're new to the game, it's a good, fun game, and there are hopes for the game since there's a modding community that might add value to the it.

It seems that this game is basically the original Cossacks, with a few minor changes. However the re-write seems to have been done very inefficiently. I have run this on 3 machines. A laptop with a dedicated graphics card, Windows 10 and 8Gb memory. A desktop with an Nvidia 1080 card, Win 7 and 8Gb memory, and my old machine which is a Win XP, with an Nvidia graphics card and 4Gb memory. The original Cossacks and Art of War both run quite happily on all 3 machines. On my XP machine they run under Steam or from the original disks. All run at a decent speed, even with thousands of troops in battle.
Cossacks 3 starts with some decent art for the load screens, which doesn't vary during load, and which needs to be there since it takes such a long time to load. Note that I only play in the random map mode, I have no interest in online multi-player.
Once loaded you can set a lot of variables, as before in the Random map mode, however this doesn't seem to be overly random. I've played or started more than 30 games (more on that in a minute), and all have been set to Very hard, bar the first which I started in normal to get a feel for the game. After my first 5 attempts ended up with all resources starting at 1,000,000, which makes it too easy, I reset this to 1,000. I aslo noticed that at VH 4 of those games had been continents, since then I've also seen mediterranean 3 times and what looked like small islands once. On continents the enemy doesn't make any effort to attack you, unlike the original where they would at higher levels. This is the second worst fault in the game as it makes it easy and boring. My gut feeling is that the randomiser isn't as random as it should be, either that or I've been unlucky so far.
The worst fault in the game is that it crashes on all 3 machines I've tried, reporting it is out of memory when you try to recover. My guess is that this has been written in one of the more modern inefficient high level languages and just suffers from code bloat, my pet hate, having been programming and designing computers for over 40 years. It only seems to crash when you get into large battles, and try to view the battle while it is running, when everything gets jerky, my old game never had this issue. You can get around this by not watching battles live (boring) and pausing the game to run your troop directions.
In general the game can be a bit jerky normally, suddenly the screen freezes for a few seconds and then picks up, again annoying. The AI doesn't seem to be as good as the old one in some respects, though a little better in others, the removal of cannons from the portugese shipyards was disappointing, the new Ukrainian ship is pretty worthless, but they are still the most fun nation to play due to their limited troop types.
I was always a huge fan of the opriginal, especially with the Art of War add-on, as were my kids and my granddaughter, to me it would have been a 9.5/10 whereas this one is more like a 3.

I like Gearbox, so it pains me to give this game a thumbs down but it just isn't worth your money anymore.
Gearbox and 2K made the poor mistake of releasing this game too close to Overwatch's release. Leading up to both game's public release, the ads were confusing as the two games looked very similar at a glance but are vastly different from each other.
Battleborn is a hero-based FPS with MOBA elements. Overwatch, well, we all know what that game is about now. But, the huge success of Overwatch is significantly responsible for the death of Battleborn. Of course there's other issues with the game to blame such as the forgettable, grindy, and obviously trying to copy Borderlands humor tackiness that is the campaign. Additionally, the absolutely horrific cluttered and very messy particle effects and visuals in game combined with the messy color scheme made it incredibly difficult to see what you're doing nor understand what's happening even with hero knowledge after some bit of playing.
All in all, this game is heavily focused on multiplayer and has a non-existant player base. Any number you see currently on steamcharts is most likely people playing single player campaigns. Last time I tried there were 50 people playing and I waited in queue for 20 minutes before closing and uninstalling the game.
It's a shame really, because the gameplay was fun and I was looking forward to the imminent balance changes and additional heroes and maps to be added. Sadly, we didn't get much of that because of the game's flop. The heroes are definitely interesting and fun, albeit some seriously unbalanced/OP heroes at launch. Some heroes just had an insanely strong kit that grossly overshadowed others.
If you're a fan of borderlands the only positive you'll find here is recognition of some of the voice actors (tiny tina) making an apperance here for various characters. The comedy of the single player campaign is hit or miss on a general scale for potential players as is all of Gearbox's work. I'm personally a fan of it, but Battleborn's comedy felt a bit too slapstick, forced, or tacky at times. Then again, I never managed to finish the campaign.
This game is NOT worth your money. Only purchase this if you have friends who wish to do the campaign with you or some of the other game modes. Even then, grab it on sale as $30 is a bit steep for a multiplayer focused game with no population.
** EDIT ** It's F2P now apparently, still not worth your time with no player base. Only get the full game upgrade during a sale as $30 is asking too much.

It's a good game for its price.  It's not a great game though.  It's just a treadmill for the sake of being one.  Everything scales to you, so there's never a sense of progression or that your character is getting better.  It's very much a resource management game as well; you can only have 5 potions, you have limited spell components, and it takes a turn to switch between items and most spells.
It has things that seem neat, but once you realize that it's pointless, they lose their fun.  There are shrines and enchanters you can use, but there's no real point to do so because the next dungeon you go in all the loot that drops will just have scaled up numbers so they'll be better.  Sure you might have a piece of gear for a few levels, but when you replace it, you won't seem like you've received a great upgrade.  It's still going to take you the same number of hits to kill everything because they scale up along with you.
You have three stats, but it's not like you can decie how you want to build the character.  They don't seem to do anything, and are just there to make you spend them to equip the scaled up thing that just dropped.  Putting stats in never actually feels like it helps you out.  It's just a resource for you to spend.
Speaking of spending, all you do is spend your gold to upgrade your shops to the next scaled up level of gear.  So that you can spend your stat points.  So that you can kill things in the same number of hits as you were before you leveled up.
It's a fun few hours, until you realise how pointless it all is.  Play it through once for the story, if you like stories, but it won't ever feel like your character is getting better as you go.

So I am going to recommend this game, but just barely.  It is a 5.5/10 in my opinion.
There are several good points.  The graphics and animations have a charm to them.  The music and sound effects are fitting.  The controls are very well presented and easy to understand.  The UI was a little large for my taste (I assume to be able to support mobile) but that was not a deal breaker.
However there are several points that hold this back.  First you are a wizard with extreme limitations on how many spells you can cast.  You are also limited in how many runes you can hold, so you can never build up a huge amount of a favorite spell even with grinding.  You basically save your spells for the bosses... which means you are really a Rogue WARRIOR not a Rogue Wizard, as you will spend most of your time with axes, bows, chakra's and staffs.
Also, switching into a spell takes a whole turn in the turn based combat, which means it is very clunky to try and use your full arsenal.  Basically, choose one weapon or one spell, and that is what you will want to stick to for an encounter to limit damage.  This is especially true when so many monsters have knockback or stun or portal or summon abilities.
The above two issues means that the game quickly becomes very shallow.  Good for a few hours of fun at most, but after that the lack of spells and the repetitive nature of the loot and monsters with no compelling end quickly gets old.
Buy on sale, if at all.

Hi guys, let's discuss Rogue Wizards for a bit here shall we..
First of all, this game reminds me greatly of the 'Braveland Trilogy' and that being said you can already create a pretty good idea about, ''if you're actually going to like it or not'' because i know such games might be a bit too boring for some.. I'm a bit of a geek so i guess i couldn't go wrong with owning a copy of this nice looking and fun to play game.
But again, it's just like i said before, you'll either going to love or hate it but that doesn't make this a bad game if you don't like it.
And that's precisely why i'm letting you guys know, why i personally like this game a lot.
Let's talk about the graphics: The game looks pretty nice and cartooney (like Braveland and such) and the animations are nicely done although don't expect blitzes all over the screen or bright flashes because this game is by all means not a AAA graphical masterpiece! But all in all, it looks pretty nice, it doesn't glitch and it works well with everything else.. So what's not good about that, right?
Let's talk about the music/sound: The music for this game is pretty much kept simple although the tunes are catchy and the animation/effects etc all sound just as one would expect from such a game. It works pretty well together impo.
Now let's talk about the gameplay: The gameplay is set up in turnbased mode as soon as you encounter enemies or obstacles such as hidden traps etc. The grid/map is also devided in tiles, so each step you make will be on one of those tiles each turn. While in battle (outside battle those limitations are absent) you'll need to do some planning as to whether to move, change weapons, cast spells or heal yourself during the turn/time you're given. Everything is done in steps so make note of that when you're used to playing a dungeon crawler and you like to rush in like Rambo because this is not such a game.. You will be whimpy at first, but soon enough you'll be wearing nice armor, wielding massive weapons and using destructive spells (you can explore, craft/sell stuff) all at the same time which i personally think is a really nice way to let you as a player experiment freely. Also you'll earn a ton of experience along the many main and sub quests, so each time you earn a level up you can invest those points into 3 separate skills such as Power, Finesse, and Stamina. (and you'll unlock more buildings along the way too that upgrade/sell you all kinds of neat stuff..)
There are 3 primary character based skills, namely: 'Power, Finesse and Stamina'..
Power: Speaks for itself as it will allow the player to boost the strength of the character, including increasing the damage output for all his attacks.
Finesse: Is your basic dodge, shield, luck counter that will affect pretty much everything you do so don't ignore that skill!
Stamina: Works hand in hand with Power, because both make sure you can remain longer in tough battles while making it possible to dish out a world of hurt to those that seek to end you (it's a Roguelike right)..
However, you're always accompanied by 1 or two minions etc that can usually hold their own pretty well, unless cornered by bosses or packs of poisonous blobs etc.
After completing missions you will be rewarded by gaining additional magic points that you can freely spend in the magic skills department which is always helpful when you would or better said will be encountering tougher enemies and bosses. Note that each enemy has resistances and weaknesses so make sure to spend those points at the earliest sign you're encountering foes that are immune to your current skill/weapon sets etc.
Don't worry though, because you can freely adjust your character within any level so just keep your eyes open when you're facing an enemy because it will be made clearly visible as to what his/her strengths and weaknesses are.

I recently completed the first Braveland, you can see its review
. So how does the second part compare against the first? Surprisingly poorly...
The graphics are one of the things that seem to have taken a step back. Lots of units are straight up reused from the first Braveland - but I don't mind that. What I do mind is that the visuals for units that have been designed for this part are worse in quality than the originals! They look like... doodles that I'd expect from free Flash games on Newgrounds many years ago. The Frost Archer's face is an example of what I'm talking about.
The worst aspect of B:W is probably the grind, especially when playing on Hard difficulty (and if you're a completionist, you have to). Compared to the first part, battle rewards (and battles in general) have been rebalanced so that accumulating gold is now
harder. To "compensate", dungeons have been added which can be repeated forever to slowly gather gold for units needed to advance the storyline. Early in the game we're talking about an approximately 15 minute grind to buy one blacksmith. And the dungeon battles are excruciatingly boring. This is some top tier design failure right here.
The engrish in the writing also seems to have taken a turn for the worse. It's understandable, even the terrible puns, but... I expected better. The English version feels like a word-for-word translation of the original at times, which makes an already uninteresting and trite story even worse.
Are there any positives? They introduced a talent tree, which has marginal impact on character development but is still cool. The music and world map have the same charm as the previous ones. The devs tried to introduce a few choices although they are as token as they come. The battles are still fun for the most part but at this point (after playing two Bravelands) boredom is firmly on the horizon, and there is still Pirate left to go.
So why the thumbs up if it's so bad? Ugh, I feel like it's not bad per se, it's... more like... aggravating and poorly designed? Also insists on wasting my time. What ended up being the decider is how easy the game is to cheat. I just wish I had checked for that sooner. I suppose I can't blame Hard for being hard but the devs here have a very asinine vision of hard.

Kathy Rain is an entertaining point-and-click adventure game in the style of Lucasarts and Sierra classics. The game is very well produced: the voice acting and dialogue stand out in particular, which really helps the player connect with the main character. It really has the look and feel of a mid-nineties product, which I imagine is what the developers intend.
The puzzles are fun - they never feel arbitrary and all the solutions obey the game's internal logic so there's always a good sense of reward on completion. However, for a seasoned veteran of old-school adventure games, they never really get too far into headscratcher territory, and some of them seem a little too easy. Sometimes this is because the character will drop hints during her narration. This does stop the puzzles from being unduly frustrating, but it does also mean you will solve them a lot quicker than you otherwise might. Part of the fun of the old classics were the gordion knots you had to unpick over a few days (or weeks). There aren't really any complex puzzle chains of the sort you'd find in Lucasarts classics either.
This does keep the story moving though, and here the game is fairly strong too. Without giving away any spoilers, Kathy Rain keeps just on the right side of cliche and touches some very adult themes. The atmosphere is more often one of unease and tension, rather than horror, and it does this well. That said, I did feel there were a few elements of the story that could have benefited from a deeper telling - and a longer game.
Kathy Rain should appeal to fans of adventure games and is a worthy addition to a point-and-click collection. It's a little too easy, and perhaps therefore a little too short, but what it does it does well.

This game is truly like a First-Person MOBA. There isn't anything P2W, but there is items for loadouts and you get the items for those in loot chests, but they are easily unlocked through gameplay rather than buying them, and some of them you can only get if you spend the time leveling up specific characters. This game is really fun, the only mistake being that they tried to compete with Blizzard and Overwatch, which was a mistake, people compared the two and OW looks better, and has a bit more developed characters making it easier to stike a chord with them. As for gameplay, your team tries to push back the other team to destroy their Scarab from Halo 2/3. Each team has two of them, one at spawn and one about 1/3 of the way in from spawn. If the match is balanced and no Scarabs were destroyed, then the team that took the least damage to their Scarabs wins, so it's not too often that there are draws. There are also buildables that take crystals that you find on around the map and a couple large ones that spawn a few times. You can also use the crystals for an item in your loadout, and stronger items will cost more. They don't give massive game changing buffs, but they aren't so small that you never notice them.
For the characters, they are all really interesting, each of their abilities are pretty unique, and they get more cohesiveness as you play in a match. In a match you level up, with 10 being the max. You get xp for damage, kills, and building, and as you level up you get to pick from 2-3 perks that add a little to your kit, meaning you can pick perks that suit your playstyle. Each character has a their own unique perks to pick from, too.

Then you would play as you learned all the basic stuff. After a while you would get used to those basic movements. You could see these weird colored bricks laying around and wonder what they meant. You could clearly see there is some weird holes around the map, you can't surely fit in those. What is the reason for them being there? I really didn't care about those, but thought to myself, what would happen to me, as the player, so that I could fit in those holes. The holes were small and narrow paths leading to somewhere. The melee moves blended nicely with the super attack moves. The fighting was versatile. You could grab the enemies and throw them back at themselves. Guacamelee is a Metroidvania-style game with a strong emphasis on platforming and brawling. As with other games in this genre, you have some freedom to explore the world, with access to new areas controlled by gaining new abilities. Exploring this beautiful Mexican art inspired world is made easy with the game's great map system and fast travel points. Blocked areas that require specific abilities to enter are color coded and are marked on the map making them easy to go back to once you have the ability to break them.
The platforming sections are mostly challenging. You'll be combining precision jumping, special moves, roll/dodge, and switching worlds to reach distant platforms. The combat provides a good challenge as well, and as a luchador you will punch and grapple your way through different enemy types that you'll be facing in bunches. As you go deeper in the game, these enemies will have different types of shields requiring a certain type of move to break. Some will also exist in one world or the other and you must be in the correct world to attack them.
It took me around 8 hours to finish this in my first playthrough, but there's some replay value to it as you can play as other characters with different attributes. There are also some side quests, collectibles, and you can continue exploring the world after you've beaten the final boss. Highly recommended.

While its cartoony appearance may suggest a more suggest a more casual gameplay experience, Rogue Wizards is a challenge and easily accessible dungeon crawler in which your weapon choice and play style aren’t dictated by character class, but by user preference. It’s suited and long and, though the story is your typical you’re-a-hero-now-save-the-world affair, it does a good job of keeping you engaged run after run. It doesn’t do anything groundbreaking, but that doesn’t make it a bad game in the slightest.
Rogue Wizard throws you right into the action and that first dungeon where you clamber around in the dim depths searching for anywhere that could lead out is a pretty good representation of the rest of your dungeon diving career. When you first enter a dungeon, you can’t see anything beyond your line of sight. Moving about, either with the WASD keys or your mouse, dispels the darkness and fills in your mini-map. As you uncover the rest of the floor, you’ll be greeted by breakable objects, treasure chests, doohickeys of magical origin that allow you to fast-travel between rooms and, of course, monsters.
Once you step into the line of sight of the dungeon’s monster denizens, it's kill or be killed. Combat is turn-based, meaning that using item and spells and changing your equipped weapon takes one turn and you’ll have to wait until all of the other enemies take their turns before moving again.
Your range is decided by the weapon you have equipped and you change them freely by using the corresponding numerical keys. There’s a good variety of both ranged and melee some with their own elemental attributes, so use whatever suits your tastes and the elemental affinity of the monster at hand. Spells can be used regardless of the weapon you have equipped and casting one costs [spell stones] of the corresponding element, and defeating monsters. Monsters also drop keys, which open chests that contain gold, equipment, and spell stones.
One of the more unusual things you can find in dungeons is missing townsfolk. Upon their rescue, they’ll return to home base and set up a business. This light city building element is complimented by the fact that you can upgrade a store and therefore its stock by buying and selling items to gain experience and then by using materials found during your run. You can also find companions, though those are a rarity.
Every dungeons has a hulking boss monster that you must defeat before leaving. These giant beasts will test you skills and keep you on your toes as they will have their own gimmicks that you’ll need to counter in order to fight effectively.
Levelling up awards you with attribute spell points. There are three attributes: strength (increases damage), finesse (increases block chance and your ability to disarm traps found in dungeons), and stamina (increases defense). Spells fall under one five elements—fire, ice, sky, earth, and cosmic—and there are four tiers of spells that can be learned by unlocking the tire proceeding it.
Your equipment can also increase in rank with regular usage and each rank will grant you with an enchantment. They have their own max rank, which means that a weaker piece of equipment can surpass a stronger one depending on its growth limit. Equipment can also be socketed with gems if they have slots available. Gems add useful effects like increased equipment rank and elemental affinity.

If you’re on the market for a title that isn’t too demanding, Rogue Wizards is a good bet. The game is like the starter version for the genre in which you’ll find an amended version of the skill trees, character customization, and other such aspects—so those who seek those gameplay elements should steer clear. As a fan of the genre, I liked what I played, but I can definitely see where there’s room for improvement as far as depth and quality of life.

Rogue Wizards is a new turn-based rogue-like dungeon crawler for PC and mobile from indie developers, Spellbind Studios.
In Rogue Wizards' story mode, you take the role of a 'Banlit': traditionally working citizens who are unable to use magic. You find a magic scroll that teleports you to a dungeon in an unknown part of the land of Rilfanor, where a friendly fighter named Pallom is waiting for you.
Progressing through the dungeon with Pallam at your side, as well as a friendly creature who joins you, you eventually find the exit portal and find yourself in the magical town of Antarit. There Merrol, an innkeeper and wizard, as well as an 'Elam' -- one of the magic-using citizens -- is raising an army of magic users to fight the evil Hosperak, all around bad guy wizard. She tells you that even though you are a Banlit, you can obviously use magic, or the scroll's magic wouldn't have worked. And she needs your help.
Hosperak has opened portals to the elemental realms, from which he is stealing magical power. He has already taken over the Guild Council, and he cares not for the disruption and destruction that his actions are having on the rest of the land.
Rogue Wizards is played from an isometric view, with dungeons (where you'll spend most of your time in the game) made up of tiles of various types. There's some variation in the tiles, with different elemental themes obvious in different dungeons, as well as the typical stone walls and floors.
Character and creature graphics are two-dimensional: large and colourful with a cartoonish style. They look very much like a modern mobile game, but work well on PC, too. It's unfortunate that you only have a choice of two character graphics to choose from -- one male and one female -- and the changes to your character as you find and equip different items are very limited; though you have multiple equipment slots, only weapon types, major armour types (cloth, leather, etc), and shield types change your character's appearance, and even then only with major equipment type changes.
Animations are good, and there's a good range of special attacks, spells, and other effects, that look nice. They do sometimes take a while, though, so after you've played through a few dungeons you may find yourself wanting to speed up the gameplay a little.
Your visibility in the dungeons is very limited: typically only five or six tiles. The game features a weird effect that I don't think I've seen before, where the world just disappears into blackness at the edge of your visibility range, but when you move the tiles in front of you at the edge of visibility drop down from above to form the map, and the tiles behind you at the extent of your range fall away off the bottom of the screen. It's sort of cool, but at the same time rather disconcerting.
Graphics options are minimal and limited to the usual resolution, full-screen / windowed toggle, and vsync. I didn't experience any graphical performance issues, but the game is turn based and quite slow to play. The Steam overlay is a little bit broken, with Achievement and other pop ups sometimes hanging about, corrupted, in the lower right of the game screen.
Music is quite nice, and exactly what you'd expect from a fantasy dungeon crawler: mainly instrumental mediaeval-style tunes.
Sound effects are okay, but nothing out of the ordinary. It's a mobile game and is pretty family friendly, so don't expect screams of terror or grunts of pain. It's the typical "swish, bash, oof" type of sounds.
There are no voices.
Rogue Wizards is turn-based, tile-based rogue-like dungeon crawler. It has two modes of play: story mode and 'gauntlet' mode. Story mode gives you a rather hackneyed plot (with plenty of little grammatical errors) and a town with people to talk to and shops to visit between dungeons, while perma-death gauntlet mode does away with all of the extras and just gives you dungeon after dungeon through which you can crawl until you die, or tire of the experience.
In both modes, the core gameplay is essentially the same: start at the first level of a dungeon, kill and loot everything until you find the portal or stairs down to the next level, and then do it all again. Each dungeon level also has up to three bonus goals: kill all creatures, loot all chests, and disarm all traps. Completing these gives you an experience bonus, which increases with dungeon difficulty and level. I don't normally bother with the traps, since finding them is largely a matter of luck and it just takes too long. In story mode some dungeons also have special bosses. Killing these tends to give you better loot, as well as move the plot along.
As with all good games in the genre, dungeons and loot are procedurally generated, though the variation in loot seems relatively limited, with only a small number of basic weapon and armour types, and a relatively small number of modifiers to them as well. Even so, there's still some pleasure to be had when finding a legendary item with many good bonuses.
Items in Rogue Wizards gain ranks as you use them, which is a nice feature. You can't tell what effect gaining a rank will have, but it's always beneficial. I think any of the item bonuses are available as rank bonuses and they seem to be randomly assigned. They also have 'sockets', similar to other games in the genre. You can insert gems into these sockets to grant certain bonuses, and, as usual, you can't remove them once added.
Spells are a staple of the genre, and they're included here, too, though with a slightly annoying caveat. Each spell uses elemental materials that you have to collect and cart about with you, so the size of your spell repertoire tends to be inversely proportional to your available inventory space. It's a bit of a pain and doesn't really add anything, in my opinion, other than frustration. Progression in the game is relatively weak, limited to three characteristics that you can increase as you level up and spell points to buy new or upgraded spells.
You can gain allies, both temporary and permanent, in both modes. The permanent ones are pets, which follow you about until they die. In story mode even death is not the end, and they'll resurrect of their own accord before too long. But in gauntlet mode that's it; you'll have to find another friend. It's unfortunate, then, that the AI is rather terrible; you'll quite often lose your companion to stupidity.
There's one design decision that makes combat much less fun than it could be for me, too: changing weapons, spells, or pretty much anything else, costs you a turn. Since you can only see a handful of tiles in any direction, each dungeon invariably turns into a battle of attrition, at least until you get an item that heals you with time, and then you just wander about aimlessly until you’re healed. Creatures that knock you back make it even worse, especially when coupled with ranged enemies.
Pros:
+ Dual modes increase replayability
+ Procedural generation works pretty well
+ Steam Achievements
Cons:
- Silly action costs for swapping active weapons/spells
- Not enough variation in loot
- Limited character graphics
- Limited progression
- Short visibility
I'm a huge fan of rogue-like dungeon crawlers, but I'm a bit disappointed with Rogue Wizards. I'd like it so much more if the developers hadn't chosen to limit visibility so drastically and then penalise you for swapping weapons or wanting to use your spells.
If you're a fan of the genre and like the style then by all means take a look. It's not a bad game; it's just not a fantastic one either.

Braveland Wizard is a turn-based strategy game with three difficulty levels, in which you have to manage your units (moves, abilities...), your equipment, spells and skill tree. The game is linear but entertaining with a cartoon style design and a nice background music.
Wizard is the second game of the Braveland trilogy. The three storylines are not related, so you can play them in any order. However, I would recommend to start with the first Braveland (
), which is way better than the second one in my opinion, so you can familiarize with the game system and the different types of units. Plus, you'll be able to answer some questions in game at some point.
This story is about a freshly graduated wizard of the Academy of Magic, who must pass a final test to become a fully qualified magician. But of course, things won't go as planned. She will meet some nice people during her journey and get help in her quest from them. There are new types of units and opponents and this second game introduces dungeons that you can farm indefinitely. And this is the negative point of this game. On hard mode, you earn too few golds per battle, but you need lots of golds to fortify your squad in order to win unavoidable fights. Basically you will have to chain dungeons for a long time until you have enough money, several times during the game.
Despite the excessive farming, Braveland Wizard is a fun game that offers around 8-10 hours of pleasure in normal mode. If you're going for the hard mode, prepare yourself for the same battles over and over again.

I don't know why I often associated this game with another series but deep down, I knew it wasn't related. It was also time for me to play it and to stop letting it rot my backlog.
Henry and Laura, with their two children Emily and Francis, are visiting their aunt Amy in Egypt. However, when Jynxie the cat escaped, the family finds itself trapped into a lost tomb, separated from each other and forced to find a way to reunite and bring together their findings to escape a deadly trap set by a Pharaoh that killed his own brother and cursed his memory.
Escape The Lost Kingdom: The Forgotten Pharaoh is a casual adventure game, with hidden objects scenes and puzzles. Each member of the family has a special item: Francis has googles with glyph visions, showing him areas of interests, Emily has the Time Amulet, showing her the previous state of a room, Laura is holding the key to many enigmas thanks to Amy's diary and Henry is carrying with him tools (hammer, shower and crowbar). Each chapter is seen through Francis, Emily and the parents first, before the kids finding themselves and exploring their areas. In the end, the family is reunited for the final push: they're each carrying items needed (staff, torn painting, etc..).
Indeed, some parts of the game can't be access unless you have Francis's Googles for example. Besides, each member is carrying items found in their part that will be useful at the end, when the inventories will fuse together. The puzzles are relatively easy, though you may need Amy's diary to find out clues. I had to resort to a walkthrough twice because I couldn't see what to do. And it wasn't because I didn't read Amy's diary. It was mainly because I couldn't understand well the meaning of the enigma.
Escape the Lost Kingdom is clearly set in an early era of the genre, though it was transitioning, as it's not hidden objects scenes set as main gameplay. But when you clear a location, it's shown. The map is also an indication of that and isn't interactive at all.
However, while the story is only about escaping and not about the Forgotten Pharaoh (everything is explained in the beginning  in other words and while you're expecting the main story to come back to that, apart one or two mentions by Emily, the Pharaoh is really forgotten), I would have expected a longer game. Even if you can choose who you'll play first when the whole family is splitted up (Emily, Henry and Laura, Francis), after that, the game is taking back the control: the kids will have to go through more trials than the parents as they found quickly the reunion point.
Besides, it's not the graphics that will reconcile people with hidden objects games as they're kinda giving the feel of being outdated. While I appreciated the drawned cutscenes, Francis seemed really an angry child and Henry very serious, where the girls are smiling. And given the scenario, it's sad that you don't have any change in their expression. I would have appreciated Emily's rolling her eyes when saying that she's a big girl now.
The soundtrack is nice, like the voice actings. That's why it's just sad that the emotions aren't matching.
The feature that showed me how old the game is (and it's not even so old) is the mention of 3D glasses use. You can play the game with it. As I don't know where my old glasses are (from the middle of the '90, mind you), I couldn't try it.
Anyway, should I recommend it? Yeah, even if I feel like the game is missing something: too short, not many use of the tools typical to each character, no real freedom of choice despite the beginning, what about the Forgotten Pharaoh and outdated graphics. But it's still an enjoyable moment to pass.
However, buy it during a sale or in a bundle. Five bucks for it seems too much for the content.

Eric Lee Smith designed an excellent boardgame covering five battles of American Civil War way back in 1992. The game was called Across Five Aprils, published by one of the wargaming heavyweights, Victory Games. Across Five Aprils was a light-weight wargame with an innovative chit-pull system for activating units. The uncertainty of chit-pulling reflected the chaos of battlefield wonderfully. One would never know if the enemy was going to pre-empt your plans by moving before you get to attack, or worse even, attack while your troops were still trying to form their lines. The system was one of my favourite ones, easy to play, exciting and very replayable. Unfortunately for reasons unknown, it never got used in other games.
What does this has to do with Gettysburg: The Tide turns, you ask? Well, this game is straight adaptation of the game system presented in A5A. And it is designed by same Eric Lee Smith - the board game took 25 years to reach computerized form. The computer version had a painful history due to original publisher Shenandoah Games not being able to bring the game out and it moved  under Slitherine's umbrella. There were apparently quite a lot of technical problems getting the game finished and finally released. I'm not going to elaborate on them, other reviews and Slitherine's comments have told the story already.
All this is irrelevant to me, as Gettysburg: The Tide Turns finally brings a forgotten gem of wargaming to public reach again, and it does it very well. The rules are clear, game is easy and quick to play with varied results each time. The graphics presentation is top notch, with the living formations making a great impression on the vintage map. My only wish is that the game had born under more fortunate stars, as I would have loved to see the same game system expanded to other Civil War battles.

I wouldn't recommend this game to my friends, because it's not a very fun or innovative addition to the point-and-click genre. Its main draw is its plot, which styles itself after Twin Peaks absurdist horror (inexplicable bald red men haunt the protragonist's dreams and then, suddenly, her real life); this 5-act piece fails to elaborate on any one plot element and instead offers a superficial take on various tropes from aliens and demons to abortion and mental illness. The characters, too, are tropes (an alcoholic tough-girl protoganist, her bland and always kind grandmother, a religious zealot villain) but at least the main concept of the story is original.
Kathy Rain would have benefited from having an editor. Most of the dialogue text is gratingly unnatural and it comes off as amateur, despite relatively strong voice acting. For instance, grandmothers don't always need to say things like "Oh, child" to convey that they are indeed grandmothers, and the characters' reactions as the plot unfolds are often one-dimensional. There's potential for some memorable and enjoyable characters here, but as a whole, the writing is jarring rather than immersive.
There's a lot of good here, and the notebook mechanic is a nice addition to item-based point-and-clicks, but in the end the game delivers too little to be considered really worthwhile.

I heard about Guacamelee when Donald Mustard was on the IGN Unfiltered podcast with Ryan McCaffrey. I had just finished Shadow Complex for the first time and was thirsty for another game in the same vein. Guacamelee delivered on this note and then some. It's one of my favorite platformers I have ever played, and there is just so much it does right. You play as Juan, an aspiring and then realized Luchador, who has to save the girl and save the world. It is set in Mexico during the Dia De Los Muertos festivities and does a great job setting the scene. 
I played the Gold edition, before finding out that Super Turbo Championship edition is about the same thing but a little newer and polished. This is info I wish I knew beforehand, but I loved the game so much that I am sure I will make time in the future to run through the newer edition. You can play co op, although I never did personally during my playthrough. If you had someone dedicated to play I can see how it would be very helpful in some situations. There are tons of great character skins for the Gold edition (Nacho Libre, Shovel Knight, The Tick, etc.) and I did see a thread on steam about how to transfer them over to Super Turbo Championship Edition, if you are wishing you had all your great old skins for the new version.
So in my books for what it's worth, Guacamelee is one of the best at what it does all time. It's difficult (prepare to rage quit), it's got a story that draws you in, it has layers of functionality in the controller scheme, and it ties all of this together in a way that just really works and keeps you hooked until the end. I remember thinking while playing the second to last boss, "there's no way it can get harder than that". I was certainly wron about that, but it doesn't push you away to the point that it seems Unreachable, you get better and it runs very smoothly when you get your pacing.

You're a convict in an Intergalactic High-Security Prison, at an unknown location.
You have managed to escape your cell and you discover an unmanned security shuttle, jump in and don't look back.

Take little glowing orbs to score and one of the 3 power-ups spread in the scenario to assist you. But keep in mind that the points and power-ups are randomly distributed, so you can't memorize your way. Keep in mind also that the speed-up power-up makes the camera wobble; the more speed-ups you take, the more the camera shake. This also happen when you either hit a black barrel with red lights coming out of it, or pass over a death item, but in a not so smooth way, making the game impossible to see for a whole second, leading the player to another death item.
