I would consider myself a veteran in adventure/puzzle games, having played most of the Sierra Quest games, all the LucasArts classics, and most recently Deponia. I also thought Machinarium was a nice little title, if a bit too heavy on the independent puzzle section.
All that said I don't recommend Samorost to anyone - veteran or new players alike.
Samorost tries to differentiate itself from adventure games by being completely dialogue free. The story is told through pictures and small animations made of smoke/clouds. It avoids the huge inventory issue in other titles, and most puzzles are solved through interacting with the environment in a precise way. Move this tube there while turning this switch on, etc.
Samorost fails in telling us what exactly we can interact it. The mouse cursor will change when hovering over objects/environment if you can interact with it, but usually only if you're close enough. Even then it won't make much sense. How exactly can I move this giant pole back and forth? Wait, you're telling me I can reach the top of a 15 ft plant? The annoyance of having to mouse-over everything is hampered further by extremely onerous travel. While samorost can 'run', some sections have far too lengthy travel between different scenes, making going between areas extremely tedious. Second, 'talking' to people brings up an uninterruptible cloud animation every time. And these aren't short! They are pushing 30 seconds + for some of them. There's also tons of things you can randomly interact with that do absolutely nothing. You can think of them as Easter Eggs but more numerous.
As this is a game you have to 'explore' on your own, I accidently looked at the hint book, not knowing I was actually 'cheating'. Thankfully the hints are mostly useless for the problems I was having. I was able to complete it without a walkthrough, but that satisfying "Ah ha!" moment you have when figuring out a particularly devious puzzle is absent here.
The same issue that bothered me about Machinarium, namely isolated puzzle segments (think solving a Rubick's Cude in the game) crop up more often than I'd like.
Aesthetically it's fine. I wasn't as smitten as some are with the art style and frankly as time wore on and the game annoyed me more and more it started feeling repetetive and even ugly.
Stay far away from this, even on sale. It's a combination of frustration and tedium in one inexpensive package.

I wanted to like this game, after truly enjoying both prequels, I was excited to wrap up my hero's story. But I found myself suddenly thrown into a linear plot where my choices didn't matter. The previous games are very open to letting you decide your own emotions and reactions, which is what you expect from a CYOA. But after being told I "have no choice", "the only way", "You know you have to"... etc, over and over, I realized I was just reading a book with buttons that I was no longer in control of. The final straw for me was the game deciding FOR ME who I romanced and kissed. Without me choosing. Also, power cost information usually leads to "wow that cost more than you thought" - which I'll admit IS in line with the plot, but ends up being frustrating when you were trying to be strategic.
I'd say buy this on sale if you really enjoyed the first two games, but be prepared to relinquish control over any major plotlines or decisions.

Lately I've been having pretty long adventure game streak, playing everything from the 90's classics to modern games. At the same time, the third season of Twin Peaks is on and I have suffered some withdrawal symptoms waiting for new episodes. So, a game that combines elements from Lynchian mysteries and classic point-and-click games seemed like a gift from heavens and I definitely wasn't disappointed. This is one of the best written small games I remember playing and that's saying a lot, because I'm a huge consumer of this genre. The voice cast is great, pixel graphics are beautiful and there's just enough music to create the right kind of atmosphere to each scene. If you are used to playing the earlier LucasArts games you might find the puzzles in this game to be relatively easy, but I was positively suprised to find that finally someone might have found a good balance between annoyingly straightforward puzzles (newer Telltale Games...) and stumpers that almost force rookies to google for some hints. In my opinion, even extremely story-driven games should provide at least some challenge.
Only some very minor things to whine about like annoyingly slow walking animations (that you have to watch every single time you arrive or leave a location!) and some pointless loose ends in the narrative. The last part of the game borrows quite heavily from Twin Peaks but for me it felt more like a tribute than a cheap rip-off.
Highly recommended

This is a really charming game that does a great job in evoking the best parts of Twin Peaks. It has a distinctly 90s retro vibe, surprisingly good voice-acting, and the best parts of the adventure game genre without ever descending into the things that made the genre also obnoxious (walking around the entire map using one item on everything until you finally find the magic combination). Many parts of the story are left unresolved, but I sense that's a combination of two deliberate decisions: the possibility of continuing the story later, and the fact that really complicated mysteries shouldn't just be wrapped up with a little bow on them. If they're that fiendishly intricate, they shouln't be neatly undone.

Oh man, this game. Where do I even start. 10 hours in, and it was fantastic. I'm not much into point&click adventure games, but i most certainly am into good stories, and this one was plain captivating, much due to the amazing main (and - to a high enough degree - side) characters, marvelous script and outstanding voice acting.
The plot grips you tight and won't let go until it's all over. And when it is, you feel so connected to Kathy it hurts to leave. Because, in addition to being a highly-likeable, witty, rebellious character packed with some charming and cunning foul language, she has some deep background and progresses as a person enormously along the storyline.
Another point this game nailed is the riddles: they are diverse, they make you think and leave you with a comfy satisfying feeling once solved, and, on top of it, all of them ACTUALLY MAKE SENSE. During the playthrough I could barely even once feel the irritation of being lost or unaware of what to do or where to go at that point.
There is one detail about the plot I feel uncertain of though. It is the fair portion of supernatural being involved into a seemingly-at-first detective story. The further you're in, the more plot swerves off into some eerie and fairly grim as-s s-hit (the darkest moments even reminded me of The Cat Lady, despite the two games being stylistically light years apart).
As long as it contributes to the intrigue, it's not a bad thing per se, but the lack of explanation leaves a mild taste of incompleteness, which, however, fails to spoil the overall satisfaction. Popular belief goes this is to prepare a solid premise for a sequel, which I'll be eagerly looking to.

This review will be very similar to my previous reviews of the UBERMOSH games, so keep that in mind.
UBERMOSH Vol.3 is the third game in the UBERMOSH series, and has a few new features and changes.
Pros
- Fun and fast gameplay
- Good visuals
- A great soundtrack that gets you pumped while you play
- The same classes from the previous two games all return in addition to a new class, which adds variety to the gameplay
- The new changes include a new class and a new enemy type. The biggest change however is the removal of cover and the restricted play-area, which gives the player much more freedom of movement
- The price
Cons
- No options menu to adjust graphics or sound settings, but the volume can be easily adjusted via Volume Mixer (For Windows users)
- The player automatically picks up whatever gun they walk over which can be annoying, however once you get the best gun in the game it stops happening
- The removal of the boundaries trivializes the survival achievements, since the player can just keep walking in one direction and outrun the enemies. However this is completely up to the player whether they abuse it or not
Like the previous two installments, I recommend this game to pretty much anyone, largely because of the price. Fans of other top down shooters like Hotline Miami and Nuclear Throne will like this game.

Dynamite Jack is like a bad version of Bomberman combined with some boring stealth elements. First of all, you have infinite bombs, but can only place one bomb at a time. Throughout the whole game. How boring is that?
About the stealth elements, basically you just avoid the enemy view cones or use a bomb detonation to lure the enemies to a spot, since the enemy AI is so bad that they literally won't do anything else than run to the location of a detonation, and then do whatever they were doing before. As you can imagine, killing enemies is very easy due to this, but some maps give you an achievement if you don't kill anyone (boooring!).
Later on, there are some more challenging enemies, but they only appear on 3 maps and also have a specific flaw which makes it very easy to outsmart them.
About the soundtrack, it really annoyed me after some time, so yeah, it wasn't very good, except for the final map theme.
The story is also basically non-existent, so the whole game just relies on it's game mechanics, which would be ok for a flash browser game, but not much more. It could have been much better.
All in all, the game isn't really bad, but it's not good either. It's a passable time-killer if you really haven't anything else to do, but you're better off playing better games. Don't waste your time with this.
Btw, it takes about 2-3 hours to beat the whole game. After that (if you really like the game) you can play community maps.

Thief town is all style and 0 substance. The game plays like this: You and your friends are on screen with a bunch of npcs that look exactly like you and your friends. The objective is to find out which one of the npcs based on movement are actually one of your friends and stab them without getting stabbed by your friends first. This is an incredibly fun CONCEPT but is executed very, very poorly in Thief Town.
Technical problems:
Firstly, every single player has to bind their controls EVERY SINGLE TIME THE GAME IS LAUNCHED. If you don't understand what you're doing and bind the wrong keys you have to walk over to the bartender to change your key bindings using the very same incorrect controlls you just bound. "Couldn't you just reset them in the menu?" you may ask. Unfortunately you still need to navigate the menu with broken controls and then you need to rebind keys for every player. "Why aren't the the controls bound to default keys like the arrow keys, wasd, or the controller joysticks and then editable in the menu therefore solving all these problems?" That's a good question reader, I have no idea.
This game's simple control scheme and design lends itself to using multiple xbox controllers and playing it on the tv, however the game designers seem to disagree. Directional controls cannot be mapped to the xbox controller's directional pad, in addition, mapping the directional controls to the analog stick PREVENTS DIAGONAL MOVEMENT. This almost would be forgivable if the controls were bound to the directional pad but no diagonal movement on an analog stick? It also almost would be forgivable if the npcs weren't able to move diagonally in game, but they are, destroying any player's ability to accurately blend in. I should say that I did make a post about this problem in the forum and did recive a responce from a developer but he blamed the lack of diagonal movement on my controller rather than on a fault of the game. I have tried 3 different controllers that work perfectly fine with any other game on steam but they all suffer the same lack of diagonal movement. So either all three of my controllers break for literally only this game or there is real problem with keymapping. I'll let you decide.
The game also has trouble dealing with high resolutions. Even when I downscaled my resolution to help the game cope I experenced high frame rate issues and screen tearing which I just had to deal with becuase if I recall, there is no v-sync feature and if there is, it does little to nothing.
Game Design Problems:
Even if the technical issues were fixed the base game itself is just badly designed. There are multiple game modes but they do little to solve the problems in design and fail to keep the game from falling into a state of repetative boredom. The premise is to hide as best you can from your friends while trying to figure out who they are. Unfortunately the small arena you are given to move around in in addition to the large size of the player sprites makes it nearly impossible to differentiate between characters. You cannot identify a player based on movement if there is no room in which to move. In addition, you cannot follow a specific character once they are identified due to the flurry of npcs constantly moving over their position. It's like trying to find a needle in a hay stack if the hay stack was bunched up in one location and the hay in the haystack was constantly moving. The best and only strategy is to throw the entire point of the game out the window and begin stabbing literally anything that gets close to you, hopefully killing a player. The game then just tuns into a stabbing death match because everyone knows who everyone else is because trying to stealth at all will just get you stabbed. Your friends might as well just flip coins for fun becase the game just turns into a game of chance with 0 skill, 0 thought, and 0 fun involved.
I paid 2$ for this game and I would have had more fun setting those 2$ on fire and betting on how long it would  take them to burn.

I was really critical of The Prodigy, the first game in this series, after my first couple of playthroughs, and I critiqued the middle instalment, The Hero Project at the same time.
I stand by my opinion on The Hero Project - it doesn't fit one whole half of the choices encouraged in the first game, it's opening act overrides choices given at the end of The Prodigy, and in general it's a random insertion of a reality-show-based stage to kill time while the third act is being set up.
The Prodigy grew on me somewhat when I revisited it, but overall, this trilogy are the weakes of the Choice of Games games I've played. This instalment finally feels like an actual superhero story from the comics, a rollicking good Big Summer Crossover Event exploring the setting's ideas, advancing storylines, and setting up new ideas for further comics, etc, where The Hero Project was clunky and The Prodigy spent too much time filling in a science-fictional world in which to place its superheroes.
However, it's still the only Choice Of Games product I've yet played which keeps putting the game mechanics in the text. And that's clunky as all get out.
A middle act that stripped out the reality show aspect of THP while doing the same conflict with the InfraOrder and the Meek, strip out the more obvious gamist intrusions and, if the game proved too hard for people to continue on without those in-text hints, some recalibration - I mean, transferring your health to beef up your power reserves as a character option ahead of combats? What? Utterly out of genre and out of narrative - and I'd be praising this series. As it stands, it's just not on the level of their best, but overall, may be worth a look if you like supers.

I have always favored games where you made real choices. In most games with such choices it's little more than a 2 way branch, or nothing but choosing a particular ally before going right back to the same path. Railroading bores me. Heroes Rise... Does not. The choices felt like actual choices, with actual consequences, influinced by prior choices and changing future choices you might have. This gave the game a fluid feeling and made it actually feel like those choices really mattered and influinced the world.
At the end of the game I got to see my choices come to a head, and got to see the results of those choices. I was particularly pleased when my decisions caused almost every conflict I was going to have, break down into infighting as half my enemies joined me instead. Knowing what I did made such a difference was an extremely satisfying feeling, one that most games do not offer. The focus on story rather than flashy graphics allowed the game to become something far greater than the pretty but. frankly, boring games I usually get to see or play, and certainly left me eager for more. I look forward to what this developer produces next.
If you like interactive novels, this series is a must buy. Good writing mixed with a plethora of choices.

Great concept, but abysmal execution. Extremely tedious and essentially impossible to actually progress the story without a walkthrough.
For every decision or action the player can make, there are seemingly several options, except most of the time the logical action is prohibited for no particular reason, and you're forced to cycle through all the possible actions in order to find which one will actually advance the story. Many times, the allowed action is either not hinted to in any way so you have to find it by chance, or it's specifically suggested in previous steps that the action is impossible or illogical. For example [spoilers?] the first time you look at or try to move the dinghy, it specifically states that it's too heavy for you to move by yourself, and doesn't give you the chance to try. Later after you're severely injured, the game finally allows you to move and unload the dinghy, but then it's raining too hard and you never get into it, and once the rain stops it's full of water which you're apparently unable to do anything about.
Maybe I just made the wrong choices along the way (20 minutes in I got completely stuck, as in zero actions were allowed, and had to use a walkthrough posted in the discussion forum), but given how restrictive the allowed actions are and how you're often not allowed to do the straightforward action [spoilers] like serach the captain's body for the desk key until you've inexplicably used the rope and hook to climb into the crow's nest for the whiskey first. If you can enter the sick bay and examine the captain's body without the whiskey, why on earth is it required to have the whiskey in order to do the single additional step of searching his pockets? Perhaps altering the narration to HINT to the player that you  require a whiskey-soaked kerchief to even enter the sick bay would be a clue, but I got the exact same narration for when I did versus did not have the whiskey, right up until the part where not having it meant I could stand in the sick bay room forever examining everying except the body I was standing directly in front of. How was I supposed to know that walking into and standing in a smelly room  looking at stuff for 10min was fine, but if I wanted to make a single hand movement in that room, I needed to leave and find some whiskey to cover my face first? And why does the nightstand ONLY contain a candle the first time I look into it, but DAYS later it magically contains additional items?
This game could seriously be improved by maintaining logical consistency (if you tell me the dinghy is too heavy to move on Day 1, why is it possible to move it days later when injured?) and some hints as to what order actions need to be performed in order to advance the story.

Thank you to the dear friend who gave me this game. Calling this game "A Detective is Born" does not do it justice.
For those who grew up loving LucasArts and those who enjoy the games of WadjetEye, this is a no brainer. I marvel at how refined pixel games are starting to look. When the game goes for pretty....it's really nice. When it wants to be creepy...it is possibly the most disturbing thing I have every seen...and I thought The Last Door was creepy. The game plays as a standard point and click, with easy controls. The soundtrack is very fitting to the game.
Kathy is a strong, irreverant, foul-mouthed, bitter young 20 something year old, and I love her to death. I have seen other anti-heroes who have bad attitutes for the sake of the game, and I HATE that; but Kathy has good reason for being the way she is. Life has happened to her, and it hasn't always been kind. In fact it never really has. Kathy feels like a real person, thanks to the incredible vocal performance. She can be funny, tough as nails, and genuinely concerned. She grows TREMENDOUSLY through the game. I don't want to tell how because of major story spoilers. She is just a well written character who, along with how great the game looks, make this game work.
Kathy is surrounded by some great side characters who give good performances. All round, I really liked the voice acting and the script. Apart from the sci-fi/religion conspiracy gamey plot, the personal relationships between the people of this game felt very genuine. The family drama in this game had me in tears, since it can be extremely relatable.
This is no point and click for the kiddos, or even the teens for that matter. This game deals in some very serious subject matter: teen suicide, teen abortion, abandonment, and being ostracized from loving familly members. The consequences of these choices are fleshed out, and at times it was hard to sit through. The language is extremely colorful. Kathy has got a mouth on her (lot of f-bombs), but what bothered me was the c**t bomb. That I felt was the writers wanting to be edgy so they gave a bad acting NPC a line with that word. It was only a moment, but it was a moment wasted trying to be edgy, and it stuck with me long enough that I felt I had to write about, so there.
Overall, this game was very enjoyable, in a reflective kind of way. To call it a detective story to me doesn't do it justice. It's more of a "solve a family mystery that is affecting the whole town while dealing with personal demons" kind of game. The ending (which was satisfying) leaves the hint of a sequel, and we better get one!

It's like LucasArts dragged itself out of a moldy sepulchre, and breath life back into 90's styled adventure games. It harkens back to old Sierra Games with it's logic and whacky characters, but it's a fresh game with it's own identity. You play as the protagonist Kathy Rain, who goes back home to Conwell Springs to attend her grandfather's funeral, and figure out why he suffered for most of his life. The best analogy I can give is "Twin Peaks" meets "King's Quest", with a minor bit of humor that would make any Space Quest fan appreciate. Buy this game folks, you'll be happy you did so!

Unless you are the kind of person who thinks, "Let me put this cassette tape on the photo scanner so I can transfer the audio to my computer", then you'll need a walkthrough. Other than that, it's pretty fun with a mysterious story.

Good, solid detective game.  Worth your time.
Puzzles are few but reasonably crunchy.  It took a while for me to solve them but I got there in the end.  Easy enough to crack without a walkthrough, hard enough to make you feel smart.  Perfect.
Story and characterization are excellent.  The heroine is likeable enough for player-identification, but has enough of a personality to be memorable on her own, a balance many games fail to strike.  Voice actors range from decent to very good.  The comic relief homeless guy is annoying and overdrawn, but he is the exception that proves the rule of a sympathetic and believable cast.
One nice feature is the game's tendency to clean up after itself.  Once an inventory item or conversation topic has been exhausted, it often disappears.  Some clutter persists to the end game, but it could have been much worse.
Game is about 8 hours, which ran a little long for my taste.  Also, there is no in-game journal keeping track of characters and events.  Play this game all at once, say in 2-3 sessions over a week at the most; otherwise you will risk forgetting important information and the game has no mechanisms to remind you.  I played the game over just 2 weeks and by the end I had to look up the names of people I'd met because there is no record of them.
That's the only downside, though.  Overall this is a solid example of how an adventure and/or detective game should play.  Grab it.

A super-dorky mashup of Gabriel Knight and David Lynch -- a combination that is intriguing and absorbing throughout, even as the game lacks some of the heft and sui generis of its two predecessors. I slammed through this game over the course of a single weekend, so obviously I had a great time with it. This would actually be a great game for point-and-click novices, as the puzzles are fairly straightforward and logical (and the almost-too aggressive hint system will no doubt help out as well). I only got stumped once, and that might have been because I missed an important hint somewhere along the way (the forest puzzle, for those curious). I also loved the character of Kathy and hope to see her in another game.
Anyway, fun game. I'd recommend it, especially at its discounted summer sale price. I'm definitely looking forward to this developer's next game (which looks pretty fab).

Dynamite Jack is a stealth game.  You have the ability to start with or pickup bombs and a flashlight in order to achieve your goal of reaching the end of the level.  In order to reach the end of the level you will need to evade or kill the soldiers protecting the mines you are walking through, collect key cards and/or destroy colored electrical fields.  The graphics are simple, but work very well for this type of game and definitely let you know if you will be seen or not.  The ability to control your character through the levels is very intuitive and fluid.  The difficulty level ramps up as you progress through the mines and special ways of beating each level are offered such as no flashlight, no deaths, or no kills.  I thoroughly enjoyed the game, beat the game and then came back to unlock all achievements.  A very approachable and fun stealth game that you shouldn't miss.

Mainland is presented more like a novella than a game. The writing style is what you might expect from a short story, and it's very linear. You can only go where the story wants you to next, and the restricted movement makes the puzzles easier to solve, which isn't necessarily bad; it just keeps focus on the story. This makes the experience more like curling up with a book. You can just relax and enjoy it. You don't need to take notes, draw maps or anything like that.
Yet it's still very much a text adventure game. You type in <verb> + <object> commands to advance the story, you have an object inventory and there's adventure game puzzles, all which help your immersion into the story and the mind of the character. And just to be very clear, as a text adventure, there's no voice acting or pretty graphics.
Thematically, perhaps the closest thing to Mainland on Steam is
. Similarities include contemplative wandering around a desert island, wounded, melancholy and near your end, to an evocative piano soundtrack.

This game is an anti-climactic waste of time. You'll spend a couple of hours trying to figure out the exact right way to phrase things to do the only series of events that will make anything happen, during which a few intriguing details begin to pull you into the illusion that there's a plot or a point to this. Then, without solving anything, discovering anything, bettering your situation, or accomplishing anything, you die suddenly and inexplicably, the end. Maybe if you knew you were going in to the game to live out the last couple of days of a dying man, that'd be one thing. But you begin searching for tools, making things happen, exploring an island, almost as if there's like, ya know, a GAME going on here. The designer changed his mind like, a tenth of the way though and decided to just randomly end it all. No sense, no closure, and nothing of value to be gained. This game is like your last relationship. You'll commit yourself, work at it, become invested in it's future, only to realize that there's nothing there at all and there was no point to any of this.

I'm pretty unfamiliar with text-input games, so I did get stuck quite a bit when I played Mainland. Nevertheless, I enjoyed the story a lot. My only qualm with it was the ending, which I felt to be a bit of a let-down, since from the beginning the player is led to root for a certain outcome, only to have everything fall apart.
Still, the music and writing were lovely. I think the slow pace of this game was mostly the fault of my ignorance on the logic. 7.5/10 from me.

Beginning sumary:
Kathy Rain starts in Kathy's room, with her stalker roommate telling her about someone with "Rain" in the name dying in Kathy's home town. Turns out it was her grandpa. She goes to the funeral and talks with her grandma. She learns that her grandpa was in vegetative state since an accident in 1981 (game's current year is 1995), but something was odd: medical exams showed his brain was totally fine, despite his symptoms of brain damage. Then the game actually starts: Kathy wants to discover what actually happened to her grandpa.
Kathy begins as your standard misfit that smokes, drinks and drives an older-than-her bike that looks like she's part of a biker gang. As the game develops, you see her kind and worried side.
Game mechanics:
It's a pretty standard point and click. You have a bag with items, a notebook with "things you want to talk about with people" and a list of contacts whom you can call to. You can combine items (like a tape and a tape recorder/player to listen to it, or your cigarete with your lighter to smoke), as well as use items on objects (key on door).
Review:
Pros:
- It touches some heavy subjects, like a teenager aborting, suicides, kathy's parents (you'll get it) and some other dark sh*t
- The game hasn't an autoplay mode, meaning you either think about the clues you have until now and do what you have to do or just try everything (which would be exhaustive, don't). Some point & click have too many clues that make the game being all about "Click this place. Now click this. Now this."
- The mystery goes really far and touches religious subjects. I'm a fan of these approachs.
- The MC is actually charismatic and has many fun dialogues and rude answers, including to priests and the sheriff. Oh and she carries a taser.
Cons:
- In a lazy gameplay, I ended the story in 7 hours. That means most of the story and character development is actually made in your mind, not by the game itself. The touches in heavy subjects are mostly shallow due this lack of time.
- Even though it doesn't have clues every freaking moment, the puzzles are pretty easy and the course of actions is rather obvious most of the time.
- Again, the 7h gameplay doesn't let the game have a great character development. Although you see Kathy growing as the game moves and see her sides, it's too fast.
- (SPOILER OF ONE "PUZZLE") You put a TAPE on a SCANNER to get the audio sound into your computer. That made me go "WTF?" Then Kathy goes on and tells me that putting fire on a wood door that i want to open is not logical. GOSH
Overall:
For the price, it's enjoyable as a casual game. Don't try finding a challenging puzzle-investigative game nor a master piece character development. It's a casual point and click game to spend time. It's worth it with at least 33% off, imo. (77% on summer sale, so 33% should be easy to get during the year)

A really solid point and click adventure. The graphics, sound, music and voice acting are all top notch. The animation is a bit clunky at times, but that's really just a very minor observation.
The story progresses nicely, and while the game holds your hand a little bit through the puzzles, I think the developers have walked the line pretty well here in keeping things intuitive and letting you know when you're on the right track.
One thing the game really nails is tone. I was drawn in from the very beginning and really got a feel for the setting of game and the people who inhabit it. I actually cared about the characters, and they really all did seem quite fleshed out, from the protagonist Kathy to her roommate Eileen, Goober the homeles man and even Hacker Dave, who's only spoken to on the phone.
Possible spoilers (really just about the feel of the game):
Some people have complained in reviews that the game takes a turn and devolves into "magic/supersition/supernatural" themes, but really the story can be read however you want to read it. The game deals with serious themes from mental illness to drug use and suicide, and any allusions to the supernatural could easily be read as forming some allegory to traumatic struggles in life.
Overall, this is a great adventure game with strong writing and a real Twin Peaks / Stranger Things / 90s nostalgia vibe. It's pretty short, and can be finished in under 5 hours, but I got it for $4 on sale and it was certainly worth all of that.

The rebindable controls are extremely basic and the animations anything makes is very minimal but not terrible.
The object of the game is to get from point A to point B one level at a time, from your starting location to the "exit." You're free to choose what levels you want to start so should you have unlocked them.
Your only real items are an unlimited supply of remote bombs and a flashlight which aren't always available to you immediately (and very few times not at all which becomes part of the challenge). There are a lot of pitch black areas to traverse through so that's where the flashlight comes in.
The bombs provided have a somewhat short range and are there for killing baddies and destroying specific key objects as well as making paths if the terrain present is at all destructible. Making a long path using bomb explosions however can get very tedious because of how short the blast radius is and the fact that you'll always have to keep your distance when placing a bomb so as not to get yourself killed. There's not a whole lot of need to do this at all.
You die in one hit and the stealth mechanics are very basic; stay out of an enemy's field of vision, watch for a pattern made by the enemies to figure out when to move, make an explosion with a bomb and soldiers available & nearby will check out the noise before going back to their scripted pattern. Not too far into the game the types of enemies will become a bit more unique and diverse. None of those new enemies will be anything like the average soldier for the most part.
I've got a few personal yet very small problems though very irrelevant; I find it a bit bothering that the game's called "
" and he's using those spherical cartoon bombs. Also, the story goes that he used to be a space marine who was captured, imprisoned, and escaped yet his methods of getting around are remarkably minimal.
By stealth game standards there isn't much of a big challenge in this game though there are in-game achievements that sort of encourage each map done specifically like beating a map in under a minute, don't kill anyone prior to exiting, kill everyone prior to exiting, etc.
It ain't a bad game though with how short it is I'd just recommend getting it for when it's seriously cheap or rather put a teeny bit of consideration if it pops up in another indie bundle.

Dynamite Jack, what can I say. It's amazing for it's price, but it just doesn't have the features to be the best.
THE GOOD:
+ Great graphics for a top-down puzzel game (shadows and sorts too).
+ Difficulty is nicely build up from easy levels at the beginning to challenging levels at the end.
+ Aggressive AI.
+ No game-breaking bugs (surprising for the price).
THE BAD:
- Not alot of variety in levels.
- Controls are poorly mapped.
- No story line.
Dynamite Jack gives you alot of bang for your buck. Packed up with some nice features and puzzel elements, this game can get real intense when playing. Especially the later levels are filled with hostile AI and difficult maps. The game features a small but clear user interface. There is no irrelevant information shown other than a somewhat annoying tutorial at the beginning of each level. For the €8.99 price tag you get enough levels to play through and the game is surprisingly free of bugs.
However, as soon as you boot the game, pay attention, an automatic cutscene/loading screen will pop-up showing the only bits of story line you will see throughout the whole game. Also, after a long gaming session some levels might feel familiar to previous levels, only to be stacked up with AI and extra objectives to complete.
One last big complaint towards the game is about the controls. They are so poorly mapped even ArmA III has better default controls. Z for your flashlight (yup, that's right), and control your character with the all familiar Unity control system: ↑ ↓ ← →.
Should I get this game for the full price?
- Yes.
Should I get this game when it's on sale?
- YES YES YES.

It's a short tale of a lone explorer on a hopeless quest.
It's a story with a well-defined ending that defined ending-philes won't like.
It's an experience on rails that you can't fail, so if you hate not being able to kill the protagonist by doing dumb things, don't play this.
More a book than anything else, it's not about the guessing game of a gameplay, but more about stirring compassion to the  narrator's ugly luck and bad decisions; we've all been there at one point or another. In a sense, it could be seen as a metaphor where you may end up guessing the right actions in life, and it's still not enough. Things happen, and efforts are lost, as we don't grow younger and perkier.
One thing I did the entire time as I read on was, where would my priorities be if I were in his worn shoes? Would I find hope in the ultimate attraction of an island afar that I could reach if not for the sudden downpour? Would I really dare to leave the comfort of home if I weren't sure I'd have a place to return to at the far end of the journey? Good old stuff or shiny new stuff (pick one)?
You're a gamer, so do waste a bit of your free time (a couple hours, really) to read this and probably gain a bit more insight about where your heart would be — or where it is.

This is the third installment of the Heroes Rise series and up to this point the finale of the trilogy itself. This story is all about you facing all those who oppose you, your ideals and the future you envision. This Choose Your Adventure story offers different story paths, relationship routes and so on, depending on the choices you take and where your alignments lie. Are you consumed by revenge that you want to crush all those that oppose you? Do you want to achieve favourable results by minimizing bloodshed? Or do you want to walk a path that lies in-between? That's all up to the choices you decide to take in this epic finale of the Heroes Rise trilogy.
It's a shame you can't do certain things regardless of your alignment (such as killing one of the bigbads because you lean towards ideals as opposed to revenge), but I guess that's just a way to prevent your character from acting too much out-of-character, but I guess that's something I personally disagree with. The game tries to give you the possibility to act "neutral" or take part in both the good and the bad, but the game definitely punishes you if you even dare to slide a bit off from past actions. I guess that's something to keep in mind when you want to unlock all the possible routes of the game, but for a first playthrough in which you just want to go all role-playing, it ain't THAT bad, just a shame it prevents you or berates you for doing certain things.
In the end, the game was overall satisfying and fascinating to both read and engage in. The entire Heroes Rise series made me reconsider the charm and fun behind Text-based Adventure games. I never thought that going through a piece of software with only text and some options here and there (no pictures, no sound, no music) could be so much fun. For the superhero-enthousiasts out there, this is definitely worth picking up, that goes for the previous two installments without saying. I definitely hope this isn't the end for the Heroes Rise series as a whole as I look forward to more adventures featuring the child of The Sound and The Fury, Jenny, Lucky, Grandma, Black Magic, and many many more.

cons

I finally got around to play this game that I got before the Planet Coaster hype, and since it got such a bad reputation I was expecting this to suck and to regret even spending time on it.
But after finally truly playing it, I found out it is actually a worthwhile product, despite the bad publicity it got for being the underdog.
RCTW offers the feature to import your own models and create custom structures by combining parts. The coaster editor is on par with the old 2D episodes. There are quite a bunch of options to embelish the park... all the key features we could expect are here.
I don't know if RCTW is the better theme park game on the market, as I couldn't purchase Planet Coaster as well yet to make a true comparison. I'll assume the masses of people are right and that RCTW really isn't as good as its big competitor... But does that really mean it's that bad?
RCTW is the very definition of a decent game. No key feature missing. No big problem. Nothing revolutionary maybe, but nothing broken and bad either. It's just a "good game", as in a 7-8 or so out of 10.
Despite its flaws, I think I can safely say that RCTW isn't a waste at least. It's not the absolute best, sure, but it's quite fine and can be enjoyed. It would be dishonest to thumb down an enjoyable product just because one another is superior.
Atari even pushed the price down to fight the initial backlash of the badly handled early access, so RCTW is actually cheaper than its competitor now.
Not being number one doesn't mean you're terrible. If you really love theme park builders, I don't see how you couldn't have at least some fun with RCTW.

If you're familiar with the "Age of Empires" series then Cossacks will feel pretty similar right off the bat. What Cossacks does differently than Age of Empires is scale up the size of the battles and adds a little more realism to the game.  In Age of Empires II (AoE2), you were limited to a maximum of 500 population. In Cossacks, you'll need at least 300 peasants/villagers alone to fill your mines, of which there are three types (Iron,Coal,Gold). Cossacks also has wood,stone and food (as found in the AoE series) for resources. While in AoE games you were free to spend up your resources until they ran out, in Cossacks that has consequences. As usual, if you run out of stone/wood, building anything becomes impossible. If you run out of food, your peasants and soldiers will start dropping like flies due to to famine. If you run out of gold, any mercenaries or ships will mutiny against you, causing more problems. There's nothing like a Ship of the Line going rogue right off the shore of your city, while you scrounge up cannon and any other ships availible to deal with it before it levels your town or your army. Running out of iron will prevent you from building units, while running out of coal will mean your gunpowder units cannot function. The battles themselves are interesting, as it can be tricky keeping track of your forces spread across the map. Fortunately most units in the game produce pretty quickly, allowing you to build up an army in little time. AoE fans will notice that you are able to build priests in Cossacks as well. However they can only heal units, and cannot convert enemy units. Enemy soldiers cannot be converted to your side in anyway, although your troops can capture enemy artillery(cannon,howitzers,mortars), buildings and peasants. Cossacks doesn't have the unit variety of say, Age of Empires 2, due to AoE covering the timespan of 700-1500 AD while Cossacks is 17th/18th century (1600/1700) only. AoE has many civs while Cossacks features 16 with the base game, all European civilizations (as the game's focus is Europe). All the civs in Cossacks do have their unique units and bonuses, similar to AoE, and all of them have different building architecture.
In the end, if you're an Age of Empires fan but up for trying something a little different, Cossacks is worth a try.

I’ve played the original Guacamelee! and now the Gold Edition as well. Both games were fantastic, but as expected, the Gold Edition had more to offer. Guacamelee! is a combination of a beat ‘em up and metroidvania, and boy is it a spectacular combination.
- Fantastic fighting/combo mechanics.
- Very well designed dodge mechanic.
- Large variety of abilities that are fun to use.
- Immaculate control scheme for fighting and platforming.
- Very fair difficulty scaling.
- Exploration is fun and rewarding.
- Very well designed maps.
- Interesting side quests and funny NPCs.
- Nice music and visuals.
- Great use of Mexican influences.
- Many video game references made into luchador posters.
- Co-op makes it a more pleasant experience.
- Plenty of fighting challenges to keep you sharp.
- El Infierno offers even more exciting challenges.
- Unlock costumes that provide both buffs and debuffs at the same time (good game balancing).
- Not sure if they fixed the co-op dimension swapping issue in this version (if one person presses the switch button, you both switch). Can be frustrating if you don’t coordinate well with your partner.
- I wish Guacamelee! was longer.
- When will a sequel come out?
- You should probably get the Super Turbo Championship Edition.
Guacamelee! is one of a kind. A truly enjoyable experience, one that I wish I could relive. I have 100%’ed this game and would do it again gladly.

A game where you roll a ball, but due to terrible framerate drops, terrible map design, and awful controls, the game is basically unplayable.
The map design is so bad, that there are often objects blocking your path that you can't even see.  There are 5 different types of levels.  Fog, Fire, Water, Dark, and Maze.  Fog is where you have to manuever through fog-filled maps with literal lines of platforming.  This "tightrope balancing" is nearly impossible when all of the fog effects randomly lower your fps at an average of 20 frames.  In Fire, you have to collect skulls to use at the end.  Many parts of the second level I couldn't even get to.  In Water, you have to fall down a 2.5D waterfall, and in the 2nd level you go through a pirate ship.  You have to avoid TNT barrels because they insta-kill you.  The 2nd part of the level is terrible.  You're manuevering through the inside of a sinking ship and the rafters are constantly blocking your vision, while the game reintroduces the "tightrope balancing", however you can't turn your camera, so you never know if you are lined up or not and will fall almost constantly.  The dark levels are the only levels that I actually enjoyed.  You make your ball glow and go through a dark maze while solving small puzzles and flipping switches.  Then it becomes a memory game.  This part was not fun at all, as you would have to memorize entire sections as there was no light.  I gave up after that and didn't even try the Maze levels.
The controls aren't the best, but the "tightrope balancing" is terrible, especially when most of the tightropes are circular objects and are extremely easy to fall off of because you can't tell if you have the right angle while approaching it.  In most levels you are not allowed to turn the camera. There were many maps that I couldn't even get to the objective because it wasn't possible to.  Other maps won't let you change the camera angle, so you have no clue if you are lined up or not with the TINY platforms.  Also, the options menu is extremely lacking.
I would not recommend this game at all.  It's a platformer with terrible map design and poor controls, which are the only things a platformer requires.

-: Everything else.  Gearbox doesn't know how to make a good free2play game.

Playerbase: Hardly anyone plays the game now.  Dead community.

Dynamite jack is a Dynamite Game in every sense of the word.
The story follows Jack in his attempt to escape from the mines, and you guide him through the caves and avoiding the guards.
The game isn't very hard if you're just trying to rush through, so challenging yourself to beat each levels 'goals' will make it a lot trickier. That said, the game doesn't take an especially long time to complete. This is where the in-built level editor, and comunity maps come in handy. There are plenty of them for you to play, allowing for extended value to the playtime.
The various types of enemy and hazard get progressively more difficult, and there is a wide enough variety that you can discover as you progress.
This game can be controlled via. keyboard or controller. I found that keyboard was easier to control, but both work well.
The graphics in this game are very nice. The maps are well designed to give the feeling that you are trapped in 'caves', even though it's all top-down. The colour accenting isn't too over the top, and the glow given off by various entities is very subtle and adds a lot of depth to the maps.

Secondly, the game is not fun at all. The main idea, which I suppose was trying to make some sort of stealth-like game using lights and shadows throughut the cave, is so heavily squeezed every single level looks just the same to the rest. ALL 28 levels looked the same. Once you've done 3 or 4, you'll know what you'll see until the end.
And the mechanics themselves are just irrational. This game is light/shadow sight-based but nevertheless the guards will never notice the bombs you've just put in their way, even if they're staring to them. The AI is absolute simplistic and lacked of any intelligence. Guards will just follow their own route and maybe notice your detonations, but with 100% predictible moves.
Overall, I can't recommend this game because it's just extremely meh. I'm sure you'll find MANY better indies than this more worthy.

I replayed this in 2015 and it's still fun. The sandbox style level design is probably the most consistent in the entire series, with each mission offering plenty of ways to assassinate your targets. The weapon upgrade system is a fun way to spend your earnings from each mission. Lots of replayability.
I do miss the brooding atmosphere of Hitman Contracts, but the farcical tone can be a lot of fun here.
I love games that let you use the gameplay systems to create your own fun. In that regard Blood Money is a classic. Give it a shot.

I mean, what can I say about Hitman: Blood Money that hasn't been said? It's a fun stealth game, full of character and creativity, allowing for some of the best moments of tension you could ever have while at the same time, allowing for creativity in terms of killing.
You like sniping? Well, there are numerous rifles to choose, including the custom Sniper you can upgrade.
You particularly like to poison people? Well, you can have multiple doses of the stuff.
You want to kill people as a chicken suited individual? It's possible and even recommended if you want to do the "Murder of Crows" mission.
Getting Silent Assassin is a wonderful felling, one where you have to think so much and relaxing, It's amazingly fun, and stressful, but getting it allows for a huge amount of relief.
If you haven't played Hitman: Blood Money before, try it out. It's cheap, fun and there's so many locations that you will remember time after time.

With every single successful gaming series, good or bad, there will always be a height in the series that the developers simply couldn't recreate. To me, and to numerous hitman fans out there, blood money is the game that hits that mark in the hitman franchise. The game does seemingly everything right. The soundtrack helps create the atmosphere, NPCs go about their day in a random pattern giving the game more difficulty, and the gunplay (albeit you wont be using guns super often) is so satisfying. The game doesn't come with its imperfections, though. They're few in number, but they exist. In pro difficulty, you'd swear cops would have wallhacks as they turn a corner with their weapons already drawn, whether or not you had commited a murder in that area. Of course, this isn't a huge issue if you play the game stealthy. Another little thing is the sheer size of some levels. Remember that bird mission? No way you could've possibly done that on your first try. Of course, though- that is completely subjective. I'm part of the gamer population who absolutely loves the trial & error that game with this game. I'd do it all again

God awful name aside this game is actually pretty good. It's definitely the best out of the 3 games in the series. Thankfully the god awful alliance mechanic is gone and you don't have to worry about being 100% lone wolf or some bull crap like that and can experience the story much more organically. In it's place a much better mechanic is introduced- balancing regaining your powers and keeping your health up. The plot this time around is also much more exciting. Your characters are constantly on the run, keeping things exciting. There are some nice twists and turns along the way and I have to mention that I was actually genuinely impressed by one of the character of Prodigal. The game actually tries to experiment a little bit with the story telling with her character. Even though she is an ex villain she gets a chance at redemption and the player gets a chance to work alongside her and even romance her in a really adorable scene with very bitter consequences. Personally I'd love to see more of experimental things like that in the future, since I hardly think any Bioware game will ever allow you to form any sort of bond with the main antagonist, it's up to indie studios like Choice of games to play around with stuff like that.
Over all I'd recommend all 3 games. They are all on the short side but for that price they are just right. They are like little pocket rpgs that you can easily digest and forget, leaving knowing you had fun.Quick, cheep and fun. Like bargain bin drugs.

So, Kathy Rain. I don't usually write reviews, so this could be a little janky, but bear with me 'cause I think this is worthwhile to say.
--Characters and World
This game shines in characterbuilding. Not a single person (except one who is meant to be) feels out of place or annoying to encounter, and Kathy as a character both suits the position she's found herself in and has a personality you immediately recognize (Jerk with a Heart of Gold). She makes for an excellent protagonist, equally intelligent and witty with a personality that not only shows through her dialogue, but also through the solutions to some of the more impromptu puzzles you face. Rarely does she overstep believable bounds, and even the clues she gives you about objects you find do not come off as patronizing.
In other words, the voice acting and writing is spot-on, just as it needs to be for a story-driven point'n'click puzzler.
Not much needs to be said about the world, as it is for all intents and purposes semi-rural America, before cellphones were invented. Nothing noteworthy is changed, a few things are added (related to the plot), but otherwise it is entirely vanilla and well-represented.
--Puzzles and Difficulty
Difficulty curve is notoriously hard to judge when it comes to puzzles, and often one individual will find some easier than others regardless of the intent. Despite that, Kathy Rain seems to have taken that a step further with puzzles that are far easier than the one that came before it found late in the game, and the hardest puzzles taking place in the second few hours. Thankfully, Kathy herself will at least let you know if you are on the right track with the harder puzzles, and stays silent when her suggestions aren't solicited. Most solutions (all but one, if I recall correctly) use a 'the easiest answer is the correct answer' policy, and (again, all but one) operate within the bounds of logic- even when reaching an area of the game where logic seems to have no meaning.
Puzzles can invariably be solved just by using the mouse- there is no keyboard usage save for where it makes obvious sense to do so (such as when typing), and even that is extremely rare. If you can't click it, you don't need to worry about it. There is no 'hunt the pixel' gameplay, either- all the items you interact with are well-lampshaded and easy to see, to the point where some of them might as well be draped in neon lights.
Overall, I found Kathy Rain very easy to get through, only having to consult a walkthrough once when I was missing a crucial item. Long-standing lovers of point and clicks will find this a walk in the park, whereas newcomers (are there any?) will find it a wading pool for the harder stuff. Most of these puzzles are character-driven as well, stemming from dialogue choices and showing the personalities and natures of those around Kathy (as well as Kathy herself), making them an integral part of the game rather than 'solve the soup can'-style pointlessness.
---Story and Pacing (no spoilers)
This is the one point where Kathy Rain falls a little short, and it isn't for lack of trying. The story begins excellently and at a medium burn, with the catalyst to adventure occuring soon after you start and with little backstory off the bat. Most of the backstory, in fact, is discovered over the course of the game with notes, dialogue and recorded messages, all of which (save one) is inevitably used in one way or another.
This persists throughout the game's middle in a way that never reaches a white-knuckle grip, but rather a leisurely jog with occasional rests that involve quick humor and fun characters (Goober, I'm looking at you). While there are the occasional twists, they never feel particularly jarring because of the slow speed with which you reach them, lessening their impact and dulling the edge- an edge that I think Kathy Rain sorely needed. Despite that, said twists and developments do grant a desire to keep playing, to remedy the events that go wrong and to wrap up the story. Players are pushed on, also, through small snippets of Kathy's past that she isn't particularly open about, but these have less of an effect both because of the ending and the way they are delivered.
As for the ending, this is where Kathy Rain loses much of its characters and world, instead making it solely about Kathy as a person- and unfortunately proving that she cannot stand on her own as an interesting protagonist. Kathy is at her best when interacting with others, but this last stretch involved only her and her own feelings amidst puzzles that are mostly 'placed' rather than 'organic', and without any of the witty dialogue or charm you find in earlier parts of the game (with a couple notable exceptions). The ending comes and goes, and it left me with a 'well, that happened' feeling that can only be described as mediocre- a sad thing for a game that had me interested and invested up until that point. Despite that, I can say that the more personal details of Kathy's choices earlier in life are handled well and intelligently (at least, on my playthrough. A different dialogue choice may yield a different result), without insulting individuals who have chosen to do the same in her place.
---End result
For a game with a new protagonist never seen before? Not half bad. Not half bad at all. For a point and clicker? Pretty frickin' decent. Is it worth fifteen bucks? That's harder to say. It is a short game, and depending on how quickly you burn through the puzzles at hand you may feel like you did not get your money's worth- especially considering the easy difficulty at hand. So since the puzzles are largely simple, lets judge it on characters and story alone. Would I hand Kathy and E fifteen bucks again, to help fund another investigation?
♥♥♥♥ yeah, I would.

I didn't think I'd fall for cute, but Promised is quite impressively likable from the 3-D characters with a lot of detail to the equally detailed and painterly 2D backdrops. This game requires some time management and resource management but it's not frantic and everything you need is at your fingertips.
3 tips...
1: If you want to transport a colonist to somewhere immediately just drag them directly out of their portrait on the toolbar: you do NOT have to hunt them down on the map to move them somewhere thankfully!
2:  You can heal unhappiness by picking up a sad colonist (one red bar of happiness left) and dropping them on another colonist when a smiley face appears. The colonists will chat and both will recover happiness.
There's a bit of randomness but also strategy in part for this game although it never feels brutal. It's more about making the best of every given situaiton: sell goods when the homeland will pay high prices, assign colonists to jobs they like and avoid jobs they don't, deal with situations that arise accordingly with new research, technology, quickly assigning almost all colonists to one job to get it done faster...etc.
There's even a mini-game similar to Angry Birds to deal with pirates that you can replay levels of to get a decent score.
Promised Land has a lot of game for a small price. You don't really fight anything and there's no groundbreaking ideas you might not have seen in other casual games but it's pleasant and engrossing and rewards your time with something new to do every few moments. You will feel some satisfaction when a building goes up, a ship returns after a good trading session or a new technology allows your colony to improve and expand.

(A lot of this review will be identical to the original UBERMOSH because the two games are VERY similar).
Just like the original UBERMOSH, Vol.3 is comparable to a top-down Devil Daggers:  You appear in an arena and are tasked with surviving 90 seconds of relentless onslaught. 90 seconds isn't much, right? And all of the enemies die in a single hit--how hard could this possibly be?
As it turns out, hard as ♥♥♥♥ing nails. Set to a thrumming metal and techno soundtrack (which is still easily one of the best things about the UBERMOSH series), you will die again and again and again. Fortunately the game subscribes to Edmund McMillen's "Super Meat Boy" model, wherein dying happens quickly and restarts are virtually instantaneous. This game doesn't want to waste your time--it just wants 90 seconds.
Depending on your class*, you may begin with a sword; use it to relieve an opponent of one of a handful of different firearms. Some of these weapons are great. Some aren't so great. Fortunately (as I previously mentioned) enemies die as quickly as you. Therefore the best weapons are those that allow you to spread death around fastest. Within 30 seconds of a single game, you'll have access to every available weapon--pick the one that works best for you.
*There are several unlockable classes that are fundamentally different takes on the same thing: One can only use a sword, one starts with the best weapon, etc. And each has a different number of allotted respawns. They impact the game, but not in a radical way.
This time around, there is also a "Brainclap" mechanic to compensate for a complete lack of cover.  The way it works, each character class automatically produces a "Brainclap" (an explosive attack that can clear most enemies from the screen) after a certain number of kills; some of the weaker classes have lower thresholds for triggering one of these explosions, making them more common.  In general, it helps provide a risk-reward mechanic for some of the weaker classes since the Brainclaps are most common (and effective) in large groups of opponents.
The game is stripped of all but the barest essentials--there's nary a plot, an economy, or an exposition.  Like UBERMOSH, Vol.3 doesn't have time for those sorts of formalities. And because of that, the game's a great shot of adrenaline whenever you've got more than a couple of minutes to stop and play it.
Who might like this game? Anybody who wants a no-frills top-down shooter that's hard as hell. People who love a soundtrack that makes you want to kill, crush, and destroy. For those who played Devil Daggers and thought, "You know, I wish this game was remade as a twin-stick shooter." For $1.99 this game is a solid deal; for $0.99--the price of a candy bar--you'd still be a fool to skip out on this game.
PROS
+ Great Soundtrack
+ Super accessible drop-in/drop-out model
+ Very challenging
+ Additional "Brainclap" mechanic is a solid addition
NEUTRAL
~ EXTREMELY similar to UBERMOSH--to the point that you could almost argue Vol.3 should have been a game mode in a previous game.  Still, you can get both games for a combined $1.49 on sale, so it's not a big deal in this case.
CONS
- No Steam Cards (even the previous Ubermosh had them)
- Weapons and enemies could still use a little more variety

Winexy is a great adventure puzzle game with fantasy elements, combining your different perceptions into solving dynamic puzzles! Interact with the environment as almost every element in a certain stage is vital to finding your way out!
The game offers a variety of levels, with different environment and interesting puzzles. Actually the environment is very important, taking you from pitch dark places to mazes, or to some other extreme conditions, where you traverse through it in a different way.
The game really reminds me of another very unique game called Ballance, but Winexy is much harder, and it is structured in a different way! The only similarities they have would be that in both games you control a sphere/ball, and throughout different stages you can change the material of the ball, to help you pass through certain areas!
Winexy combines those old ideas into a brand new adventure puzzle game, with many more extras and beautiful and unique environments, a lot of collectibles, and achievements!
Recommended for ppl who like puzzle games that will probably have you tickle your brain!

Based on the trailer, I was expecting to really enjoy Winex. This game has a lot of great ideas, but the small amount I have played are very poorly executed.
PROS: Pretty good art execution and the music is nice. Nice puzzle solving and some unique mechanics.
CONS: Brutally difficult and very bad pacing. I died more than 10 times on the first level. Some from not being able to see the ball, some from not knowing where to go and mostly from failing to balance on the tiny path. These are all fine mechanics, but not at the very begining of a game. There is a sequence at the very start where you have to charge your ball with electricity. While this could be a simple gate you roll through, it stops the game for 13 seconds to do this. While it may be cool the first time. Its very annoying the 3rd, 4th, etc. The second level has some interesting mechanics but they are not fun to replay. No checkpoints during levels means redoing the same steps many times. Challenge in a game is great as long as you can get back to the part that you are struggling with quickly.
While I would like to see a lot of the cool looking content in the trailer, I can tell by the first two levels that the frustrating moments will outweigh the great ones.

Winexy is graphically amazing - an impressive 3D rendered world - with a pleasant enough music backdrop. The precision skills required to direct the ball and not fall off the girders is initially high, but you'll soon get the hang of it. All round, a graphically impressive game.

I literally powered through it because I felt like I was inside of a summer movie, full of mystery, explosions, great character development, explosions, unexpected reunions, tons of explosions, and an all out war between several factions (which included both powered and unpowered types risking their lives for their beliefs).  Not all is what it seems in this tale, nor are the characters as clean cut but with good reason.  Enemies become friends, friends become enemies, and others become frenemies. This series could easily be a trilogy of motion pictures, or at least 3 solid seasons of any primetime slot.  No character is weak, nor due they simply serve as plot devices or story fodder.
